In the beginning of the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping” (selskabstømmersager) came into existence in Denmark. It related mainly to a criminal activity whereby the persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud. Approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion Danish kroner (DKK) were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994. In addition to the criminal cases, tax asset stripping gave rise to a large number of cases for damages relating to the sellers’ and the buyer banks’ liability for the loss arising when the companies were stripped of their funds.

The applicant's lawyers made several applications for an adjournment of the trial, on 30 March and 4 April 1989. The President of the Assize Court declined to adjourn the trial. He found that the applicant had been absent without good cause. The applicant was found guilty on 300 out of 302 counts of forging documents and of a like number of counts of fraud. He was also found guilty of forgery of documents for procuring the signing by his secretary of seventeen false receipts for expenses in a name she no longer used. The Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. It also made an order excluding him from Swiss territory for ten years. The jury assessed the amount of alleged damage at approximately 1,000,000 Swiss francs. On the other hand, the applicant was acquitted by the jury on 672 counts of. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court. The Court of Justice held, in particular, that the applicant had been seriously at fault in not transmitting his medical knowledge to other practitioners despite knowing from 1 February 1984 onwards, the date of his release, that he would one day stand trial. The Court of Justice described the applicant's attitude as irresponsible. The applicant was also held to be at fault for having delayed in appealing against the decision of the American court. The appeal had been lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun, and his application for an adjournment had been dismissed. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal as unfounded, holding that he had brought about the situation that had prevented him from leaving his patients and appearing before the Assize Court by his own conduct. It held that the argument concerning the refusal to remit the case had been conclusively disposed of in its judgment of 27 June 1990. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. He alleged a violation of his right to be heard and to attend his trial. The Federal Court dismissed his appeal. It considered that the applicant had misled the American court by making inaccurate statements, notably regarding Swiss procedure. It held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not preclude a trial being held in the defendant’s absence if the defendant refused to attend or was unable to attend through his or her own fault. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant's argument concerning the legal definition of the offences of fraud and forging documents. The applicant could not avoid his obligation to appear before the Swiss courts by relying on a decision that was ultimately based on equivocal and even knowingly inaccurate statements. On 26 July 1995 the applicant was arrested at Munich Airport (Germany) on his way to a conference. He was extradited to Switzerland and transferred to Champ-Dollon Prison. An application he made for a pardon was refused in February 1996. He served the remainder of his sentence, spending part of it in a secure wing of Geneva Cantonal Hospital. On 20 December 1996 he returned to the United States. The Federal Court’s opinion, it was possible to infer from the foregoing that it was the applicant's own fault that he had been unable to attend his trial. The applicant had not given the American court accurate information about the procedure that would be followed or the sentence.

The jury heard the case for the first time on 11 June 2013. It was the first hearing of the case since it was brought in 2010. On 9 May 2002 the Kars Criminal Court declared that it lacked jurisdiction. The proceedings should be initiated before the Assize Court on account of torture. The applicant joined the proceedings as a civil party. The court found it established that the police officers had intentionally ill-treated the applicant to extract a confession. It accordingly sentenced each of the policeOfficers to one year imprisonment under Article 243 of the former Criminal Code, and banned them from public service for six months. At the end of the trial, on 15 June 2010, the court reduced their sentence to ten months' imprisonment and five months’ ban from public Service. It subsequently suspended the pronouncement of the judgment in accordance with Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 10 May 1996 he applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (“FDB”). The case was settled at the Polish Court of Appeal in Warsaw, where it was heard for the first time on 30 May 2000, and the application was dismissed on 1 June 2000, with the judge ruling that the applicant was not entitled to any compensation at all.

The case was adjourned until after the European court of human rights was seated in Madrid in May 2007. The applicant was born in 1973 and lives in Istanbul. She sought to enrol in the Faculty of Theology of Marmara University. She provided, among other materials, an identity photograph which showed her wearing a headscarf. The identity photograph she had supplied did not comply with the regulations in force and the person concerned could not be enrolled. She lodged an application for judicial review with the Istanbul Administrative Court. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment. The applicant appealed on points of law.

The jury court resumed its examination by laying out general principles for the assessment of the credibility of evidence by witnesses. It considered that the applicant’s own submissions, according to which he could not have been present at the crime scene as he first entered Swiss territory in January 2002 – and thus after the victim had been killed – were contradictory and thus lacked credibility. Conversely, the court considered the testimony given by the anonymous witness, who submitted that he had seen the applicant shooting the victim, to be credible. The principle of a public hearing had been safeguarded by allowing the press directly to follow the interrogation from the separate room in which the defence was seated.

The jury court considered that a criminal conviction must not be exclusively based on testimony given by an anonymous witness. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the German Government on 10 August 1992 and by the European Commission of Human Rights on 11 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 15473/89) against Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 11 July 1989 by two German citizens. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3 and 8. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (Art. 43) and Mr Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The first applicant, a social worker, drew up outside the back entrance to the block of flats in Lemgo where she lived. She was accompanied by her daughter Monika, who, at the time of the incident that gave rise to the complaint, was eight years old. After she had opened the gate she was stopped by two police officers who had followed her and were standing in the gateway. They accused her of having driven through a red traffic light and of having tried to get away - an allegation denied by the applicant. The police officers claimed to have detected a strong smell of alcohol on her breath when they checked her driving licence. She agreed to be breathalysed. Despite having been shown what to do, she proved unable to provide a specimen of breath. The applicants claim that Mrs Klaas agreed to have a blood sample taken, but explained that she wished first to accompany her daughter to a neighbour. The precise course of the events is disputed by the applicants (see paragraph 7 below) and the police officers. She was charged with obstructing a public officer in the execution of his duties contrary to Article 113 of the German Criminal Code (Strafgesetzbuch) and of driving. The blood test showed the level of alcohol in her blood to be 0.82 per ml (milligrammes per millilitre) She was subsequently released. The first applicant underwent two medical examinations and was put on sick-leave until 8 February 1986. The first applicant had been very aggressive when told that she had to undergo a blood test. She had tried to escape into the darkness of the back-yard. The applicant's guilt in resisting the police officers had been minimal. The criminal proceedings against the first applicant were discontinued by the public prosecutor’s office (Staatsanwaltschaft) at the Detmold Regional Court. In November 1986 the competent administrative authority imposed an administrative fine of DM 500 for having committed the “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) of driving with a blood. while under the influence of alcohol contrary to Article 316 of the said code. First applicant laid an information against the police officers concerned. She alleged that they had assaulted her contrary to Articles 223 and 230 of the Criminal Code. A driving ban of one month was also imposed. The Lemgo District Court confirmed this decision. The first applicant’s subsequent appeal to the Hamm Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) and to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht?) were dismissed. She maintained that the blood test showed the level of alcohol to be 0.80 per ml. It was argued that the degree of force used against an unarmed woman was incomprehensible on an objective or subjective analysis. The first applicant instituted civil proceedings in April 1987 against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia and the police officers concerned. Her request to take her daughter to a neighbour’s first was granted. When the first applicant opened the door and tried to enter with her daughter, one of the police. officers held her right arm fast, whereupon she started to kick and to hit out with her left hand. She had to be handcuffed. It was not accepted that her head knocked against the window-ledge at any moment in the course of the arrest. On 10 July 1987 the Detmold Regional Court, in a partial judgment, dismissed her complaint. Police Constable Wildschut confirmed the general circumstances of the first applicant’s arrest as described by Police Constable Bolte. He said that Mrs Klaas had vehemently resisted arrest which was why he had taken her left arm and twisted it behind her back and then handcuffed her arms in that position. He confirmed that she had requested that the handcuffs be removed but did not remember her complaining about any pain - in particular pain in her left shoulder. The second applicant, Monika, gave evidence. She stated that she remembered the incident and that she could not exclude the possibility she could have knocked her head on the wall or on something else. She continued, without success, to resist accompanying them. Monika was arrested with her mother and two police officers in their back-yard. She was not aware that one of the police officers had forcibly kept the door open. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion. The Detmold Regional Court dismissed the first applicant’s compensation claims against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia. It held as follows: “The plaintiff has no claim under Articles 839 and 847 of the Civil Code (Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) taken together with Article 34 of the Basic Law’. Arrest itself was not unlawful, even if the plaintiff had no intention whatsoever to abscond, the situation nevertheless appeared otherwise to the police officers. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the policeOfficers went further than was necessary, by handling the plaintiff too roughly and in so doing injuring her or even by deliberately inflicting the injuries on her. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof. With respect to the origin of the graze, the evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff’s daughter, conflicts. In the light of these circumstances the arrest does not appear to be disproportionate either, but a perfectly reasonable means of ensuring the further investigations could be carried out. The two police officers could certainly expect disciplinary proceedings and a resumption of the criminal investigation if these proved to be the facts, while witness Klaas has a natural interest in supporting her mother’s claim and account of the facts. It is not clear to the Chamber which of the statements corresponds to what really happened. The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. In the process her head could easily have knocked against the wall; the shoulder contusion could also have occurred when she struggled while being restrained by the police and when the handcuffs were put on her. For these reasons the claim must be dismissed. Monika Klaas, the second applicant, contended that the aforementioned treatment of her mother in her presence had violated her right to respect for her private and family life. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the various separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government in their memorial of 12 November 1992 invited the Court to find “that the applicants did not suffer violations of their rights under Article 3 ( art. 3) or Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention’”. The Court ruled that there had been a violation of Article 3 in respect of the first applicant.

eval_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Ukrainian national. The court repeated the grounds previously given for the applicant’s continued detention. In addition, it underlined the need to obtain a report from an expert in graphology. In the retrial proceedings the applicant made numerous, unsuccessful applications for bail. On 19 August 1998 the applicant was committed to Międzyrzecz Remand Centre. Since that date he has been detained. On 5 December 2001 the Gorzów Wielkopolski Regional Court convicted the applicant as originally charged and sentenced him to 25 years’ imprisonment. On 16 May 2002 the Poznań Court of Appeal upheld the first‑instance judgment. The applicant submitted that between 1999 and 2000 his legal-aid lawyer had never met him to prepare the case and had put forward an ineffective defence. The court observed that the applicant had given an account of his own wrongdoing. It observed however that the remainder of his testimony had not been credible and had not be taken into consideration by the trial court. The applicant maintained that during most part of his detention he was held in overcrowded cells in conditions which did not comply with the basic standards of hygiene. On 10 December 2007 the applicant was transferred to Hrubieszów Prison where he is currently detained. The Government submitted that the period of the applicant’s detention in cells in which the statutory minimum requirement of 3 m² per person had not been respected amounted to some 979 days. This submission was not contested by the applicant. The applicant did not bring a civil action in tort to seek compensation for the infringement of his personal rights. The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Zawiercie. He married A.N. in 1993. In 1994 they had a son, D. In 1997 the Katowice Regional Court dissolved the applicant's marriage. It awarded parental rights to his ex-wife, limited the applicant in the exercise of his rights and ordered that D.'s permanent residence be with his mother. The applicant was allowed to participate in decisions about the child's education and health. He was able to visit the child every Tuesday and every first Saturday and third Sunday of the month, between 4 p.m. and 6.30 p. m. The child stated that he had not wished to see his father.

The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Zawiercie. In 1993 the applicant married A.N. In 1994 they had a son, D. Subsequently, the applicant and A. N. separated. The applicant was allowed to visit the child every Tuesday and every first Saturday and third Sunday of the month, between 4 p.m. and 6.30 p.M. The police intervened on 12 occasions in order to facilitate the applicant's contact with his child. On one of these occasions the child stated that he had not wished to see his father. According to its terms the contacts were to be enforced. On 9 December 1999 the applicant. and his ex-wife concluded a court settlement.

The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Zawiercie. In 1993 he married A.N. In 1994 they had a son, D. In May 1997 the Katowice Regional Court dissolved the applicant's marriage. The applicant and his ex-wife concluded a court settlement concerning the visiting right. According to its terms the contacts were to be enforced. The settlement was reached on 9 December 1999. It was agreed that the contacts would be enforced on pain of a 100 PLN fine. The applications for fines to be imposed on the applicant under Article 1051 of the Code of Civil Procedure were withdrawn after he withdrew the applications.

The mother failed to comply with the access arrangements. The court obtained reports from two experts including a psychologist and heard evidence from several witnesses. It considered that A.N had not turned the child against his father. The mother was allowed to participate in decisions concerning the child's education and choice of profession. The applicant appealed, and on 28 December 2000 the Katowice Regional Court gave a decision granting custody to the applicant and ordering that D.'s permanent residence be with the father. His subsequent interlocutory appeal was dismissed on 15 November 2001. On 12 October 2001 the Zawiercie District Court modified the decision of 28 December2000.

The mother failed to comply with access arrangements. A.N. was ordered to make the child available for a visit (by 1 May 2000), on pain of having to pay a fine. The applicant appealed and on 28 December 2000 the Katowice Regional Court gave a decision granting custody to the applicant and ordering that D.'s permanent residence be with his father. The mother was allowed to participate in decisions concerning the child's education and choice of profession. The court held that A.n. should be granted full custody over D. and that D.'s place of residence should be with the applicant. The application was dismissed by the Zawiercie District Court on 15 November 2001.

A.N. applied for full custody of D. under supervision of a court appointed guardian in order to protect D.'s well-being. The mother failed to comply with the access arrangements. On 5 January 2000 the applicant asked the Zawiercie District Court to impose a fine. On 19 December 2000 the District Court dismissed that request. The court considered that A.N had not turned the child against his father. It noted that the child had not wished to attend the meetings with his father and had started suffering from anxiety and fear. The applicant's further appeal was dismissed by the Katowice Regional Court on 28 February 2001.

The child was living with his mother, with whom he had very close relations. The court held that the child's own statements that his mother had not obstructed his contact with the applicant. It was D. himself who had avoided contact with his father. Between 2001 and 2005 the applicant had not attempted to contact his son and to exercise his visiting rights. Their contact was limited to occasional meetings on the street, since they lived nearby. The applicant filed an application to be granted full parental rights. His application was dismissed by the Zawiercie District Court on 28 July 2006. The appeal against this decision was dismissed in September 2006 by the Czestochowa Regional Court.

The application for custody of the child was made in 2001. The child was living with his mother at the time. The court held that it was in the child's best interest to leave him with her. The application was dismissed on 27 September 2006 by the Czestochowa Regional Court. The case is still pending in the Zawiercie District Court in Poland. The boy has since moved back to his mother's home in the town of Ażż. He is now the father of a seven-year-old girl, who was born in 2000. She was born on the same day as the applicant.

Court ruled that the child should stay with his mother. Further appeal lodged by the applicant was dismissed by the Czestochowa Regional Court on 19 December 2001. The court held that the applicant had not had a good relationship with his child and that the boy was afraid of him. The applicant again requested that D. be restored to him in October 2005. The Zawiercie District Court refused his request and the applicant did not appeal against that decision. On 16 December 2005 the applicant filed an application to be granted full parental rights. On 22 June 2006 the District Court dismissed his request. His application was dismissed on 28 July 2006.

The applicant was born in 1981 and lives in Antalya. In 1995 he enrolled at a vocational high school specialised in communication. He said that he had intended to obtain a high-school diploma and then go on to study communication science at university with an eye to becoming a journalist. But the Higher Education Council issued a circular based on Law no. 2547 introducing a new system amending the rules on admission to university. The applicant considered that applying a weighting to the average marks used for calculating the results of the entrance examination gave an advantage to students from ordinary high schools. In his view the new selection system tended to direct holders of diplomas from such vocational schools into two-year technical training programmes.

The applicant, having obtained his high school diploma, sat the national entrance examination for higher education. He calculated that had it not been for the 0.2 weighting on his average high school marks, the marks which he had obtained in the examination would have been sufficient for him to enrol in the faculty of communication sciences of his choice. His request was rejected by the Ministry of Education on the ground that the legislation did not allow students to move from a vocational or technical college to an ordinary high school. The State Counsel asked the relevant Section of the Supreme Administrative Court to declare void the clauses relating to implementation of the 30 July 1998 circular.

The applicant, having obtained his high school diploma, sat the national entrance examination for higher education. On 6 September 1999 he received his results, which were insufficient for access to a faculty of communication sciences. Relying on the principle of equality among holders of the different types of high school diplomas, he complained of the unforeseeable nature of the changes introduced under the reform. He contended that the immediate implementation of the new rules on vocational guidance and the lack of a transitional period had had a negative impact on vocational high school students. On 1 May 2001 the 8th Section of the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s application. It explained that the changes provided an advantage to students who wished to take a university course in a field closely related to secondary studies.

The applicant applied to the Supreme Administrative Court for judicial review of the decision in question. He complained of the unforeseeable nature of the changes introduced under the reform carried out during his final year in secondary education. He contended that the immediate implementation of the new rules on vocational guidance and the lack of a transitional period had had a negative impact on vocational high school students. On 1 May 2001 the 8th Section of the Supreme. Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s application. It began by explaining that the changes. introduced in the 1998-1999 academic year provided an advantage as regards university. entrance to students who wished to take a university course. in a field closely related to their secondary studies.

The applicant had been in a vocational school for over a year when the Higher Education Council introduced a facility for transferring, under specified conditions, from a vocational to an ordinary high school. The combined sections of the Supreme Administrative Court, endorsing the arguments of the 8th section, rejected an appeal on points of law lodged by the applicant. As [counsel for the Secretary of State] submits, there is a broad spectrum of approaches among democratic societies, and the United Kingdom falls into the middle of the spectrum.

Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned, and like McLachlin J in Canada, I would accept that the tailoring process seldom admits of perfection, so the courts must afford some leeway to the legislator. As [counsel for the Secretary of State] submits, there is a broad spectrum of approaches among democratic societies, and the United Kingdom falls into the middle of the spectrum. In course of time this position may move, either by way of further fine tuning, as was recently done in relation to remand prisoners and others, or more radically, but its position in the spectrum is plainly a matter for Parliament not for the courts.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) On 8 July 2003 it was declared partly admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of Mr M. Pellonpää, President, Sir Nicolas Bratza, Mrs V. Strážnická, Mr R. Maruste, Mr S. Pavlovschi and judges. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 April 2005. Observations were also received from the AIRE Centre and the Government of Latvia, which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure. The parties replied to those comments at the hearing mentioned below. The Court heard addresses by Mr Singh and Ms Krause. The Government each filed a memorial. The applicant’s tariff (that part of the sentence relating to retribution and deterrence) expired on 25 June 1994. His continued detention was based on considerations of risk and dangerousness, the Parole Board considering that he continued to present a risk of serious harm to the public. There is more than one element to punishment than forcible detention. Removal from society means removal from the privileges of society, amongst which is the right to vote for one’s representative. In Europe only eight countries, including the United Kingdom, did not give convicted prisoners a vote, while twenty did not disenfranchise prisoners and eight imposed a more restricted disenfranchisement. Lord Justice Kennedy concluded: “... I return to what was said by the European Court in paragraph 52 of its judgment in Mathieu-Mohin. Of course as far as an individual prisoner is concerned disenfranchisements does impair the very essence of his right toVote.” Convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed, the Working Group said. to be disenfranchised that must be in the pursuit of a legitimate aim. In the case of a convicted prisoner serving his sentence the aim may not be easy to articulate. The European Court also requires that the means employed to restrict the implied Convention rights to vote are not disproportionate, and that is the point at which, as it seems to me, it is appropriate for this Court to defer to the legislature. ... If section 3(1) of the 1983 Act can meet the challenge of Article 3 [of the First Protocol] then Article 14 has nothing to offer, any more than Article 10. An application for permission to appeal was filed on behalf of Mr Pearson and Mr Feal-Martinez, together with a forty-three-page skeleton argument. On 15 May 2001 Lord Justice Buxton considered the application on the papers and refused permission on the ground that the appeal had no real prospect of success. The applicant’s renewed application was refused on 18 June 2001, after oral argument, by Lord Justice Simon Brown. On 25 May 2004 the applicant was released from prison on licence. His. claims were accordingly dismissed as were those of the other prisoners. His appeal was dismissed on the basis that he had no right to appeal.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Rules of Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicant filed with the District Court an application for permission to carry out works on the gas supply to his apartment. The District Court gave a preliminary decision (postanowienie wstępne) on 22 December 1989. It determined that the house in question consisted of two apartments, basements and an attic. On 9 July 1990, on the applicant’s appeal, the Regional Court quashed this decision. On 4 March 1992 the District court rejected the applicant's request for an interim order authorising works to be carried out on the attic of the house. In April 1993 the parties paid an advance fee towards the costs of the inspection, as ordered by the court. By a letter of 8 April 1994 the applicant and his lawyer informed the court that the inspection had not taken place. The court ordered the Institute of. Construction Technology to appoint an expert to take charge of the. preparation of the report ordered by the court. On 22 November 1995 the court received the expert report and served copies on the parties. The hearing was adjourned on 3 February 1997 on account of B.G.’s poor state of health. On 16 December 1997 the District Court again stayed the proceedings because B. G. had died on 3 October 1997. On 30 August 2000 the court appointed G.G., the petitioner, as guardian of the estate. On 8 February 2000 the Regional Court upheld that decision. The applicant filed an application on 20 March 1996 for permission to carry out works on the gas supply to his apartment. The Warsaw-Praga District Court ruled that the applicant’s sons, T.G. and E.G., were the heirs to his estate. The proceedings are still stayed and, therefore, remain pending before the Warsaw- praga district court. The applicant's lawyer requested the President of the Civil Division of the District Court to expedite the proceedings. The court refused to do so and the proceedings remain pending. The case was settled out of court in 1999. It is now being appealed to the European Court of Human Rights, the High Court of Justice, and the Supreme Court of the Republic of Poland. The application was filed by the son of the applicant, who is now deceased.

The man is believed to be in his 40s and to have been in his late 20s. He is thought to have a daughter and a son-in-law who are still living in the U.S. and have been married for 30 years. The applicant claimed that he did not remember how he had been brought before the Bursa Magistrates' Court and that before the judge he had just sat there while the verbatim record was written, which he had not signed. The applicant's legal representative submitted that some of the evidence in the case file had been unlawfully obtained. The Court of Cassation, relying on Article 318 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, dismissed the applicant's request for an oral hearing and upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 17 December 2004 the Bursa Criminal Court, taking into account the relevant provisions of the new Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), ordered the applicant's release from prison. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was the President of the City Council in Knyszyn (Przewodniczący Rady Miasta) The applicant accused K. Ch. of adopting an inappropriate timetable, unjustified division of students into groups, increasing overtime, which caused additional costs. The school manager found the accusations defamatory and untrue. The Białystok District Court found the applicant guilty of presenting untrue statements during the session of the City Council. Criminal proceedings against the applicant were launched in March 2005. The case was adjourned until January 2009. The judge ruled that the applicant's statements of 28 February 2005 weredefamatory. The applicant was awarded a suspended prison sentence of two years and four months. The sentence was suspended for three years and two months. The Białystok Regional Court partly amended the first-instance judgment. It found that taking into consideration the social consequences of the prohibited act and the conduct of the applicant, as well as his personal and family situation, it was unnecessary to sentence the applicant. The court also ordered that during a session of the Knyszyn City Council the applicant should make a statement that his accusations had been untrue and apologise to K.Ch. The applicant's lawyer requested the Ombudsman to lodge a cassation appeal on the applicant's behalf. The Ombudsman refused her request, finding that the arguments contained in the judgments of the first and second-instance courts had not raised any doubts. The applicant's lawyer lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court (Trybunał Konstytucyjny) arguing that Article 212 of the Criminal Code was incompatible with the relevant provisions of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court refused to hear the constitutional complaint (odmówił nadania dalszego biegu skardze), holding that a similar matter had already been examined by the court in its judgment of 30 October 2006. The applicant apologised to the court for the K.Ch.C. judgment and apologised to K. Ch.C for its handling of the case in the first place.

The application was brought by Ms M. Gąsiorowska, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołęsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The court based its decision on Article 587 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and others, which allowed statements made by both witnesses and accused in another set of proceedings to be read out. It agreed that it had not been obvious whether this provision could be applicable to a situation where the actions of foreign authorities hadn't been taken at the request of the Polish authorities. However this doubt had been dismissed by the Supreme Court in its decision of 28 March 2002. The applicant was convicted of the following offences, committed on an unspecified date between 1997 and 15 December 2000: storing and possessing large quantities of psychotropic substances, particularly amphetamines. The court found that the applicant had acted together with three accomplices; however it acquitted him of the charge of leading an organised criminal gang. The trial court sentenced the applicant to nine years’ imprisonment and a fine. Some of the evidence referred to above had been collected in another set of criminal proceedings against the applicant (regarding charges severed in 2001, see paragraph 10 above) The court examined at length the results of the searches of the laboratory. The written reasons of the judgment in this respect are detailed and extensive. The drugs found abroad had in fact been produced in the laboratory in B.C. confiscated in several European countries, notably in Austria. The trial court considered that W.P. in his statements had been incriminating himself to a far greater extent than the applicant. The President of the Fourth Section decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) The President gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. In August 2003 the applicant's wife informed the prosecutor that her son had been kidnapped by the applicant. In May 2004 the parties and A were examined by experts from the RODK (Regional Family Consultation Centre) Their opinion was that A should live with his mother, although the applicant should enjoy extensive contact rights. On 22 November 2004 the court changed its decision of 19 November 2003 and made a residence order for A. The applicant was granted contact rights and was ordered to return the child to his wife. On 8 March 2007 the applicant was arrested for the kidnapping of his son, B. The court allowed the applicant contact rights in respect of both his sons. In March 2008 A ran away from his mother's and went to his father's house, 100 kilometres away. The applicant took him to the police station and A was returned to his mother. On 4 December 2009 the Krakow Regional Court quashed that judgment. It appears that the proceedings are pending before the trial court. The child apparently felt that he had been treated differently from his brother B and that his mother had threatened that he would be taken to a children's home. The child obviously had a stronger attachment to his father. The court did not consider that there was enough evidence to issue an interim order changing the earlier decision of A's place of residence before the case was ready for a decision on the merits. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was dismissed on 20 July 2009. On 15 February 2010 the Kraków District Court allowed the applicant's request of 8 April 2008, granted him full parental responsibility and ordered A's stay with him. The court considered that A's negative attitude towards his mother, which manifested itself during the period when he was under her care in 2007, had been caused by the lengthy period of total deprivation of any contact between them. The court concluded that the best interests of the child required all contact between him and the applicant to cease. The applicant appealed against this decision, but on 11 June 2010 the Dabrowa Tarnowska District Court rejected the appeal for failure to lodge it in accordance with formal requirements, namely by lodging it out of time. A further appeal against the latter decision was dismissed on 20 July 2010 by the Tarnów Regional Court.

He fled from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan because of pressure from the police. In 2005 he arrived in Iran, where he settled in Zahedan. In 2007 he decided to flee from Iran following deportation threats. He claimed that the threats had been a response to certain disagreements with the Iranian authorities over their living conditions. In November 2007 the applicant entered Turkey illegally through Van and went to Ankara to apply for refugee status at the UNHCR. The Van office issued him with an asylum seeker certificate. Subsequently, he registered with the Van police headquarters and started the domestic temporary asylum procedure. Thereafter he was given a temporary residence permit until 24 September 2008. The applicant was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. Iran together with the applicant were granted similar certificates and permits after following the same procedural steps. The asylum seekers contacted some other Uzbeks who had managed to escape deportation from Turkey and obtained the ransom fee. The smugglers made them walk for three days to Yüksekova, a town close to the Iranian border of Turkey, where they were released. They requested legal advice from the Van Bar Association, which, along with two Turkish non-governmental organisations, published a report on 28 September 2008 regarding the Uzbek asylum seekers’ collective expulsion. It was argued in the report, inter alia, that the expulsion of the Uzbek by the Turkish State authorities had had no legal basis. The applicant has been living in Turkey in hiding since 2007. He has not received any information from the Turkish authorities as to his request for asylum. The application for refugee status under the mandate of the UNHCR is still under consideration. The applicant's application for asylum in Turkey is under review by the UNHCR's Ankara office, but no decision has yet been made on whether or not to grant it. He is the only Uzbek national to have been deported from Turkey to Iran since the beginning of 2008. The move was condemned by international human rights groups, including Amnesty International and the Human Rights Commission of the Parliament of Turkey. The asylum application is still being considered by the UN Refugee Agency. The applicant cannot appoint a lawyer to undertake the necessary legal and procedural actions on his behalf before the domestic authorities. He does not possess the necessary identity documents required to issue a power of attorney before a notary public. He was subsequently deported to Iran, a safe third country, where he was recognised as a refugee by the UNHCR. His identity documents were not confiscated. According to a document signed by two police officers and one military officer, submitted by the Government, twenty-nine Uzbek and Afghan nationals, including the applicant, were deported on 12 September 2008. The Government, the applicant was not deprived of his liberty. Moreover, his identity Documents were not confiscated.

Mr Gürsel Coşar (“the applicant”) was taken into police custody in connection with a murder investigation in January 2004. In his statement to the police, the applicant confessed that he had been involved in the murder of a certain İ.G. The applicant was born in 1961 and is currently serving his prison sentence in Muğla Prison. He was represented by Mr M. A. Altın, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The applicant was taken before the public prosecutor and the judge. The judge ordered his pre-trial detention and the applicant was placed in Fethiye Prison. The other co-accused, Y.A., who had allegedly killed İ.G. according to the applicant’s statement, was arrested. The applicant complained of pain in his left ear and that he should therefore be examined by an ear, nose and throat specialist. The doctor found two bruises 5-6 cm wide and 30 cm long, and one bruise 5-8 cm wide on the applicant's back. The injuries rendered the applicant unfit for work for three days. Y.A. and the applicant were charged with homicide under Article 450 (4) of the former Criminal Code. The applicant had tied an iron bar to İ.G.’s leg and together they placed the body on the tyre inner tube that they had bought earlier. They then swam 100 metres away from the shore with the tyre, dropped the body into the sea and then returned to the shore. On 30 June 2004 the Fethiye Assize Court convicted the applicant and Y.A of homicide and sentenced them to life imprisonment commuted to sixteen years and eight months’ imprisonment. The case is still ongoing. The court noted that, according to the police statements from the accused, they had hit the victim on the head with an iron bar and had thrown the body and the bar into the sea. The applicant appealed. In his appeal petition, he stated that the only evidence against him was the statement taken by the police during the investigative stage, which had been obtained under duress and should therefore not be accepted as evidence. He also pointed out that the police had not discovered a body or a murder weapon. On 18 October 2006 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 13 July 2005. The investigation into the applicant’s allegations of ill‑treatment continues. The applicant complained that he had been ill-treated while in police custody at the organised crime department of the Fethiye Security Directorate. The public prosecutor issued a decision not to prosecute anyone on the basis of the applicant’s allegations. The medical reports issued at the beginning and the end of the. applicant's detention did not reveal any sign of ill-treatment on the applicant's body. The doctor who examined the applicant on 16 January 2004 said he had not observed any injuries on his body and the doctor who carried out the examination on 17 January 2004, claimed that he did not remember the applicant in particular. According to the public prosecutor, the applicant had sustained the injuries after his police custody had ended. The public prosecutor considered that the applicant could have caused these injuries by hitting himself on the walls or his bed while in prison. In this connection, the public prosecutor relied on the statements of the doctor who had examined the applicant on 19 January 2004. On 15 December 2004 an objection by the applicant was dismissed by the Muğla Assize Court. The judge ruled that the application was not a case of false imprisonment, as the applicant had not shown that he had been beaten. The appeal was dismissed on 16 December 2004, and the case was settled out of court on 18 December 2004. The applicant was given a suspended sentence of two years and one month.

It was decided to examine the merits of the case at the same time as its admissibility. Both applicants confessed to their involvement in a criminal organisation, according to a document. Doctors noted in their reports that there were no signs of ill-treatment on the applicants’ persons. One of the weapons found in the car of the first applicant’s brother had been used in the shooting of 14 February 2001. The applicants disputed the accuracy of the evidence against them, including the medical reports issued following their detention in police custody, which stated that there was no sign of physical violence on their bodies. The court refused to release the applicants, relying on the seriousness of the offence and the evidence in the case file. The first applicant, Rif, was killed on 1 November 2001. The applicants were charged with causing grievously bodily harm to third persons. The applicants were convicted of forming a profit-making criminal gang and sentenced to three years and four months’ imprisonment. In December 2006 the Aydın Criminal Court acquitted the applicants. The court noted that the applicants had formed a criminal organisation with a view to making a profit, and that the shooting of the two persons on 14 February 2001 had been a result of the activities of that organisation. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the İzmir State Security Court to release the applicants in May 2003. The application is still pending in the court of cassation. The first applicant complained about the ill-treatment he had allegedly suffered in police custody. He asked his representative to secure him a medical examination. On 29 March 2001 the first applicant was taken to a clinic attached to the Aydın Governor’s office. A doctor examined the applicant and drafted a report in which he noted that there was no sign of ill- treatment. The applicant further submitted that the doctor had noted in his report that he was suffering from cervical disk syndrome. The doctor sent the applicant's x-ray to the prison. On 4 April 2001 a doctor sent a letter to the Prison Administration, requesting the latter to send the applicants for medical examinations. The applicant filed a complaint with the Aydın Public Prosecutor’s office against the police officers who had allegedly ill‑treated him, and the prison authorities. He also complained about the doctors who had not examined him in accordance with the regulations and had failed to note his injuries in their reports. The court considered that the decision to discontinue the proceedings was justified given the lack of sufficient evidence capable of substantiating the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. In his decision, the public prosecutor relied exclusively on the medical reports issued in respect of the applicant on 15, 16 and 21 February 2001 and the medical report issued during the investigation.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3994/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was lodged by a Polish national, Mr Jarosław Kąkol (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2002. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The trial began on 28 December 2001. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. The trial court ordered the removal of the applicant and two other defendants from the court room. They disrupted the trial by screaming when the prosecutor was reading the bill of indicted. The Court of Appeal instructed the trial court to hold more than 3 hearings per month. The Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's requests for the presiding judge to withdraw the case against him. The court ordered that the applicant be kept in custody until 31 October 2001. The Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant and his 17 co-defendants be kept in custody until 30 June 2003. It held that the grounds invoked in its previous decisions were still valid. In addition to the grounds previously relied on, the prolongation of his detention was justified by the volume of evidence to be heard at the trial. In September 2003 a new legal-aid counsel was appointed for the applicant. The previous counsel was discharged by the trial court from his duties at his own request and following a number of the applicant's requests. The trial was adjourned until the end of December 2003. The appeal was dismissed on 30 July 2003. Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention on several occasions. Court of Appeal stated that the grounds previously given for his detention were still valid. By March 2006 the trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. It heard more than 400 witnesses. The applicant filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. He maintained that the length of his detention was excessive and that the charges against him lacked a case to answer. The trial court dismissed the applicant’s application for release on health grounds, relying on the report prepared by the Gdańsk Medical Academy. The case was adjourned in 2004 due to the illness of the judge rapporteur. On 21 March 2005 the Gdańsk Regional Court made a severance order with a view to expediting the proceedings. On 18 October 2005 a different panel of the Court of Appeal quashed the impugned decision and ordered the applicant's release under police supervision. It also imposed on him a prohibition on leaving the country. The applicant was released on 19 October 2005. It appears that the proceedings are still pending before the first-instance court. The case is still pending in the first court of appeals. It is likely that the case will be heard again in February or March 2015.

In 1978 he had been formally registered as a secret collaborator (a “TW”) The court referred to the definition of collaboration contained in the 1997 Lustration Act and reiterated that collaboration had to be intentional, secret and consist of passing on information. The applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment. He argued that the registration of Mr J.M. as a secret collaborator by the services, in light of generally known facts, had allowed him to conclude that he had been a collaborator. But the court noted that no. documents confirming that the claimant had agreed to be a collaborator or that. he had actively reported to the secret services were available. It concluded that registration by the. secret services alone was not sufficient to consider that someone had been. a secret collaborators. The court accepted all the findings of the first-instance court regarding the facts of the case. It considered that when personal rights had been breached by a statement of alleged facts, the illegality of such action could be excluded only if the statement contained truthful information. In the present case there was no evidence, in the form of either documents or witness statements, proving that Mr J.M. had indeed actively collaborated with the secret services. The applicant was ordered to reimburse the claimant a further PLN 2,000 for the costs of the cassation proceedings. The text of the apology to be published by the applicant was as follows: “I apologise to Professor J.m. for having made the untrue assertion that he had been an informer of the [communist-era] political police” The court agreed with the facts as established by the lower courts in particular as regards the conclusion that the statement made by the applicant had not been true. According to the conclusion of this resolution a journalist’s actions would not be considered illegal if they were made in the public interest and the duty to act with due diligence was fulfilled. Imposing an obligation on a journalist to prove the veracity of each statement would unjustifiably limit the freedom of the press in a democratic society. Making false allegations was illegal, whereas the question of due diligence would be taken into account only when assessing the fault of the defendant. Therefore, the interpretation of the law adopted by theLower courts was correct.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the national authorities had failed to carry out an effective investigation into the disappearance of her husband. The application was communicated to the Government on 23 October 2012. The facts of the case as submitted by the parties and as they appear from the documents submitted by them, may be summarised as follows. The investigation carried out between 2005 and 2006 was described as a ‘preventive operation’. Mustafa Sayğı was taken to a military base near Yoğurtçu village in June 1994. His mother and two other villagers claimed they had been stopped by soldiers. The soldiers said they were checking their identity papers and let them go. But Mustafa was not released and his family was unable to find him. An investigation by the Suruç prosecutor found no evidence that Mustafa had been detained by the military. The prosecutor also questioned the two villagers who had claimed they were stopped by the soldiers at the time of Mustafa's disappearance. However, the soldiers said that they had not been at the site at that time and that they were looking for someone else. Mustafa Sayğı was unlawfully detained by the military in the temporary military base near Yoğurtçu village. The prosecutor did not attach any weight to the denials of the military personnel. The applicant lodged an objection against the prosecutor’s decision with the Siverek Assize Court and submitted that nothing had been heard from her husband after his unlawful detention. She argued that similar unlawful detentions had peaked in that area in 1994 and that the relatives of those who had disappeared had been too frightened to complain to the authorities. The objection lodged by the applicant was rejected by the Sverek Assise Court on 29 November 2006. The remains of a red motorbike were found during the excavation. The family of Mustafa Sayğı told the prosecutor about the eyewitnesses who claimed to have seen his brother in the hands of the soldiers. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 28 April 1997. The applicant alleged that the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. On 6 April 2000 the application was declared partly admissible. On 9 November 2000 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, unanimously, that there had been a violation of Article 6. The respondent State was to pay the applicant FRF 10,000 (ten thousand French francs) The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. The Court heard addresses by Mr Dinç, Mr Özmen and Mrs Bulutlar Ulusoy, and their replies to questions from individual members of the court. The case was decided by a panel of Judges Makarczyk and Türmen. The judgment was published on 9 November 2000. The applicant later claimed that he was not permitted to contact his family or consult a lawyer. On 31 July 1995 the office of the public prosecutor of Karşıyaka decided not to bring charges against the applicant (takipsizlik kararı) for lack of evidence. The decision was served on the applicant on 19 August 1995. In the petition, the applicant's lawyer stated, inter alia, that the applicant, while in detention, had been tortured and ill-treated by being beaten and insulted for two hours and deprived of his right to contact family and lawyer. As a result of his detention the applicant was granted four days' sick leave by his employer. The judge found that the evidence obtained was sufficient to enable him to draft his report and decided in the exercise of his discretion under section 3 of Law no. 466 that it was unnecessary to hear the applicant. The public prosecutor recommended that the applicant be granted compensation for non-pecuniary damage in an amount to be assessed by the court. This opinion was not served on the applicant, however. The applicant was detained for two days and qualified for compensation. The court awarded the applicant TRL 1,500,000 for his legal costs. The applicant's lawyer and the Treasury both appealed against the award. On 17 October 1996 the Principal Public Prosecutor submitted his opinion on the merits of both parties' appeals. He advised that both appeals be rejected and that the first-instance judgment be approved. On 7 November 1996 the Sixth Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation approved the judgment. The applicant never applied to obtain the compensation awarded to him by the Karşıyaka Assize Court. The judgment of 7 December 1995. having regard, inter alia, to the opinion of the Principal Public Prosecutor, upheld the judgment. The District Court held that the evidence obtained in the case had not sufficiently justified the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed slander. The applicant had not been informed of his rights and obligations as an accused. The alleged offence only carried a fine or a penalty of restriction of liberty (such as a community service order) but not a custodial sentence. The applicant was released from detention in the morning of 13 January 2003 (a Monday) Upon his release he received copies of the three documents translated into French. The applicant went on to describe in general terms a local economic development programme, which had been presented to him by a businessman. He finished his article with the following paragraph: ‘This is not a venture of the quail variety by some smart poser or populist who is able to sell his dull bosses dung nicely wrapped in words. And he actually sells it’ The private prosecutors sought an order requiring the applicant to publish an apology in the weekly newspaper. They further sought reimbursement of their legal costs and payment by the applicant of 5,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) to a charity. The Radomsko District Court ruled that it did not have jurisdiction in the case, and transmitted the private bill of indictment to the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court. The trial court held two hearings. The court held that the use of the words “numbskull”, “poser” and “dim‑witted official” in respect of K.H. had amounted to insult. The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. The trial court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media, which was to serve the State and society. It is difficult not to agree with the position that the word “numbskull” (“palant”) in the analysed context, although its literal meaning is legally irrelevant. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The court observed that his acts and motivation had been reprehensible. It imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt.“Dull” meaning not sharp, unintelligent, intellectually retarded. “Dung” used in the title of the article has a cruder equivalent, and undoubtedly that equivalent was meant to describe K.H.’S contribution to the development of local entrepreneurship which was accepted without reservation by his “dull bosses” The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The judgment was served on the applicant on 29 May 2006. The applicant appealed. On 18 April 2006 the Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court (“the Regional Court”) upheld the first-instance judgment. It further held that, although fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted, the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been shot in the leg and then beaten up by a number of gendarmes who had been carrying out an operation in the prison where he was being detained. As the remaining facts of the case are disputed between the parties, they will be set out separately. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr Nurettin Peker (“the applicant”), on 12 October 2006. The operation, named “Return to Life’, began at around 4.30 a.m. on 19 December 2000. The applicant was handcuffed and dragged through a 100-metre-long human corridor formed by the gendarmes. While the prison governor and other civilian authorities were checking the inmates' identity documents, a gendarme dragged the applicant into a corner and beat him up there. He was subsequently taken to Gebze State Hospital but was brought back to the prison four days later, before his treatment was complete. The Government's submissions on the facts of the case were published online at:http://www.dailymail.co.uk/. The operation was to take a number of prisoners who were on hunger strike to a hospital. When the inmates refused to co-operate, force had to be used to remove them from the prison. A doctor examined the applicant at Gebze hospital on 20 December 2000, noted a gunshot wound on his left foot and began treating it. The applicant and five other inmates who were injured in the operation were also taken to hospital. He alleged that the gendarmes had opened fire on the inmates. The inmate and over 200 of his fellow inmates were accused of obstructing law-enforcement personnel in the execution of their duties and causing criminal damage. Three pistols and thirty-three bullets were found in the prison on 22 January 2002. Neither officer S.Y. nor any of the gendarmes under his command had fired shots during the operation. In a letter of 27 May 2004 the Gebze prosecutor requested permission to prosecute two gendarmerie officers allegedly responsible for the applicant's injury. The Regional Administrative Court in Sakarya examined the objection lodged by the applicant against the governor's decision on 10 January 2005, and quashed the decision. It held that a judicial investigation should be carried out into the incident. On 13 September 2005 the applicant filed an appeal against the decision and won. The two officers were sent to the Gebze Prison in Istanbul for questioning. On 18 November 2005 they were told they were no longer working at the prison. The inmate lodged an objection to the decision on 26 December 2005. The objection was dismissed by the Kartal Assize Court on 14 March 2006. On 12 March 2009 the case was dismissed as the period of limitation had already expired. The prisoner was released from the prison in 2004. The case was brought by the inmate and his fellow inmates against the Gebze Prison in Istanbul. The court ruled in favour of the inmates and dismissed the case on 20 March 2009. The trial is still ongoing.

Ankara Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s case. It held that before its publication, the book in question had been examined by a Rapporteur appointed by the publications advisory board. It is not clear from the documents in the case file whether or not the applicant lodged an appeal against this decision. The conclusion to the book “The Gypsies of Turkey” read as follows: ‘The most important links connecting the Gypsy. society to each other are their familial and social structures as well as their traditions.’ ‘Natia’, one of these social structures, can no longer be sustained in today's Turkey. The liveliest characteristic of Gypsy is their way of living. The secret world of the Gypsies reveals itself through their beliefs, in particular through their superstitions and taboos. In our opinion, these people, who suffer from humiliation and rejection everywhere, could be transformed into citizens who are an asset to our State and our nation once their educational, social, cultural and medical problems are solved. The only thing that needs to be done is to focus on this issue with patience and determination.“In December 1998 the Language Association, a non-governmental organisation, published a dictionary entitled ‘Turkish Dictionary for Pupils’. The publication of the dictionary was financed by the Ministry of Culture. In his letter, the applicant submitted that certain entries in the dictionary were insulting to and discriminatory againstGypsies.” ‘Gypsy wedding’ (Çingene düğünü): a crowded and noisy meeting. “Gypsy fight” (Ångene kavgası): verbal fight in which vulgar language is used. ’Gypsy money’: coins. 'Gypsy pink' (Ángene pembesi): pink. ‘ Gypsy pink’ means ‘a dirty and poor place.’ ‘Gypsies’ is a derogatory term for the Gypsies. The applicant asked the Language Association to correct the definitions of the aforementioned words and to remove the discriminatory expressions from the dictionary. On 16 July 2003 the Ankara Civil Court dismissed the applicant’s case.

The case of a woman who tried to leave Turkey using a forged Canadian passport. She was held in detention at the Aliens Department of the Istanbul Security Directorate until 26 March 1998. After the intervention of the Ankara branch office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) she was accommodated at a hotel in Istanbul. The applicant lodged an asylum application but the police rejected her application as it had been submitted out of time. She later realised that she was going to be sent to Iran and told Aliens Department she was an Iranian national. The application was rejected as she had not lodged her application for asylum within five days of her arrival in Turkey.

The applicant met a man in Iran while attending a secretarial college in 1995. She fell in love with him and after some time they decided to get married. In June 1997 X married another woman. The applicant continued to see him and to have sexual relations with him. In November 1997 the applicant entered Turkey illegally. In February 1998 the applicant went to Istanbul, from where she tried to fly to Canada via France using a forged Canadian passport. When the applicant arrived at the airport in Paris, the French police found her to be in possession of a forged passport. Following her arrival at Istanbul Airport at 1 a.m. on 5 February 1998 she was arrested by policemen. She was brought before the Bakırköy public prosecutor on the ground that she had entered Turkey using a forging passport.

In November 1997 the applicant entered Turkey illegally. In February 1998 the applicant went to Istanbul, from where she tried to fly to Canada via France using a forged Canadian passport. She was held in detention at the Aliens Department until 26 March 1998. The public prosecutor ordered her release, finding she had not entered Turkey of her free will. The applicant was handed over to the Istanbul Security Directorate with a view to her deportation. When the applicant realised that she was going to be sent to Iran she told the Aliens department she was an Iranian national. The police rejected her asylum application as it had been submitted out of time. Thereafter, following the intervention of the Ankara branch of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), she was accommodated at a hotel in Istanbul.

The case was heard in the Supreme Court of Turkey. The judge ruled there was no need for a stay of execution. The case is still being heard by the High Court of Justice. The decision was made under the European Convention on Human Rights, not the Turkish Constitution. The court ruled that the case should go to the full High Court, rather than be decided by a lower court, as the case was in this case. The ruling was upheld by the Court of Appeal, who ruled that it was not a case of illegal deportation. The appeal is still pending and the case is likely to be heard again in the next few months.

On 16 February 1998 the UNHCR granted a petition to stop the deportation of a woman to Iran. The woman was concerned that she would be subjected to death by stoning. The court ruled that the request was not in breach of the European Convention on Human Rights. The decision was made to allow the woman to return to her native Iran. She was given the right to appeal the decision to the Supreme Administrative Court of Turkey, which ruled in her favour. The case is still pending, but has not been heard by the Court of Appeal, which has ruled in favor of the woman's right to stay in Turkey. The U.S. Embassy in Ankara says the decision was “the right of the person concerned to remain in Turkey’s custody.”

The case was brought under the Geneva Convention. The case was dismissed on the grounds that there was not a need to suspend the order of deportation. The decision was made on the basis that the order was not an act of war, but of self-defence, and that the woman was not at risk of being killed. The judge found that it was the woman's right to stay in Turkey, and not the government's duty to protect her. The woman was allowed to return to Turkey, but not until after the case had been heard in court. She was then forced to leave the country, but was not allowed to leave Turkey until the case was heard again.

Turkey has ratified the Geneva Convention and the 1967 Protocol thereto. It has exercised the geographic preference option under the 1951 Convention in order to limit the grant of refugee status to asylum-seekers from European countries. For humanitarian reasons, Turkey issues temporary residence permits to non-European countries who are recognised by the UNHCR as refugees pending their resettlement in a third country by that organisation. A person who enters Turkey illegally and does not apply to the Turkish authorities within five days of his or her entry cannot be accepted as a refugee. Foreigners whose requests are not accepted are liable to be deported by the local authorities. An asylum-seeker whose application has been refused may now appeal within fifteen days of the refusal to the competent governorship.

Turkey has ratified the Geneva Convention and the 1967 Protocol thereto. Foreign nationals arriving in Turkey to seek asylum must submit their asylum application to the police within five days of their arrival. Non-European asylum-seekers who receive a positive decision may then submit their cases to the UNHCR for resettlement. Foreigners whose requests are not accepted are liable to be deported by the local authorities. An asylum-seeker whose application has been refused may now appeal within fifteen days of the refusal to the competent governorship. The appeal is to be assessed by the superior of the official who took the initial decision to refuse asylum. In its 1999 Annual Report, Amnesty International concluded that judicial punishments amounting to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment continued to be reported.

The report stated that no traces of gunfire were found on either the shirt or the vest of HalimBayram. The applicant appealed against the decision not to prosecute him. Cavit Özalp was killed by an explosion on 26 August 1995. His legs were severed as a result of the explosion. His corpse was then given to a member of the Kamberli village assembly. The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Department of Social Security to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 19 May 2005, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required.

The Courts Act gives judges the power to order immediate imprisonment as a penalty for contempt of court or for disturbing order in the courtroom. However, the case-law of the Supreme Court made it clear that these powers could not be used in situations where insults or disparaging statements about a judge or a court had been made in writing. The Court of Appeal noted in passing that there was disagreement in the doctrine as to the scope of judges’ powers to apply section 49 of the Courts Act. On 18 January 2005 the Supreme Court adopted a resolution (no. III SPP 113/04) in which it ruled that while the 2004 Law produced legal effects as from the date of its date of entry into force (17 September 2004), its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date.

We regard conduct of the sort involved here, that is to say working to create a false market in shares in companies involved in a City takeover, as a very serious matter. Not only may it lead to a fraud on shareholders, but it causes considerable damage to the reputation of the City of London. We consider it very unlikely, therefore, that when such conduct comes before the courts for sentence that a Community Service Order could ever be sufficient punishment. The right sentence in his case, we believe, would have been 30 months’ imprisonment. The applicant had already completed the community service to which he had originally been sentenced.

Two defendants chose, as was their right, to appeal against conviction. The right sentence which should have been passed on him by a trial judge upon conviction, additional to compensation and the costs order, was 3 years’ imprisonment. We have no hesitation in concluding that it was inappropriate, that is to say too lenient, in respect of the conduct in this case. The applicants were born in 1955, 1973 and 1962 respectively and live in Istanbul. The cases were remitted to the first-instance court of the Civil Court of General Jurisdiction. The Court of Cassation quashed the three judgments of the first‑instance court and held that the court should have taken into account the tax registration records and accepted the applicants' claims only in respect of the parts of the plot which were used for agriculture. In its judgment, the court stated that the plot in question was not designated as “meadowland” in the tax register.

The case originated in an application (no. 48983/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Mr Refik Timuçin Bektaş, a lawyer practising in Ankara. On 26 October 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the following complaints to the respondent Government: the national authorities' delay in paying additional compensation for expropriation and damage sustained by the applicants as a result of the low interest rate applied to State debts, despite the high inflation in Turkey. The Court informed the parties that it would decide on both the admissibility and merits of the application.

The applicants alleged that their plots of land were illegally seized by the administration for a dam construction without any payment. The court established that a committee of experts had assessed the value of the expropriated land in advance and that the authorities had paid the resulting amounts to the owners registered in the local land registry. It ordered the administration to pay the applicants an amount of increased compensation, plus interest at the statutory rate, starting from 1986 when the land was submerged in the waters of the dam. The cases were then quashed by the Court of Cassation, who ruled that the cases should be characterised as compensation claims arising from de facto expropriations rather than claims for illegal seizures.

The court ordered the administration to pay the applicants an amount of increased compensation, plus interest at the statutory rate, starting from 1986 when the land was submerged in the waters of the dam. The Court of Cassation quashed these judgments, holding that the cases could not be characterised as compensation claims arising from expropriation. It proceeded to quash the judgments of the first-instance court only in respect of the date from which the statutory rates of interest began to run.
