eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27770/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was convicted of offences of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. He arrived in the United Kingdom on 7 May 1995 and claimed asylum. The asylum claim was refused but he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State for the Home Department issued the applicant with a decision to make a deportation order. In early 2003 the applicant was interviewed by probation officers who found that he was not suitable for parole. The applicant claimed to be a member of the Isaaq tribe, which comes from Somaliland, an autonomous region in north-west Somalia. He also claimed that his parents were born in Hargeisa, but it was accepted that he was born in Mogadishu, in south-central Somalia. As the applicant did not co-operate with the provision of bio-data, the Government decided that it would be preferable to remove him to Somalia. In July 2006 the Government concluded an agreement with African Express Airlines which made enforced removals to Somalia possible. The first enforced removal to Somalia took place on 30 November 2006. On 25 September 2006 the applicant was granted permission to apply for judicial review. The applicant was issued with removal directions set for 29 November 2006. He sought leave to apply for judicial review of the removal directions and the directions were cancelled pending a decision on that application. Mr Justice Calvert-Smith in a judgment handed down on 7 December 2006. The judge held that the applicant’s detention after 30 June 2006 was lawful as once again there was a prospect of immediate removal. Both the applicant and the Secretary of State were granted leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The applicant was granted interim relief in the form of an order that he be released from detention but an application for interim relief  was refused. On 1 February 2007 the Secretary of State issued a decision refusing to revoke the deportation order. On 10 May 2007 the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal ordered reconsideration of the Immigration Judge’s decision. The rehearing took place on 18 December 2008 and, in a determination promulgated on 1 July 2009, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal. In a judgment dated 23 April 2010 the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding that the applicant would be at risk of ill-treatment if he were to be removed to Mogadishu. On 6 December 2010 the applicant was issued with removal directions to Somalia. The removal was to take place on 8 December 2010. The Court granted the applicant interim measures under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his removal. In April 2006 the Home Office introduced a ‘secret’ policy creating a presumption in favour of the detention of Foreign National Prisoners pending their deportation. The policy was not disclosed until mid-2008 and was not formally published until September 2008. The lawfulness of this policy was considered by the Supreme Court in the cases of Walumba Lumba and Kadian Mighty v. The applicant met his girlfriend Miss V. (‘V’) in May 1986. They lived together from February 1987 until February 1988. Around Christmas 1987 they decided to have a child. On 29 September 1988 V. gave birth to a daughter S. of whom the applicant was the father. V. had made arrangements to have the child adopted and on 17 November 1988 she had the child placed by a registered adoption society with the prospective adopters. The applicant subsequently instituted proceedings before the Circuit Court to be appointed guardian under section 6A, sub-section 1, of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964, which would have enabled him to challenge the proposed adoption. He also applied for custody of the child. The Circuit Court appointed the applicant guardian and awarded him custody.

The High Court found in July 1989 that the applicant was a fit person to be appointed guardian and that there were no circumstances involving the welfare of the child which required that the father’s rights be denied. Mr Justice Barron of the High Court stated: “I am of the opinion that in considering the applications both for custody and guardianship I must have regard to circumstances as they presently exist’” The High Court ruled in favour of the applicant and awarded him custody of the baby. The baby was placed in the care of a registered adoption society. The child was given up for adoption by the prospective adopters on 17 November 1988. The adoption order was made without the consent of the mother and the applicant.

The applicant also complained to the Parliamentary Ombudsman (justitieombudsmannen, JO) who replied in a letter of 25 February 1976 that he was well aware of the problems which could arise as a consequence of lengthy building prohibitions.

The applicant's property is situated in Rönninge. The building prohibition covering his property had ceased to be effective on 6 June 1984. The applicant appealed to the Government, which rejected the appeal on 8 November 1984, referring to the on-going planning work. In a decision of 21 August 1984, the Building Committee conceded that a mistake had been made and quashed its decision of 12 June; however, it took a new decision of similar content since a new building prohibition was valid as from 11 July 1984. In the decision it was noted that the Municipality planned to carry out certain work during 1984 for the purposes of establishing the necessary plans.

Hans Fejde, a Swedish citizen, is a businessman residing at Västra Frölunda in the South-West of Sweden. In connection with the bankruptcy of the applicant’s removal firm in 1984, a rifle was found among the goods stored on its business premises. The applicant was charged, on 2 March 1984, with illegal possession of a weapon (olaga vapeninnehav) contrary to the Weapons Act 1973 (vapenlagen 1973:1176; “the 1973 Act’). Section 1, sub-section 2, of the 1973 Act expressly included within the definition of weapons unusable items which, if made usable, would count as weapons.

A rifle was found among the goods stored on the premises of the applicant’s removal firm in 1984. The applicant was charged, on 2 March 1984, with illegal possession of a weapon. The court sentenced him to 30 day-fines (dagsböter) of 10 kronor each, i.e. 300 Swedish kronOr in total. The daily amount of the fines was fixed on the basis of Mr Fejde's financial situation, and the court also upheld the decision to charge him with the offence. The weapon in question was owned by R.T., who was married to his mother, who is now 82 years old.

The Court heard the case of Hans Fejde, a Swedish citizen. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government, Mrs Thune for the Commission and Mr Arnewid for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. The Chamber decided unanimously, under Rule 51, to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The case was heard in connection with the bankruptcy of the applicant’s bank account. Mr Cremona, the Vice-President of the Court, replaced Mr Ryssdal as President, the latter being unable to take part in the further consideration. A rifle was found among the goods stored on a business premises. The rifle lacked a breech-block and there was never any ammunition. The court finds that [the applicant] cannot avoid being held responsible for the possession of the weapon, but that the violation of the Weapons Act is of a minor character.“ The court sentenced him to 30 day-fines (dagsböter) of 10 kronor each. The daily amount of the fines was fixed on the basis of Mr Fejde’s financial situation.’ The court also upheld the earlier decision taken by the police to seize the rifle. In October 1984 the Court of Appeal told the applicant that his case could be dealt with without a hearing. The applicant was asked to indicate in his reply any evidence on which he would rely. He requested the appointment of a defence lawyer under the free legal aid scheme. In a letter of 11 March 1985 the applicant reiterated his argument that the rifle could not be considered a weapon within the meaning of the 1973 Act. He was also told that he should submit his final written observations within ten days. On 6 March 1985 he was refused the applicant’s request for a defence defence lawyer. The case was settled in favour of the applicant. Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s request for a trial hearing as this was found to be manifestly unnecessary. Court of Appeal, taking the latter submission to be an application for leave to appeal, referred the matter to the Supreme Court (högsta domstolen), which refused him such leave on 19 June 1985. On 15 April 1986 the Supreme. Court refused an application by Mr Fe to appeal to the. Supreme Court. The request for confiscation of the rifle is therefore rejected. No such action has been taken in this case. An action for. confiscation should be directed against the owner of the gun in accordance with Section 17 of the Act of 1946 on promulgation. of the new Code of Judicial Procedure. Jde is fighting to have his case re-opened. He was accused of raping a woman in 1993. He says he is innocent and the case should be reopened. Jde is appealing to the U.S. Supreme Court to re-examine his case. The case is currently on hold until the case can be re-heard by the court. The applicant was charged with the murder of Patrick Quinn in 1990. The case was controversial in the United Kingdom on account of missing and conflicting police evidence. The applicant alleged that the police had framed him for the murder in order to cover up their own wrongdoing. In 2000 the applicant made subject access requests to MI5 and GCHQ under the Data Protection Act 1998 (“DPA” – see paragraphs 21 to 22 below). The object of the requests was to discover whether information about him was being processed by the agencies and to obtain access to the content of the information. Both the applicant and the victim were found not guilty of the charges.

The applicant was convicted of the murder of Patrick Quinn in 1991. His conviction was overturned on appeal in 1993. Following his release, he became active in campaigning against miscarriages of justice generally. In 2000 he made subject access requests to MI5 and GCHQ under the Data Protection Act 1998 (“DPA” – see paragraphs 21 to 22 below). The object of the requests was to discover whether information about him was being processed by the agencies and to obtain access to the content of the information. Both requests were refused. The application was dismissed and the case against the applicant was dismissed as a miscarriage of justice. The case was reopened and the appeal was dismissed. The applicant was sentenced to nine years' imprisonment.

In 1996, he became active in campaigning against miscarriages of justice generally. He subsequently started a removal business called Small Moves, undertaking small moves and van hire in London. He alleged that local calls to his telephone were not being put through to him and that he was receiving a number of time-wasting hoax calls. He suspected that his mail, telephone and email communications were being intercepted.

The applicant lodged two complaints with the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (“IPT”) on 6 July 2001. The applicant complained that his communications were being intercepted in “challengeable circumstances”, within the meaning of section 65(7) RIPA. The information requested was exempt from the disclosure requirements of the 1998 Act on the grounds of national security under certificates issued by the Secretary of State on 22 July 2000 (MI5) and 30 July2000 (GCHQ). The applicant also complained under the Human Rights Act 1998 that there was an unlawful interference with his rights under Article 8 of the Convention. The application was rejected on the basis that the information requests were exempt from disclosure requirements.

There is a reasonable likelihood that interception and processing ... has taken place and continues to take place (Hewitt and Harman v. UK, 12175/86, EComHR Report 9.5.89, paras. 26-32). The Tribunal ruled that there had been no interception or that any interception which took place was lawful. The ruling dealt with a number of matters relating to the extent of the Tribunal's jurisdiction in respect of the applicant's complaints relating to conduct prior to the entry into force of RIPA. The IPT then proceeded to examine the specific complaints in private. The applicant was told that no determination had been made in his favour by the IPT on 17 January 2005, meaning that no interception had taken place. The Tribunal then ruled that the applicant was entitled to compensation under s 67(7) RIPA and damages sustained by the Complainant in consequence of the matters complained of.

Lord Bingham CJ stated that section 35(2) of the 1991 Act conferred a broad discretion on the Secretary of State to direct the release of mandatory life prisoners. The applicant alleged that he did not receive a fair trial on account of the absence of interpretation at his hearing on sentencing. In September 1994 the applicant was declared bankrupt as a result of civil proceedings brought by the Inland Revenue to recover unpaid tax. The various companies were all registered for Value Added Tax (VAT) purposes but failed to make any VAT payments or returns to the Customs and Excise authorities. The resulting loss of VAT was assessed at approximately 460,000 pounds sterling (“GBP”) and the accumulated losses in respect of Income Tax and National Insurance contributions were assessed at GBP 360,000. The applicant was represented throughout the proceedings by a Queen's Counsel, who was also a Recorder, a very experienced junior counsel and two different firms of solicitors. The applicant was convicted of all charges and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He applied to the Court of Appeal Criminal Division seeking leave to appeal against sentence. In his application, the applicant was represented by the same legal team that had defended him at trial. The applicant did not maintain in his application that he had been unable to understand the proceedings at the trial or to communicate effectively in court. He did not allege that he should have been provided with the services of an interpreter. The court agreed to make use of the applicant's brother, but he was never requested to translate any statement during the course of the hearing. The application was rejected. The applicant pleaded guilty to GBP 800,000 fraud but claimed the real amount of the fraud was GBP 140,000. Leave to appeal was refused by the Single Judge on 3 May 1996 and by the full Court of Appeal on 15 July 1996. The Home Secretary forwarded the applicant's case to the Criminal Case Review Commission (“the Commission’). The applicant himself applied to the Commission, claiming inter alia that his lawyers should not have allowed him to plead guilty to the GBP 880,000 Fraud. The Commission noted that it had interviewed the applicant via an Italian interpreter and that it was apparent from telephone conversations between the applicant and the Commission that he did not have a good command of English. The Commission accepted that the applicant would have been able to understand the generality of the prosecution case but expressed the view that an interpreter ought to have been present when the case was explained to the applicant by his own representatives. The Commission concluded that there were grounds for finding that the plea was uninformed because the applicant had not fully understood the nature of the case to which he was pleading. However, the Commission noted that the Court of Appeal no longer had the power to allow an appeal against conviction if it did not think the conviction was unsafe but was dissatisfied in some way with the trial process. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13284/04) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that, if deported from Sweden to Syria, the first applicant would face a real risk of being arrested and executed. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court declared the application admissible on 26 October 2004, and it was assigned to the newly composed Second Section on 1 November 2004. The applicants claimed they had left Syria legally, flying from Damascus to Turkey and then on to Stockholm. They had travelled using their own passports but had destroyed them upon their arrival in Sweden. The Migration Board rejected the family's application for asylum and their request for residence permits and ordered their deportation to Syria. The applicants appealed to the Aliens Appeals Board (Utlänningsnämnden), relying on the same grounds as they had before the Migration Board and adding that Kurds were being persecuted and discriminated against in Syria. They also claimed that they had paid 6,000 United States dollars for false passports which they had subsequently discarded. The first applicant was convicted of threatening behaviour against his four-year-old daughter and a brother-in-law. He appealed to the Court of Appeal of Skåne and Blekinge, which on 24 February 2004 upheld the conviction and the suspended sentence. In January 2004 the family lodged a new application for asylum to the Aliens Appeals Board and requested a stay of execution of the deportation order. They referred to a judgment that had been delivered on 17 November 2003 by the Regional Court in Aleppo which stated that the first applicant had been convicted, in absentia, of complicity in a murder and sentenced to death. They were also ordered to pay 1,000,000 Syrian pounds to the victim's family. The court went on to state: “[T]his judgment has been delivered in the accused's absence. [It] can be reopened.” It would appear that the judgment has gained legal force. The applicants also submitted some further documents concerning the proceedings in Syria, including a summons dated 10 August 2003 requiring the first applicant to present himself before the court within ten days. The first applicant claimed that he had not been involved in the murder as he had been in Beirut at the material time. The applicant was represented by a lawyer in Syria whose contact details had been provided to the Aliens Appeals Board. The embassy said that the lawyer had also stated that it was not unusual for the Syrian courts to impose the maximum sentence possible when an accused failed to appear for trial. The court found that the first applicant in the case was of Kurdish descent. The court ruled that he would not be able to return to Syria if he was convicted. The case was dismissed on the grounds that there was no proof that the case would be re-opened. The judge also ruled that the death sentence was not the most serious charge against the first person, as he had been found guilty of a lesser charge of murder. The majority of the judges agreed that the man was guilty of the more serious charge of killing his brother-in-law. The verdict was upheld on the basis that the murder was a case of mistaken identity and that the victim had no right to be believed. The stay of execution of the deportation order until further notice is still in force. The dissenting member of the Aliens Appeals Board considered that, having regard to all the facts of the case, the applicants did have a well-founded fear that the first applicant would be executed if returned to Syria. The family should therefore be granted residence permits in Sweden. On 19 April 2004, following the Court's indication under Rule 39, the Migration Board granted a stay of Execution of the Deportation Order until further Notice. The stay is currently in force and continues to be applied to the case of a Syrian family who want to move to Sweden.

It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Stephanskirchen. On 25 March 2000 the applicant, driving on the A1 motorway in the direction of Linz, was stopped by a traffic patrol. The officers noted that he had been driving at 200 km/h, thus exceeding the speed limit. The applicant was convicted of four traffic offences, namely speeding, breaching the requirement to drive in the right-hand lane, unjustified use of fog-lights and failure to carry his driving licence with him. The applicant alleged in particular that the Independent Administrative Panel had failed to hold a hearing. The Administrative Court partly quashed the decision in 2004 and upheld the conviction as upheld in 2004. The court also ordered the applicant to pay a fine and procedural costs of 7,000 Austrian schillings (508.71 euros) and 236 hours’ imprisonment in default. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that two police officers had been following the applicant over a stretch of over 1,000 metres. The Administrative Court remitted the case to the Independent Administrative Panel. The hearing was held on 29 November 2004 in the absence of the defence. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 30 December 2004. The applicant did not lodge a complaint with the Administrative Court or the Constitutional Court. The case was dismissed on 13 December 2004 and the case was not heard again until 6 January 2005. The two police officers were heard as witnesses. The application was dismissed and the decision was filed on 13 January 2005, and the appeal was settled on 16 March 2005, when the applicant was sentenced to three years in prison. By a decision of 10 October 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The applicants and another man, Jean-Pierre Terrasson, were convicted of illegally importing 18 kilograms of cocaine (with a street value of GBP 2‑3 million) into Heathrow Airport, London, in 1990. Two people travelled from Brazil to London in 1990. Their luggage was intercepted by customs officers. It contained 18 kilograms of cocaine. The pair were arrested and the cocaine was returned to its rightful owner. The case remains open in the UK and in the U.S. but no one has yet been convicted of any offence related to the possession of the cocaine in the 1990s. It is currently being investigated by the US Department of Homeland Security in Washington D.C. and the US Attorney General’s office in New York. Armand Terrasson, Thierry and Mr Smolny were all arrested at Heathrow in 1991. All three men were interviewed and denied any knowledge of or participation in the offence. The trial, which started in May 1991, was that Armand had organised the importation, using Mr Smorny as the courier from Brazil to Copenhagen and London. There was no forensic evidence and the prosecution case was that Armand had instructed Mr Terrass on the trip to collect Mr Smurny’s suitcase as if in mistake for his own. The defence said that the only relevant evidence held by the prosecution which had not been disclosed to the defence was two tapes of interviews with the applicants’ South London relatives. Armand Atlan and his two co-defendants were accused of smuggling cocaine. The case centred around a dispute between Armand and a rival jewel trader based in Brazil called Rudi Steiner. The applicants contended that Mr Steiner was an informer for Customs and Excise. The judge summarised the defence by saying: ‘...Steiner had long since either directly or through the Brazilian authorities informed British Customs and. Excise that the applicants were preparing to smuggle cocaine to England. In that way had induced the Customs and excise here to mount a prolonged and labour-intensive observation of those three men.’ Brazilian businessman Steiner set up the alleged drug deal in Copenhagen. He got Armand Atlan to believe that it was worthwhile going for the third time to Copenhagen for a delivery of diamonds. Steiner provided initially some samples of diamonds worth seven or eight thousand ... US dollars. He lost the cost of sending [his representative] diagonally across the world and back [with the sample] with a bit of time in a hotel. Stole 18 kilograms of 90 plus percent pure cocaine in Brazil. It would be difficult for Steiner to ask the British Customs and Excise about Terrasson’s suitcase for that purpose without revealing that he himself was engaged in setting them up. Armand Thierry was sentenced to eighteen years’ imprisonment and a confiscation order of GBP 1,918,489.60 with a further ten years' imprisonment to be served in default of payment. The applicants learned from the French press (Libération) that a Swiss undercover police officer, Commissioner Cattaneo, had written a report. In early 1995 the applicants’ solicitor obtained a copy of the report. It mentioned Rudi Steiner, describing him as one of three regular informers of the Brazilian, Danish and French police. He was said to have an interest in stolen jewels and a long-term involvement in the traffic from Brazil to Europe of large quantities of cocaine. The Court of Appeal heard arguments over the use of the Mato Grosso Report in the case of Rudi Steiner. The applicants maintained that the report substantiated their suggestion at trial that Mr Steiner had access both to stolen jewels and cocaine. The application for leave to appeal against conviction and to bring new evidence commenced on 18 December 1995. The hearing was adjourned on 19 December 1995 and legal aid was granted to enable their solicitor to travel to Italy where, it was believed, Steiner was awaiting trial on a charge of smuggling cocaine. However, the Italian authorities were unwilling to assist the applicants without the backing of a formal letter of request from a competent authority. The applicants' solicitor was able to obtain a number of documents relating to the Italian proceedings. He also obtained a statement from Commissioner Cattaneo, the Swiss police officer who had prepared the Mato Grosso Report. Mr Steiner was released on bail and his whereabouts were unknown at the time of the applicants’ appeal hearing in February 1997. The applicants added a further ground of appeal, alleging that the prosecution had failed to make full disclosure of the evidence in its possession. The lack of full disclosure rendered their convictions unsafe. Mr Crago was called by the defence to give evidence. He was refused authorisation to attend the hearing by his superiors. Court of Appeal ruled that justice did not require disclosure by the Crown of the public interest immunity evidence. Court of Appeal dismissed the application for leave to appeal on 20 February 1997. It observed: “Little, if any, of the material ... would have been admissible at the trial’. The applicants and their lawyers were not permitted to be present when the court delivered its judgment on disclosure. The court noted that much of the evidence was hearsay and irrelevant to the central issue in this case, namely whether British Customs and Excise officers conspired with Steiner to ‘frame’ the Atlans. The decision was announced on 16 February 1997 and was made in the absence of defence lawyers. Prosecuting counsel suggested that Steiner could have been sure of achieving such an end. Such a conspiracy between Steiner and the officers would have been hard for them to organise to an assured outcome. In the Court’s view, there is force and hard logic in those submissions. There are also a number of other questions indicating the impossibility of the Atlans’ defence. Why, if they thought they were to collect diamonds from Steiner, not drugs, did Thierry and Terrasson immediately check their luggage onto the return flight without apparently enquiring by telephone why he had not turned up or whether he had been delayed? Why did the two of them make no contact in Copenhagen and ignore each other on the plane to Heathrow? Prosecuting counsel’s submission, which echoes considerations voiced by the judge to the jury in the summing up, provides a logical and complete answer to the complaint. The evidence against them, which had been thoroughly and robustly tested at the trial, was overwhelming. All that activity pointed only to their involvement in the high value and high risk activity of drug smuggling, not some black market dealing in gems under Brazilian law. ...” Whatever Steiner's possible role as an informer, the Atlans’ guilty participation in cocaine smuggling is clear.’”“If the jury had had before it information matching our assumptions, it might have led them to conclude that Steiner may have provided some information, direct or indirect, to the United Kingdom Customs and Excise, but it could not have left them with any doubt.

The applicant was transferred to the post of specialist without any team-leading responsibilities. The job profile did not state that any employees or civil servants were to be under his direct supervision. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Appeals Commission on 18 May 2006. He argued, inter alia, that his actual work had not changed sufficiently to justify the lower grade. The Appeals Commission replied on 30 October 2006 and stated, referring to the Constitutional Court’s case-law, that the rights and obligations. arising from employment in public service did not amount to civil rights and. obligations. The application was dismissed without an oral hearing on 21 July 2006. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2007 that the European Convention on Human Rights did not apply to the case. The European Court ruled that there was no need to hold an oral hearing on the matter. The case was dismissed on 11 July 2007. The court ruled that the case should not have been heard in the first place because it had been decided by the European Court. It was the first time a European court had ruled on the case since the case was brought before it in 1987. The decision was made to allow the case to be heard by the full European Court for Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, on 17 July 2007, but only after the case had been heard by a jury.

Regarding the remaining five families, who are represented by the same lawyer, statements of claim were issued in October 1993, alleging that the shooting of the deceased represented excessive force and was unnecessary and unlawful. On 3 March 1994, the Ministry of Defence served their defence, stating inter alia that the force used was necessary to prevent the deceased committing unlawful acts and to protect lives and personal safety.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants, next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987, alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Jordan v. the United UK ( no. 24746/94), McKerr v the United. UK (no., 28883/95) and Shanaghan v the UK (No. 37715/97) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff. The applicants accepted that the summaries below are an accurate reflection of the written statements made by the official personnel involved, without making any admission as to the credibility, consistency and veracity of these statements. A decision of 4 April 2000, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The application was brought by the Irish. Human Rights Commission on 23 March 2000, which had been given leave by the. President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36. § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61. § 3). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 1999. The RUC station, which operated on a part-time basis only, was opened as normal at 9 a.m. on 8 May 1987. Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. The men said they wanted to borrow the digger and one of the sons was brought outside to fill it with diesel. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house and placed in the bucket of theDigger. The owner, Mr McGrath, waited four hours and reported the incident to Coalisland RUC at approximately 6.50 p.M. The incident at Loughgall took place between 7.15 and 7.30 p.m. The soldiers reported a number of sightings of the blue Hiace van passing in front of the RUC station in both directions. Reports that the van had been hijacked, and that a digger was acting suspiciously in the area, were also received. Given this information and the knowledge that diggers had been used in previous terrorist attacks, the soldiers were on full alert when the incident occurred. The digger stopped and shortly afterwards there was an explosion which caused masonry and dust to fly everywhere. Soldiers A to F and Constable A were unhurt by the blast which damaged a large part of the station. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station and continued to fire at the men near the van. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Some of the soldiers stated that they came under fire. Shortly after the bomb exploded, Soldiers K and R observed what they thought was a gunman lying in the grass behind the police station. He failed to stand up when challenged to do so, and both soldiers fired several rounds at what turned out to be a large lump of wood. Before the bomb went off, a white Citroen car began to reverse towards the soldiers in position 5. Soldiers S, T and U opened automatic fire on the car and when they stopped firing the vehicle was about 20 metres away. The front seat passenger got out of the car despite a warning from Soldier U not to move. Almost immediately, he was hit by gunfire and he fell to the ground. Later realising that he was still alive, Soldiers S and U moved him onto the pavement and put two field dressings on his wounds. When the shooting ceased the soldiers and members of the RUC were airlifted back to their barracks. Police investigation of the incident began at 7.35 p.m. The pathologist observed at least twenty separate missile wounds (i.e. bullet and fragment) and found that discharge abrasion on an entry wound on the front of the neck indicated that when the gun was discharged the muzzle was within several feet of the body. The post mortem examination revealed at least a dozen wounds to the torso and head. The eighth body (Gerald O’Callaghan) was lying on its right side on the pavement at the Loughgall side of the lane-way. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. The sixth body (Eugene Kelly), which had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere, was seated in the driver seat. Post mortem examination showed twenty-nine wounds (bullet and shrapnel) Police took possession of the firearms used by Soldiers A to X. In total, 678 spent cartridge cases were recovered, 78 of which were from IRA weapons. The DPP concluded that the evidence did not warrant the prosecution of any person involved in the shootings. The inquests were adjourned pending the determination of the Devine case, before the Court of Appeal (and subsequently the House of Lords), which concerned the powers of Coroners and the procedure at inquests. Judgments were given by the Court. of Appeal on 6 December 1990 and by the House. of Lords on 12 December 1990. The inquest into the deaths of the men in the present case was opened on 30 May 1995 in public before a Coroner and a jury of 10 members. The Coroner made available the maps and photographs but did not permit counsel (other than those instructed on the Coroner’s behalf) to see witness statements until the witness was giving evidence. The families of the deceased asked for the proceedings to be adjourned to allow them to seek judicial review of the decision to refuse access to the witness statements. This step was taken on 31 May 1995 following consultation with the families and because it was felt “utterly impossible for the applicants’ interests to be fairly or adequately represented”. The inquest concluded on 2 June 1995 that all nine men had died from serious and multiple gun shot wounds. The family of Declan Arthurs sought judicial review of the Coroner’s decisions not to allow the legal representatives to see witness statements before they gave evidence. The judge placed considerable emphasis on the character of an inquest as a fact finding exercise and not a method of apportioning guilt. In his judgment of 24 May 1996, Mr Justice McCollum in the High Court refused to quash the coroner's decisions or the jury verdict. The families of the eight other men who died are represented by the same lawyer. Seven of the families issued civil proceedings against the Ministry of Defence on 2 December 1988, 20 March 1990 and 4 May 1990 respectively.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53911/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicants run a fishing farm in Schalchen, Austria. They claimed that the regulation works on a small river in the vicinity of the applicants' estate without permission under the Water Act (Wasserrechtsgesetz 1959) constituted an interference with their water-rights. On 20 June 2002 the First Section declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The applicants' predecessors filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) as the District Authority failed to decide within the statutory six months time-limit. The Federal Minister for Agriculture and Forestry (Bundesminister für Land- und Forstwirtschaft) allowed the appeal as a consequence of which the Regional Governor had to take a decision on the merits. The Administrative Court, upon a complaint lodged by the applicants, quashed this decision and found that the administrative authorities had not properly decided. The case was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECH) in Strasbourg, France. The water rights of the applicants were not prejudiced by the regulation works. The applicants filed an appeal against this decision. Several technical experts were appointed in order to establish whether the works had damaged the well. The Federal Minister dismissed the applicants appeal on 14 October 1996. The Minister found that the regulationWorks had not damaged the applicants' well and dismissed the request for compensation. On 27 April 2000 the applicants challenged the experts appointed by the Federal Minister for bias (Ablehnungsantrag) in the Constitutional Court of Germany. The decision was overturned on 6 August 1998 on the ground that the experts had failed to take into account the expert reports submitted by the applicants. The proceedings are still pending. The applicants agreed with the Federal Minister on the further conduct of the proceedings. The Federal Minister would furnish a questionnaire to the expert in order that he supplemented his report. Thereafter the applicants would be given the opportunity to comment on the revised report and another hearing would be held. The applications are due to be heard on December 5. At the time of lodging his application, he was detained in Berlin. The applicant was extradited to Germany and subsequently held in detention on remand on account of the arrest warrant issued in 1990. The court accused the applicant of having prepared, with others, a bomb attack at the ‘La Belle’ discotheque in Berlin on 5 April 1986 in order to kill as many members of the American armed forces as possible. During this terrorist attack, three people had been killed and 104 seriously injured. Berlin Court of Appeal repeatedly ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand. It held that the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged resulted, among other things, from the confession of one of the other suspects. The danger of his absconding still persisted because the applicant was extradited to Germany only in May 1996 and had neither a fixed dwelling nor social ties in Germany. eval_texts: The applicants alleged that the procedure at first instance and before the Court of Appeal, allowing non-disclosure of certain relevant evidence, was inconsistent with the Court's case-law. The applicants denied any involvement in the bombings but admitted having carried out experiments with TATP and model aircraft. The sole purpose of the experiments, they said, was to develop and test techniques which they said were necessary to develop new technology. The Crown's case was that both were members of, or sympathisers with, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) The applicants were born in 1967 and 1965 respectively and, prior to their sentences of imprisonment, lived in Rugby. Both condemned the bombings, regarding them as short-sighted. They alleged that a Palestinian known to them as “Reeda’, whom they were unable further to identify, had supplied the TATP found in the lock-up and accompanied Mr Botmeh to buy cars at auction. The Crown, pursuant to its duty to review disclosure during the trial, unsuccessfully tried to find evidence confirming his existence. On 11 December 1996 both applicants were convicted and on 16 December 1996 they were sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment and recommended for deportation. They lodged appeals against conviction and sentence. In November 1997 the applicant's solicitors drew the attention of the Crown Prosecution Service to a press article quoting a former intelligence officer, David Shayler, who declared that the United Kingdom's intelligence agency, MI5, had been warned that such an attack was imminent. The Home Secretary signed a public interest immunity certificate in respect of a bundle of documents. The documents ‘concerned the part played by the Security Service in events prior to the prosecution of the defendants’ The material had not been placed before the trial judge prior to, or during, the trial. On 3 May 1999, the Court of Appeal granted leave to appeal against conviction on grounds relating to the lack of full disclosure. The substantive appeal was first listed for hearing on 24 October 2000. It began with inter partes submissions on the procedure to be followed. On behalf of the applicants it was submitted that it would be inconsistent with Article 6 of the Convention. Court of Appeal ruled that it should view the material ex parte and rule on the claim for public interest immunity. It ordered the following summary of the undisclosed evidence to be released to the applicants and their representatives, but declined to order any further disclosure of the material in question. “Some months prior to the bombing of the Israeli Embassy in London on 26/7/94, the Security Service and MPSB [Metropolitan Police Special Branch] had received information from an agent source that a terrorist organisation, unconnected to these appellants, was seeking information about the location and defences of the embassy. The Security Service took immediate steps to bring the document to the attention of the CPS [Crown Prosecution Service] and Counsel. The hearing of the appeal was adjourned for reasons unconnected with the present application. It resumed almost a year later, on 16 October 2001, when the applicants repeated their submission that the present case was indistinguishable from Rowe and Davis v the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, ECHR 2000-II (see paragraphs 37-38 below) The Court of Appeal rejected the argument that it could never be appropriate for it to conduct an ex parte hearing to determine a claim for public interest immunity in respect of material which had not been placed before the trial judge. It also specifically considered whether there was disclosable material relating to any warning by the Israeli ambassador or any involvement in the bombing by Mossad. We are unpersuaded that the Crown's system and strategy in relation to disclosure ... is flawed. We are satisfied that no injustice was done to the appellants by not having access to that matter at trial. We say this, first, because the matter added nothing of significance to what was disclosed at trial and, secondly, because, for whatever reason, no attempt was made by the defence at trial to exploit, by adducing it in any form before the jury, the similar material which had been disclosed in court. Thirdly, no one has attempted to conceal from this court any relevant or potentially material matter. Fourthly, public interest immunity has been rightly claimed because it affects national security at the highest level. The jury could not have failed to realise that there were many possible candidates for carrying out bombings of this kind. Expert evidence was called for the defence that the bombers could have come from many different places, though responsibility was not attributed to any particular group or organisation. The judge's summing-up rehearsed these matters in what [counsel for the applicants] called 'commendable detail' No complaint of any kind is directed to the summing up. We do not take the view that deliberate malpractice is a necessary or proper inference from repeated human error, particularly in the light of the explanation given to us in the ex parte proceedings. The Court of Appeal concluded that there had been no breach of the applicants' Article 6 rights and no reason to regard their convictions as unsafe. The applicants petitioned the House of Lords for leave to appeal against the judgment of the Court of appeal, but were refused leave on 14 November 2002. In December 1981 the Attorney-General issued guidelines, which did not have force of law, concerning exceptions to the common-law duty to disclose to the defence evidence of potential assistance to it. One of these categories (6(iv) was “sensitive” material which, because of its sensitivity, it would not be in the public interest to disclose. In R. v. Ward, the Court of Appeal stressed that the court and not the prosecution was to decide whether or not relevant evidence should be retained on grounds of public interest immunity. It outlined three different procedures to be adopted. The first procedure, which had generally to be followed, was for the prosecution to give notice to the defence that they were applying for a ruling by the court. The defence would then have the opportunity to make representations. The third procedure would apply in an exceptional case where to reveal even the fact that an ex parte application was to be made would in effect be to reveal the nature of the evidence in question. The leading case on disclosure at the time of the applicants' trials was the judgment of the Court of Appeal in R. v Keane ([1994] 1 WLR 746) The Lord Chief Justice held that the prosecution should put before the judge only those documents which it regarded as material but wished to withhold on grounds of public interest immunity. “Material” evidence was defined as evidence which could be seen, “on a sensible appraisal by the prosecution: (1) to be relevant or possibly relevant to an issue in the case; (2) to raise or possibly raise a new issue whose existence is not apparent from the evidence which the prosecution proposes to use; (3) to hold out a real (as opposed to fanciful) prospect of providing a lead on evidence’. The requirements of disclosure have since been set out in a statutory scheme. Under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996, the prosecution must make ‘primary disclosure’ of all previously undisclosed evidence which, in the prosecutor's view, might undermine the case for the prosecution. The defendant must then give a defence statement to the prosecution and the court, setting out in general terms the nature of the defence and the matters on which the defence takes issue. The prosecution must then make a “secondary disclosure” of allPreviously undisclosed material “which might reasonably be expected to assist the accused's defence as disclosed by the defence statement”.

However, that hearing was postponed to 15 May 2000 as agreed with the parties. The court declared that the parties did not need to take any action.

On 13 May 2004 the Berlin Court of Appeal upheld the decision, arguing that S. had suffered from the persistent conflict between his father and his mother. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court, which the court refused to admit on 14 July 2004. On 19 July 2004 the decision was served on the applicant. The child has since made a full recovery from the psychological damage caused by the incident. The court has now decided that the applicant has no right to contact his father in the first place. The boy has been reunited with his mother. The case has now been settled out of court, and the boy has returned to his mother's care. The application is still pending, but the court has ruled that the child does not have any contact rights with his father and that the case should be dismissed.

The applicant found out about the child’s removal from Romania to the United Kingdom in January 2003. The applicant sought a ruling that the child’s removal from Romania had been illegal. The case was adjourned until 8 December 2003. The mother appealed to the European Court of Human Rights, to which the case was referred. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had failed to sign the application and that the mother had not signed her request for adjournment.

The judge expressed concern that since his decision of May 2003 a number of documents from Romania had become available which seemed to indicate that the child’s removal from Romania by his mother was wrongful. If these documents were available earlier, the judge said, he would not have sought a declaration under Article 15. The mother submitted her observations concerning the applicant's actions in the Romanian proceedings and introduced a counter-action seeking, inter alia, a ruling that the applicant did not have a right of custody over the child.

The case was brought before the Bucharest Third District Court (“District Court’) seeking a ruling that the child’s removal from Romania had been illegal. On 16 March 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the respondent Governments. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. The child and the mother were located by the British authorities; however, their place of residence was not disclosed to the applicant. The High Court was presented by the applicant with documentary evidence emanating from the Ministry of Justice, the Romanian President’s Office, the Child Protection Authority and the Ombudsman. However, the court was not convinced and, in accordance with Article 15 of the Hague Convention, requested a Romanian court decision on the matter. The judge in charge of the case indicated that since his decision of May 2003 a number of documents from Romania had become available which seemed to indicate that the child's removal from Romania by his mother was wrongful. The case was to be heard in the District Court in Bucharest, Romania. The mother submitted her observations concerning the applicant’s actions and introduced a counter-action seeking a ruling that the applicant did not have a right of custody over the child. The judge expressed concern about the time that had elapsed in the proceedings and indicated that if the 8 December hearing in Romania was not conclusive he would discharge the order he had made in May and proceed to adjudication. The parties appealed against the judgment and the case file was transmitted to the Bucharest Court of Appeal and the latter fixed 6 April as the date of the hearing in the case. The mother filed her observations with the Bucharest Court of Appeal on 15 March 2004. The court examined the applicant’s action on the merits and dismissed it as ill-founded. The judge in charge of the case ordered that the final hearing should take place as soon as possible after receipt of an authorised translation of the decision of the court. The case file was sent back to the Court of Cassation of Romania on 16 March 2005 and the first hearing in the case was scheduled for 16 June 2005. It appears that during that period the Romanian Code of Civil Procedure was undergoing changes and that it was not clear which court was competent to examine the applicant's appeal. Under Romanian family law, after divorce the parents of a child do not have equal rights in respect of their child. The case originated in an application (no. 60682/00) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant’s admissible complaints concerned the compliance with Article 6 of prison adjudication proceedings against her. By a decision of 11 October 2005, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed further written observations.

The applicant suffered from cerebral palsy, a disorder of the central nervous system which can inhibit voluntary muscle control. She used a wheelchair and could only walk a few steps with assistance. She did not have voluntary control of her bladder meaning that on occasion she either could not urinate for several hours or she urinated uncontrollably. The condition did not affect her intelligence but rather her ability to process information so that she required explanations in plain language and sufficient time for full comprehension. The applicant was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment. It was her first time in prison. She was accorded an unconditional release date of 23 January 2000.

The applicant was detained in the medical wing of the prison since the normal prison cells were not wheelchair accessible. The applicant alleged that she said that she would not be able to produce a sample: the Government did not accept this. She claimed that she began to explain why she could not provide a sample but that her explanation was brushed aside. She was offered a cup of water, which she declined. She maintained that this was because she knew that the water would not assist because the problem was not whether her bladder was full or not. The Government maintained that she simply refused to provide a urine sample. It seems rather graphically to have brought home to her the consequences of some of her own actions – actions for which she had been unable to envisage consequences.

The applicant was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to eighteen years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed the conviction and was released in 1992. On 23 August 1993 the Linz Public Prosecutor's Office filed a bill of indictment charging the applicant with murder. On 3 April 1995 the applicant filed a request under Section 91 of the Courts Organisation Act (Gerichtsorganisationsgesetz) to order the Regional Court to fix a date for the trial. On 30 October 1995 the DNA test results were transmitted to the court. The trial commenced on 19 August 1996 and finished on 29 August 1996. The Assize Court acquitted the applicant on 29 September 1996.

The applicant was convicted of murder and sentenced to 18 years' imprisonment. The applicant was released after the applicant's appeal was granted. In 1995 the applicant filed a request under Section 91 of the Courts Organisation Act (Gerichtsorganisationsgesetz) with the Linz Court of Appeal. The DNA test results were transmitted to the court on 30 October 1995. The trial began on 19 August 1996 and finished on 29 August 1996. The Assize Court acquitted the applicant of murder on 29 December 1996. He was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 18 years. He is currently serving a life sentence with a maximum term of 24 years.

The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention as regards the length of the criminal proceedings against the applicant. On 14 January 1999 the Panel of the Grand Chamber decided that the application would be examined by one of the Sections. The applicant submitted a memorial on 16 April 1999, and the Government on 17 May 1999. The applicant was charged with murder in 1991. On 11 December 1991 the Linz Regional Court dismissed the applicant's request for the re-opening of the criminal proceedings against him. The applicant's trial commenced on 19 August 1996 and finished on 29 August 1996. The Assize Court acquitted the applicant on September 29, 1996. A DNA test of hair and skin parts which had been found on the victim and the applicant’s clothes was transmitted to the court on 30 October 1995. The DNA test results were transmitted on 30 January 1996 and the trial began on 19 February 1996. On 28 May 1996 the applicant was acquitted of the murder charge.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44647/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained about the disclosure to the media of closed-circuit television footage, which resulted in images of himself being published and broadcast widely. He relied on Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section.

Brentwood Borough Council installed a CCTV surveillance system in Brentwood in April 1994. In August 1995 the applicant was suffering from depression as a result of personal and family circumstances. On 20 August 1995 at 11.30 p.m. he walked alone down the high street towards a central junction in the centre of Brentwood with a kitchen knife in his hand and he attempted to commit suicide. He was unaware that a CCTV camera, mounted on the traffic island in front of the junction, filmed his movements. The CCTV footage later disclosed did not show the applicant cutting his wrists, the operator being solely alerted to an individual in possession of a knife at the junction.

The applicant was told by friends that they had seen him on 9 March 1996 in trailers for an episode of “Crime Beat” which was to be broadcast soon. On 11 March 1996 he complained to the Council about the forthcoming programme, at which stage the Council became aware of his identity. The Council contacted the producers who confirmed that his image had been masked. The applicant's image was masked in the main programme itself but the Broadcasting Standards Commission (see below) later found that masking inadequate. Many of the applicant's friends and family who saw the programme recognised the applicant. The BBC were also to consult with the police to ensure they had “no objection to recordings being shown because of sub judice issues”.

The Press Complaints Commission (PCC) rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing. The applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material. The High Court rejected the application for judicial reviewed. The PCC considered that, whether or not the applicant was identifiable from the photographs, the events in question took place in a town high street, open to public view. It did not consider that the juxtaposition of the photographs and the articles implied that the applicant had committed a crime and it had been made clear that he was released without charge. It found that the purpose of section 163 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 (“the 1994 Act”) was to empower a local authority to provide CCTV equipment.

The PCC rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing and the decision was communicated to the applicant by letter dated 2 August 1996. On 23 May 1996 the applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material. On 26 June 1996 a single judge refused leave. The High Court granted leave on 18 October 1996 to amend the application to include a complaint that the disclosure was irrational, even if lawful.

The PCC rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing and the decision was communicated to the applicant by letter dated 2 August 1996. On 23 May 1996 the applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material arguing that that disclosure had no basis in law. On 26 June 1996 a single judge of the High court refused leave. The High Court granted leave on a renewed request and leave to amend the application to include a complaint that the disclosure was irrational, even if lawful.

The High Court found that the Council had the power to distribute the CCTV footage by virtue of section 111 of the Local Government Act 1972. The applicant had argued that by failing to consult the police to see if he had been charged with a criminal offence, the Council facilitated an unwarranted invasion of his privacy. The High Court judge had some sympathy with that submission but did not consider it correct in law. Unless and until there is a general right of privacy recognised by English law, reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise, in order to try and avoid such undesirable invasions of a person's privacy.

The applicant argued that by failing to consult the police to see if he had been charged with a criminal offence, the Council facilitated an unwarranted invasion of his privacy. The judge had some sympathy with that submission but did not consider it correct in law. The footage showed a man walking in the High Street carrying a large knife in his hand. It did not show him attempting to commit suicide. It was plainly a potentially dangerous situation which the Council's employee quite properly put to the police, as a result of which the man was arrested.

Unless and until there is a general right of privacy recognised by English law, reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise, to try and avoid such undesirable invasions of a person's privacy.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44647/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained about the disclosure to the media of closed-circuit television footage, which resulted in images of himself being published and broadcast widely. He relied on Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. By a decision of 15 May 2001 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The Council installed a CCTV surveillance system in Brentwood in April 1994. It was fully operational by July 1994. In August 1995 the applicant was suffering from depression as a result of personal and family circumstances. On 20 August 1995 at 11.30 p.m. he walked alone down the high street towards a central junction with a kitchen knife in his hand and he attempted to commit suicide by cutting his wrists. He was unaware that a CCTV camera, mounted on the traffic island in front of the junction, filmed his movements. The Council's first press feature, the CCTV News, was released on 9 October 1995 and included two photographs taken from the CCTV footage of the applicant. The applicant's face was masked at the Council's oral request. However, that masking was later considered inadequate by the Independent Television Commission. The applicant's distinctive hairstyle and moustache made him easily recognisable to anyone who knew him. It appears that a number of people recognised the applicant. A letter of 25 April 1996 from the Yellow Advertiser opined that the applicant was not identifiable. The article included the name of a Council employee in the event that readers wished to obtain copies of the pictures. The application was rejected by the Court of Appeal on 15 September 1995. The hearing was adjourned until 28 November 1995. The BBC agreed to mask the faces of the stars of 'Crime Beat' on the basis that the show would be shown to the public. The BBC did not reveal the agreement until late 1997, after the star's name had been made public in a newspaper article. The man's identity was revealed in a TV documentary, 'The Man in the Mask', which was shown on BBC1 on March 31, 1998. The programme was pulled from the BBC's schedule after the show, but the rest of the programme was shown. The Man in The Mask was shown for the first time on BBC2 on April 11, 1998, when it was shown to a crowd of more than 2,000 people. The Broadcasting Standards Commission (BSC) upheld both of the applicant's complaints. The BBC was directed to broadcast a summary of the adjudication of the BSC with the episode of ‘Crime Beat’ on 12 June 1997. The Independent Television Commission (ITC) found that the applicant’s identity was not adequately obscured and that he was readily identifiable and easily recognisable by those who knew him. The ITC noted that the implication was that a man carrying a knife was likely to be intent on a criminal act. Given the admission and apology by Anglia Television, no further action was taken by the ITC. The applicant later chose to speak publicly about this incident.  applicant complained to the PCC in respect of the articles published in the Yellow Advertiser. The PCC rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing and the decision was communicated to the applicant by letter dated 2 August 1996. The applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material arguing, inter alia, that that disclosure had no basis in law. The High Court rejected the application. It found that the purpose of section 163 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 was to empower a local authority to provide CCTV equipment in order to promote the prevention of crime or the welfare of victims of crime. High Court judge had some sympathy with that submission but did not consider it correct in law. He argued that by failing to consult the police to see if he had been charged with a criminal offence, the Council had facilitated an unwarranted invasion of his privacy. Unless and until there is a general right of privacy recognised by English law, reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise, he said. The evidence is that the CCTV cameras in public places play an important role in both crime prevention and crime detection. In this case, the film footage showed a man walking in the High Street carrying a large knife in his hand. It did not show him attempting to commit suicide. Anglia TV failed to mask the applicant's identity adequately. The BBC failed to disguise the applicant at all in the trailers. Brentwood Borough Council were aware of the identity two days before the programme went out. The council contacted the BBC and received assurances that his image had been masked. In the event, unknown to the Council, it had not been adequately masked in the programme. An application to the High Court for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal was rejected. The subsequent leave application to a single judge of the Court in January 1998 was rejected as the Council was neither acting outside its statutory authority nor irrationally in making the film and photographs available to the media.

The applicant was the head of the Federal Bacteriological Serological Research Institute in Linz. He was found guilty of having violated his professional duties under the Non-Discrimination Act (Bundes-Gleichbehandlungsgesetz) and sentenced to a fine of approximately 2,400 euros (EUR) It found that the applicant inter alia had made statements about some of his employees amounting to sexual harassment. On 4 September 2003 the Administrative Administrative Committee of the German Federal Ministry for Public Service and Sport partly dismissed the applicant's appeal. It reduced the fine to approximately EUR 1,600. The applicant was allowed to remain in his position.

The Federal Minister for Work, Health and Social Affairs recalled the applicant from his post with immediate effect (Abberufung mit sofortiger Wirkung) and transferred him to a post with a lower grade. The Appeals Commission at the Ministry for Public Service and Sport dismissed the applicant's appeal without holding a hearing. It noted that the authority deciding on the transfer did not necessarily need to wait for the outcome of pending disciplinary proceedings but could assess itself whether a civil servant had violated his professional duties and whether such a violation requested a transfer. There were, therefore, no reasons for his transfer, the Appeals Commission said. It further acknowledged that it was in fact not clear whether the applicant had made one of the statements at issue.

However, it confirmed the Federal Minister's finding that the applicant could no longer be trusted to perform the managerial duties.

The applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) in 2000. He complained that the fact that the Appeals Commission had taken its decision after a private meeting was in violation of his right to court proceedings under Article 6 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's complaint on 26 November 2001. It found that rights and obligations which resulted from an employment as a civil servant could not be considered as ‘civil rights’ within the meaning of Article 6. It followed that Article 6 was not applicable to the applicant’s case. It further found that there was no indication of arbitrariness in the proceedings at issue.

Hamburg Regional Court heard proceedings in November 1996. Dentist K. claimed payment of medical fees amounting to DEM 20,708 (some EUR 10,587) for the applicant's dental treatment. Medical expert M. examined the applicant on 19 December 1997. He found that there had not been any malpractice in K.'s treatment. Expert S. examined applicant on 27 February 2001 and found there had been malpractice. The court granted the applicant legal aid and ordered expert S. to submit his report on pain of a fine in the event of non-compliance by 11 June 2001. The Hamburg Regional Court dismissed K.'s appeal against this decision in January 2002.

The applicant was a shareholder in a limited liability company, but assigned his shares to another shareholder in 1985. Subsequently, the company went bankrupt. A bank which had extended credit to the company filed an action against the applicant with the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht) on 8 April 1986. On 29 April 1986 the first hearing was held and on 14 July 1986 the second. On 18 November 1987 the court appointed a banking expert. On 19 January 1989 the Regional Court granted the bank’s claim having regard to the submissions of the parties, witnesses and the expert, to documentary evidence and to the case files of the bankruptcy proceedings.

The application concerns land consolidation proceedings involving land belonging to some 500 owners, including the applicant's husband. The applicant appealed on 21 August 1995, claiming that some of the plots of land which had belonged to her late husband and had been allocated to another party, were of special value. The Supreme Land Reform Board (Oberster Agrarsenat) decided to suspend the appeal proceedings pending further amendments of the consolidation plan. On 26 May 1998 the Administrative Court quashed the Supreme Land reform board's decision and ordered it to continue the proceedings. The judge ruled that the applicant was represented by counsel in these and the subsequent proceedings.

Acquitting the applicant and Mr Jensen could only be justified by reasons clearly outweighing the wrongfulness of their actions. In this connection, the interest in protecting those grossly insulted by the statements had to be weighed up against that of informing the public. The majority had regard to the fact that the statements, which were brought to a wide circle of people, consisted of inarticulate, defamatory remarks and insults spoken by members of an insignificant group. Their news or information value was not such as to justify their dissemination and therefore did not warrant acquitting the defendants. This did not mean that extremist views could not be reported in the press, but such reports must be carried out in a more balanced and comprehensive manner than was the case in the television programme in question.

An appeal by the applicant to the Supreme Court was rejected by three votes to two on 30 September 2011. The appeal had been directed at the High Court’s assessment of evidence as well as its application of the law. It concerned the interpretation of the first paragraph of Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, according to which journalists may refuse to answer questions as to who is the source of information confided to them for use in their work. The majority observed that it did not appear that it was relevant whether the source had disclosed his or her role or that this role had in other ways become known. However, the wording could not be given decisive weight.

The majority observed that it did not appear from the wording of Article 125 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that it was relevant whether the source had disclosed his or her role or that this role had in other ways become known. However, the wording could not be given decisive weight. There was no cogent reason to think that the legislature had not taken a stance on the issue at stake in the present case.

The majority disagreed with the applicant’s view that there was no reason to treat a situation, where the informant had identified himself or herself as the source, differently from those cases where the source had consented to being identified. A person who so consented could do so, trusting that the recipient of the information would respect the protection of sources as long as the identity of the source was unknown. Once an informant had confirmed that he was the source and had confirmed his or her role, this fact would become known. In such a situation an exemption from the obligation to give evidence would in reality not constitute a protection against having to disclose the source. It would rather be a right to avoid contributing to the elucidation of a criminal case. If the state of the evidence was such that confirmation by the journalist could not be said to assist in identifying the source it seemed unquestionable to maintain the obligation.

Protection of sources by journalists is ‘one of the basic conditions for press freedom’ The purpose was not to protect the source, but rather the public interest in free communication of news and opinions. If the hearing of evidence on the identity of a source were to be allowed, the media’s working conditions would become considerably more constricted. The protection of sources by journalists was, according to the European Court’s case-law, ‘one of the basic conditions for press freedom’ The purpose was not to protect the source, but rather the public interest in free communication of news and opinions. If journalists were allowed to protect their sources, they would obtain information enabling them to uncover matters in society that were worthy of criticism more easily than they would otherwise. If it were a precondition for the protection of journalistic sources that no other proof of the source had been presented, such protection would be undermined. This would enable a source to be tracked down, even if a requirement for waiver of source protection was that the source be identified with a criminal standard of proof.

Under Belgian law, journalists and editorial staff may be compelled by a judge to disclose information sources only if they are of a nature to prevent crimes. Such restrictions must be genuinely exceptional and subject to the highest standards, implemented by judicial authorities only. Such situations should be limited to investigations of the most serious crimes or the protection of the life of other individuals. National laws should ensure that protections apply strictly, with extremely limited exceptions. The same conditions apply to investigative measures, such as searches, and to the right to freedom of opinion and expression.
