eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been denied fair trials, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 10 September 2002, following a hearing on admissibility and the merits, the Court declared the applications admissible. On 1 July 2003 the Court decided to join the two applications (Rule 43 § 1) The applicants were represented by Mr P. Maynard, a lawyer practising in Tonbridge, and, at the hearing, by Mr B. Emmerson QC and Mr J. Hall. The first applicant's defence was that at the time of his arrest he believed he was taking part in a transaction to sell stolen jewellery. He alleged that his participation had been organised by a man named Geoffrey Lerway, whom he had met the previous year while both were detained on remand in Brixton Prison. In the van was a briefcase containing 4.83 kilograms of 50% pure heroin. On 7 April 1995 the applicant was convicted in Snaresbrook Crown Court of possessing a Class A drug with intent to supply and was sentenced to nine years' imprisonment. The first applicant agreed to accompany Lerway to a public house where, at approximately 12.45 p.m., a red Jaguar car and a white van drew up. Of all the participants in the above transaction, only the applicant was arrested and charged. The applicant suspects that the other participants were undercover police officers or informers acting on police instructions, but their identities and status have never been revealed to him. At the time of the alleged dealings, Lerway was on bail to the Middlesex Crown Court in respect of a large scale conspiracy to supply cannabis. It was known to the applicant that Lerway had acted as a participating police informer in that case and it was further known that the police officers involved in the applicant's case had also investigated the conspiracy. The Government revealed for the first time that the. material placed before the trial judge included information indicating that the applicant had been involved in. the supply of heroin before the start of the undercover operation. The trial judge, who directed himself in accordance with the approach set out by the Court of Appeal in R. v. Keane, decided that the evidence in question would not assist the defence and found genuine public interest grounds in favour of non-disclosure. The defence made an application to the trial judge under section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (“PACE”: see paragraph 29 below) to exclude the evidence of Graham, on the basis that the applicant had been entrapped into committing the offence. The judge held that in the course of the ex parte application he had heard nothing and seen no material which would have assisted the defence in their argument that evidence should be excluded. The application was made by a man claiming to have been entrapped by undercover police officers. The judge ruled that most of the information sought was subject to public interest immunity. The application also asked the judge to order the prosecution to withhold certain material evidence on grounds of publicinterest immunity. This request was denied by the judge on the grounds that the information was not in the public interest and the application was not supported by the evidence. The case against the applicant was dismissed on appeal and the case was adjourned until the case against him was heard in November 2014. The trial is expected to last at least until the end of the year, when the judge will deliver a verdict. A second submission was then made on the applicant's behalf to exclude the evidence of undercover police officers under section 78 of PACE. Defence counsel sought guidance from the judge as to the areas of cross examination which would or would not be allowed, given that certain issues relating to the investigation were covered by public interest immunity. The submission was withdrawn and the applicant entered guilty pleas to the indictment on 12 November 1996. On 20 November 1996 he was sentenced to a total of four and a half years' imprisonment. The applicant made a complaint about the conduct of the RUC at the scene of the shooting in denying Dr Stewart access to the body and in failing to call an ambulance. This complaint was investigated by an assistant chief constable, under the supervision of the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (the ICPC) The Inspector concerned was given advice which was recorded in the Divisional Discipline Book. The RUC conducted further enquiries and reported to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) The applicant's daughter sent a copy of the unofficial inquiry report to the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland (see below) Inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the murder was organised by family and friends after the conclusion of the inquest. The inquiry, conducted by the Castlederg-Aghyaran Justice Group and chaired by a retired United States Judge, heard thirteen witnesses over the period from 17 to 19 September 1996. Evidence was given alleging that police officers had frequently stopped Patrick Shanaghan in the street and issued threats, that the police warned people to keep away from him or they would end up being shot. The Judge concluded that the applicant had been murdered by the British Government and, more specifically, with the collusion of the RUC. No further steps have been taken. In January 1999 the DPP decided that there should be no prosecution in relation to the shooting.

The application was communicated to the Government on 3 February 2016. The court will hear the case from 7 to 9 March 2016, and the case will be heard at a later date. The public prosecutor asked for a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 until that day. He asked the bank not to reveal the request to the applicant. The bank complied with both requests for information and submitted the information to the public prosecution office. A list of fifty-three transactions deemed to be relevant was included in the investigation file as evidence. Everyone who had access to the case file, such as the lawyers of the co‑accused, also had access to the applicant's banking information, including the names of his clients who had transferred. The information received was analysed by the police and the public prosecutor. The applicant, as the lawyer of the accused, was granted access to the investigation file. From the case file he learned, for the first time, of the investigative measures concerning his own bank account. He asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to hand over to him all data received from the bank and destroy all related data at the public prosecution office. On 2 May 2012 the Bochum Chief Public prosecutor refused the applicant’s request. The applicant appealed against the decision. The court found that the investigation was lawful, that the bank had provided the information voluntarily, and that the documents could only be returned to the bank. Nonetheless, in order to safeguard the client‑lawyer privilege, it also decided to separate the documents in question from the general court file and only grant access to them if reasons proving sufficient interest were provided. The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed the decision of the Regional Court in September 2012. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint, without providing reasons (case no. 2 BvR 2268/12) The court found that the decision was proportionate and that the safeguards were not applicable, in particular since the bank could not be considered a person assisting the applicant or a person involved in the professional activities of the applicant under Article 53a of the CCP (see paragraph 27 below). The court also ruled that the applicant had acted voluntarily and that there had been sufficient suspicion for such an extensive analysis of his banking transactions.

It held that the assessors of the Regional Appeals Commission were independent in exercising their duties and that no circumstances giving rise to doubts about their impartiality or independence had arisen in the present case. Jowitt J. described the test of bias under English law in the following terms (pp. 93-96 of the judgment): ‘(1) Any court seized of a challenge on the ground of apparent bias must ascertain the relevant circumstances and consider all the evidence for itself so as to reach a decision’. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias. Having done so, he has to go on to show that on a proper examination by the court of the evidence before it there is demonstrated a real danger of injustice having occurred.

Jowitt J. then applied the test of bias which he had set out to the facts of the case, and concluded that, on the evidence before him, he could not say that the applicant had established that there was a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias. He said: “When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty, which cannot be done by reason of bias, the court must necessarily be asking itself whether there is areal danger that the decision-maker was unconsciously biased” He concluded that there had been no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. The Court of Appeal said it was not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different.

Jowitt J. concluded that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. He said: ‘When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty, which cannot be denied, the court must necessarily be asking itself whether there is a real danger that the decision-maker was unconsciously biased’ He said that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias, the ‘doctrine of necessity’ fell to be considered. The court is [not] concerned strictly with the appearance of bias but rather with establishing the possibility thatthere was actual although unconscious bias. It is not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different but for the bias.

The court must reach its own factual conclusion. Is there a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias? By ‘real’ is meant not without substance. A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. It is not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different but for the bias. What must be established is the real danger. of bias having affected the decision in the sense of having caused the decision-maker, albeit unconsciously, to weigh the competing contentions, and so decide the merits, unfairly.” Jowitt J. then applied the test of bias which he had set out to the facts of the case. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 55287/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1983 and is currently detained at HMP Whitemoor. He is represented before the Court by Mr G. Bloxsome, a lawyer practising in Croydon with Blackfords LLP. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Grainger of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The facts of the case may be summarised as follows: The applicant’s case was that he had been involved in a drug deal with Mr Pearman and Mr Bartlett. The applicant’s trial for the murder of Mr Bartlett started on 11 August 2008. Mr Pearman was asked to make a statement or give evidence at the trial but refused to do so. The defence objected to their admission in evidence but the judge ruled that they should be admitted. The judge stated that he was satisfied the evidence had extremely strong probative value. The admission of the telephone calls was made in accordance with section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (see paragraph 40 below). The prosecution sought to adduce the recordings to disprove the applicant's defence. The court ruled that the recordings had “extremely strong Probative value’. The judge said that he was satisfied the evidence in question was ‘extremely important’ He indicated that Mr Pearman could not be called because he refused to give evidence, but noted that all the enquiries carried out by the police to date had confirmed his lack of involvement in the killing. He said that as the conversations were taped the evidence was clearly reliable. The trial judge said he did not consider that there would be any real prejudice to the applicant from the tapes being played. The applicant admitted that when arrested on that occasion he had been dealing in drugs, but denied possession of the firearm. The prosecution also relied on the applicant’s previous arrest when he was found in possession of a firearm. Witnesses saw a white van in the vicinity of the shooting at the relevant time. The van had orange writing on the side, and was similar, if not identical, to the van that had been hired from AVA on the same date. Cell site evidence also demonstrated that the applicant and his co-accused were in the area between 8.01 and 8.17 p.m. on the evening of the murder. The jury heard evidence from a ten-year-old boy and a witness who saw a car matching the Vectra’s description leaving the scene. The applicant's mobile phone was switched off between 7.28 and 7.50 p.M. at the time of the killing. CCTV footage showed the applicant arriving in the white AVA van, wearing a baseball cap and making telephone calls to an associate at 1.47 a.m. The number dialled by the applicant was in the vicinity of the cell site covering the road where the Vectra was found. The prosecution’s case was that Mr Pearman, a man in his fifties, did not match the description of the gunman given by the eye-witnesses. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty by reason of diminished responsibility. The verdicts were returned by the jury after a three-day trial at the Crown Court in London. The Court of Appeal heard that Pearman had a tendency to be a drug dealer, carry a firearm and commit murder. The jury asked and were allowed to hear the tapes of Mr Pearman’s telephone calls again. The application for leave to appeal was initially considered and rejected by a single judge in February 2009. It was renewed before the full court on 14 November 2009 and leave to appealing was granted. In doing so, the court found it to be arguable that the trial judge did not make sufficient investigations with regard to the production of Pearman. The court also observed that it is a long standing principle that unless there are compelling reasons to the contrary, the best available evidence should be put before the jury. The full court heard the case and dismissed the appeal, reserving its judgment. The court observed that the tapes of Mr Pearman’s telephone calls should not have been admitted without calling, or trying to call, Pearman to give evidence. The prospect of any sensible evidence being given by Pearman was, on any realistic view, nil. All that the defence could have obtained was the advantage of having him brought up before the jury. The judge considered this evidence to be important and to have strong probative value. We do not know whether the jury shared this view. The defence were able to say, as they did, that the statements were self-serving, made by a serious criminal who knew that they were being recorded. The Court of Appeal said the only evidence of Pearman’s involvement was that of the Appellant. Because of the lateness of the allegation, the telephone records for telephones used in the murder for which Pearman had been convicted only went back to 23 April 2006. The judge's decision was not marred by legal error; he took all relevant matters into account; and the decision to admit the recordings in evidence was not one that no judge could sensibly have made. For these reasons, we reject this ground of appeal. However, we would in any event have upheld the safety of the conviction. Evidence of Rita Willott, described by the judge as an extremely important witness, was not challenged and was read at the trial. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40060/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Court of Appeal’s decision to dismiss her appeal and uphold the judgment making a possession order constituted an unjustified breach of her right to respect for her home and her family life. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 May 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms A. Sornarajah, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The Gypsy Council issued a claim for possession against the applicant and five members of her extended family, including her parents. The applicant indicated that she intended to leave the site when her parents left. Judge Bidder QC gave a judgment on the preliminary issue of whether the applicant could challenge the making of a possession order in her case. He concluded: “58. ... I do not consider it to be arguable that the decision of the claimants to seek possession against her was unreasonable or that their decision to invoke their domestic law rights could be castigated as unreasonable ... 58. ... It is impossible to say ... that there is a seriously arguable point raised ...” The judge made an order for possession against the applicant. He was, however, satisfied that her son, who resided part of the time with her, had been involved in an incident on site in which he threatened someone with a gun. It was not clear whether the gun had been real or merely an imitation; and had dumped garden refuse on the site. The applicant indicated in a recent statement that she intends to move from the site when [her parents] leave, that is on or before 4pm on 24th November. I do consider it appropriate to suspend enforcement of the possession order against her until the same time and date. But I am clear that the behaviour of [her son] on this site and his attitude towards the Farrows [the family of the site manager] is such that I have to impose conditions on her continued possession. The applicant, who was still resident at the site, was granted permission to appeal the possession order to the Court of Appeal. A stay of execution of the order of 28 July 2006 was also ordered. In November 2007 a bill which would amend the Mobile Homes Act 1983 was introduced to Parliament. The effect of the proposed amendment was to allow a defendant in possession proceedings such as the applicant to challenge before the County Court the reasonableness of making a possession order. On 12 December 2007 the applicant’s appeal was dismissed. The real difference between the present case and Connors is not that the appellant had been in occupation for a shorter period than was the family in Connors. In Connors, once the licence had been terminated, the authority was entitled to eviction. Dyson LJ concluded that since the amendment to the 1968 Act, it was difficult to conceive of a case in which a public law defence would succeed. He found that the main reason for the narrowing of the margin of appreciation in Connors was that the complete absence of any procedural safeguards was a serious interference with the applicant’s Article 8 rights. However, the precise scope of these safeguards was in his view, a matter for the national authorities to determine. He considered that provided that a reasonable degree of protection was afforded by the domestic law, the Strasbourg Court would not interfere. He accepted that the vulnerable position of gypsies as a minority meant that some special consideration should be given to their needs and different lifestyle. The court was bound not merely to make an order for possession, but to order the eviction of an occupant such as the appellant provided that the 4 weeks’ notice was given. Absent a public law challenge, the occupant had no opportunity to challenge the reasons given by the local authority for seeking possession and the court had no jurisdiction to take the reasons into account. The local authority’s reasons were irrelevant as were the occupant's personal circumstances. Nor did the court have power to suspend a possession order even in circumstances of extreme hardship. The court is, therefore, required to conduct an examination of all the circumstances of the case ...” House of Lords refused the applicant’s request for permission to appeal. She claims that her departure was the result of the refusal of leave to appeal and in the face of further threats of eviction. Dyson LJ considered that by addressing the lack of procedural safeguards for gypsies of local authority sites, the amendment had also gone a long way to meeting the discrimination point. While discrimination would not be cured completely until the 1983 Act was amended, it had been much mitigated. Thus to the extent that the discrimination persisted, the decision not to eliminate it altogether fell within the margin of appreciation accorded to the contracting States.

This decision can be appealed against to the Ministry of Justice... The applicant, represented by counsel, explained inter alia that she had refused to give her name to the ticket inspector partly because she was angry, partly because he already knew her. She had handed over various belongings among those, she believed, various letters from public authorities bearing her name. They claim they have been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway. The applicants own property close to Umeå, in the vicinity of a Natura 2000 area, the European network of nature protection areas established under the EU Habitats Directive of 1992. The NRA applied to the Government for permission, under the Environmental Code (Miljöbalken), to construct a 10 km long railway section in a river area in the north of Sweden (constituting the final section of a railways called “Botniabanan”) Proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. Six of the present applicants own houses or land within the mentioned “corridor” The properties of the other twelve applicants – houses and land in their ownership or owned houses located on non-freehold sites – are situated outside the “Corridor’s’ ‘neighbouring’ area. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for a judicial review of the case and requested that the Government's decision be quashed. NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. In 2006 the Environmental Court of Appeal (Miljööverdomstolen) in Stockholm quashed the judgments. The appellate court found that the Government’s decision had not contained a detailed examination of measures necessary to compensate for environmental harm caused by the railway project. On 21 June 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. Twelve applicants – all but Ms Holmström, Mr Härestål and Mr Höjer – appealed to the Government against the railway plan. They essentially complained of the specific stretch of the railway, invoking, inter alia, nuisance such as noise and vibrations affecting the enjoyment of their property. All applicants except Mr Osterman appealed against the part which concerned the permit to construct the bridges. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railroad plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. The Government’s permissibility decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. The Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissability of the railway project and the designation of the “corridor” in which the railway could be located. These issues could not be examined in the third stage of the decision process. The Supreme Administrative Court further stated that, if private interests were affected by the location of a railway project, judicial review could be obtained by petitioning the court in proceedings against the Government's decision. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The case was heard at the High Court in Dublin and the verdict is expected later this year. The applicants alleged a violation of their right to freedom of expression. The application was communicated to the Government on 26 June 2014. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal and the jury returned a verdict in favour of the applicants on 2 July 2014. It is expected that the case will be heard again on 6 July 2014, and that the decision will be made on 3 August 2014. The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged a violation of their right to freedom of expression as guaranteed by Article 10 of the convention. The applicants were born in 1977 and 1961, and live in Copenhagen and Åbyhøj respectively. They are represented before the Court by Mr Tyge Trier, a lawyer practising in Copenhagen. The Danish Government was represented by their former Agent, Mr Jonas Bering Liisberg, succeeded by their present Agent, Tobias Elling Rehfelt. The application was communicated to the Government.

The programme concerned the treatment of pleural mesothelioma cancer at Copenhagen University Hospital. It focused on two types of chemotherapy medication, Alimta and Vinorelbine. The programme followed four patients and their relatives, who told their stories, and a narrator spoke as a voice-over throughout the programme. In September 2004 the European Union had approved the marketing of AlimTA in combination with Cisplatin for treatment of patients with inoperable cancer. In July 2007 the Minister for Internal Affairs and Health replied to various questions posed by Members of Parliament. The Minister replied, inter alia, that there was no proof that an alimta-only treatment was more effective than a combination of the two drugs.

The applicants are journalists employed by one of the two national television stations in Denmark. The first applicant produced a television programme, described as a documentary, called ‘When the doctor knows best’ The programme focused on two types of chemotherapy medication, Alimta and Vinorelbine. The programme followed four patients and their relatives, who told their stories, and a narrator spoke as a voice-over throughout the programme. It was broadcast at 8 p.m. on 24 September 2008, and seen by 534,000 viewers. The second applicant was the first applicant’s superior and responsible for the content of the show.

Copenhagen University Hospital sent a memorandum to DR in June 2008. It said the combination of Vinorelbine and Cisplatin resulted in a one-year survival rate of 50% and a median lifetime of 12 months. The memorandum also referred to a fund aimed at developing research on pleural mesothelioma cancer, in the amount of 90,000 Danish kroner (DKK), equal to approximately 12,000 Euros (EUR) The money had been used to pay nurses and students and for data collection. It emerged that there had been no financial profit for the doctors involved in the study.

Copenhagen University Hospital sent a memorandum to DR on June 11, 2008. The memorandum said that the combination of Vinorelbine and Cisplatin resulted in a one-year survival rate of 50% and a median lifetime of 12 months. It also said that international studies had not shown that any two-combination regime was superior to other two‑combination regimes. There had been no direct comparison of the two treatments, and that there was no internationally accepted standard chemotherapy for the treatment of pleural mesothelioma cancer. There was no financial profit for the doctors involved in the research. The money had been used to pay nurses and students and for data collection.

Copenhagen City Court found in favour of Copenhagen University Hospital and S in defamation case against Director of DR and two applicants. The applicants maintained that the latter, in the programme in question, had made direct and indirect accusations, covered by Article 267 of the Penal Code (Straffeloven), of malpractice against certain patients suffering from pleural mesothelioma cancer. The first applicant stated, inter alia: “... that she had not criticised Copenhagen University. Hospital for improper treatment causing death.” The applicants, S, and Medical Director H for Copenhagen. University Hospital gave evidence before the City Court. The proceedings before the courts concluded that S’s claims were not substantiated.

Copenhagen University Hospital and S instituted defamation proceedings against the Director of DR and the two applicants. The applicants maintained that the latter, in the programme in question, had made direct and indirect accusations. The proceedings before the courts were settled in favour of the applicants on 27 October 2008 in Copenhagen City Court (Københavns Byret) The application was brought under Article 267 of the Penal Code (Straffeloven) which covers malpractice. The first applicant stated, inter alia: “... that she had not criticised Copenhagen University Hospital for improper treatment causing death.” The second applicant said she had wanted statements from both H and S as the programme would be unbalanced if they were not heard.

The law was changed in 1990 to make it easier for the public to claim benefits. The law was amended again in 2001 to make the law more flexible. The new law was approved by the European Court of Human Rights. The European Court ruled in favour of the new law in 2009. The case is still pending in the EU Court of Justice, which has the power to overturn the law. The original law was passed by the German parliament in 1990. It was amended in 1991, and the law continues to be applied today. The decision was made on the basis that the law provides for the right to claim a certain amount of money. It does not provide for a right to a full refund.

The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 1989 that the European Convention on Human Rights did not apply to children born in 1989. The European Court's ruling was upheld on the grounds that the EU’s human rights law does not give the right to a ‘right to a child’. This is based on the assumption that the child was born with a right to some form of human rights protection. The decision was appealed to the European Court, and the case was rejected. The case was decided in favor of the mother, but the father was not allowed to be compensated. The father was allowed to stay in the U.S. for two years.

The Constitution does not allow the government to deny benefits to children born without their parents' permission. The law was passed in 1788, and the law was never amended. As a result, the law cannot be used to deny the right to a child without parental consent. The right of parents to be compensated for the loss of a child’s earnings is not part of Article 26 of the Constitution. It is therefore unconstitutional to deny children the benefits of their parents’ income. The child's right to be able to earn a living is not subject to the same rules as that of the parents, it is the child's duty to pay for his or her education and health care.

The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). In accordance with the relevant legislation, an inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. The hearing was adjourned until 14 June 1995, when the applicant was allowed to apply for an extension to his appeal. Inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. The size, layout, and original external appearance of the buildings and their detailing did little to change that view.” Buildings lie in part of the green belt but outside the village policy area for Higher Whitley. The use of domestic-style eaves and gable barge boarding. to that view. The residential look of the ‘porch’ to No. 1 building. And the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food’s view about the uneconomic layout of both buildings as originally built all add to the impression that these buildings were not designed for agricultural purposes, albeit they have since been modified and adapted for such a use. I shall also consider the effect of the development on the countryside surrounding the village. (17) ... (18) The appeal buildings have neither enhanced nor preserved the appearance of the conservation area. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order’. The appeal on ground (h) (21) ... Mr Bryan wanted more time in order to erect a replacement or replacements before demolition. I see no need to insist on a period which would make undue difficulty for him. I will increase the period to 6 months ... (22) I have taken account of all the other matters raised, including the possibility of your client putting up a large steel-clad building under permitted development rights, but find they do not affect my decision. The applicant had been given more time to erect a replacement or replacements. The question whether the alterations proposed to a building were, as he evidently thought, a ‘matter of cosmetics’ and would not meet the main objections was entirely a matter of planning judgment for him. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.“At the hearing held before the European Commission of Human Rights on 14 October 1993, the applicant’s representatives stated that, although they had not represented the applicant before the High Court, they surmised that the challenge to the inspector's ground (b) reasoning had been raised in the Notice of Motion and then abandoned at the hearing.”

A medical expert noted that she suffered from symptoms of schizophrenia and had diminished intelligence. She did not acknowledge her own psychological condition. The domestic court concluded that she remained a danger for the general public and a continuous stay in a psychiatric hospital had to be ordered. In November 2009 the applicant was granted privileges in the hospital. She also started working full‑time in the laundry department of the clinic. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 December 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was born in 1954. At the time of the lodging of his application he was detained at HM Prison Whatton, Nottingham. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff (i.e. minimum term to be served before eligibility for release arose) of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection. The applicant’s tariff expired on 18 December 2008, by which time no Parole Board review had taken place. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings, the delay in fixing a hearing. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The panel concluded that the applicant had 'no more than a superficial understanding of the reasons why you committed the index offences or of the risk management strategies' The panel made no recommendation to the Secretary of State on the occasion of this review. It accepted that there had been a breach of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention in that the hearing had not taken place speedily. The High Court handed down its judgment in the judicial review proceedings on 23 June 2009. The judge outlined the background to the applicant’s claim, as follows: “4. a breach, having regard in particular to the fact that the pre-tariff advisory opinion of the Parole Board had effectively made it clear there was no chance of release upon expiry of the tariff (see paragraph 7 above)” The judge considered that it followed ‘inevitably’ from it that the panel, if asked, would not conceivably have directed the applicant's release. It is common ground that Article 5(4) of the European Convention on Human Rights requires there to be a speedy hearing.  Article 5(4) requires a speedy hearing to determine the lawfulness of the detention. In this case the cause has been the lack of man power in the Parole Board which has meant that it has been unable to provide the necessary panel. ‘Speedy’ does not indicate a particular period, and I accept entirely that it is fact sensitive. What may be required in a particular case may not be needed in another, depending upon the circumstances.’ He concluded that the September 2008 advisory opinion in the applicant’s case could not address the question whether the post-tariff detention was lawful. However, it did mean that any breach would not require payment of damages, because it was plain that in any case the Paroles Board would not have ordered the applicant's release.  applicant had originally sought a mandatory order requiring that his case be heard in September. Judge agreed with the decision not to pursue the claim for such an order. He said it would be inappropriate for an individual, seeking judicial review, to ‘jump the queue’ at the expense of those who did not seek judicial review. He decided: “I have already recorded that there was a breach, but it is a breach that will not provide, for this particular claimant, any great advantage. It does make the point, and it needs to be made, that there is an independent requirement under 5(4) for a speedy period” The judge noted that the measures put in place to alleviate the problem will not have immediate effect. He said it is not now appropriate for any prisoner to take proceedings against the Parole Board alleging breaches of Article 5(4) Unless there are very special circumstances, something has gone badly wrong despite the new arrangements in that prisoner’s particular case. It will not be helpful, either to the prisoner or to the court, if claims are brought which in reality, because of the existing situation, are not likely to achieve any sensible redress and merely add to costs. We cannot make orders which are only going to create difficulties for others and are not in any way desirable. The applicant was advised by his counsel that no appeal would be successful as the Court of Appeal would be bound to conclude that it could not prioritise any individual case. But, this has at least brought home to the court, and enabled the court to make the point, that the situation that existed was unsatisfactory, potentially contrary to law, and the court welcomes the steps that are clearly being taken now to ensure that that situation does not continue. The Parole Board recommended that the applicant be moved to open conditions. The Secretary of State accepted the recommendation. The case was heard at the High Court in London on Tuesday. It is expected that the hearing will last for up to two days.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the convention. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The decision was made to uphold or reject the application on the basis of the merits. The Court's decision was appealed to the European Court of Human rights (ECHR), which is expected to take the case further. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994. The applicant was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The court's record of the applicant's statement reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships. Henceforward he would only have sexual relations with other HIV infected persons. also tell his dentist [about it]. Moreover, the applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm.” The County Administrative Court ordered that the applicant should be kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The order took effect immediately, but the applicant failed to report to the hospital; the police accordingly took him there on 16 March 1995. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. On 27 September 1995 he ran away again and was at large until the police found him on 28 May 1996. He ran away for a fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. He explained that before 1994 he had had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. The owner of the farm hostel gave evidence on the applicant's behalf. The applicant had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. He had lost all sexual desire and would in future have to decline all sexual relations. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant continued to drink beer. He also spent money on lottery games and drinking beer. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. The county medical officer, who gave evidence before the court, recorded, inter alia, as follows: “During the last two years when he was on the run, [the applicant] sought medical treatment twice and it has been established that both times he said that he had the HIV virus’ The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons. “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years.” “He has consistently declined the help offered by the consulting physician and the psychiatrist at the special care facility at the hospital and has instead responded with aversion and mistrust – and by escaping. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection. During [the applicant's] contact with the doctors in question, they did not discuss the risk of spreading the disease at all” The applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. He had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. In the meantime, he relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated, inter alia, the following: “The opinions [by other psychiatrists and one psychologist] resulting from previous examinations were fairly unanimous in their conclusion that [the applicant] was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol.” The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [ the applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued and that this entails a risk of the infection spreading. The applicant showed empathy as far as other people from those years were concerned. He was partly able to shoulder responsibility for his own mistakes, without blaming others. From 1996, he had not experienced feelings of persecution, inter alia since he had secured his own liberty. With regard to sexual relations, [the applicant] has stated that he preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17. He had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill.” In conclusion, C.G., found that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for a paranoid personality disorder, and that, judging from previous information, the applicant suffered from misuse of alcohol. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court, which referred to the fact that the applicant’s whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the. applicant's whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical. officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the applicant.'s further involuntary placement in isolation. The application was made in December 1999. The applicant was placed in isolation from 5 October 1999.

The applicant is a farmer living in Piesendorf, Salzburg. He applied to the District Agricultural Authority for declarations that the share in an agricultural association (Agrargemeinschaft) represented by a certain parcel of land belonged to him. On 24 June 1991 the District Authority found that the applicant had not made out his claims, and it declared the share and the grazing rights belonged to a third person. The applicant appealed to the Regional Land Reform Board (Landesagrarsenat, the “Regional Board’). The Regional Board dismissed the applicant's appeal on 8 May 1992. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant’s constitutional complaint on 14 October 1992. It remitted the case to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof).

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The application was heard by the Court’s Fifth Section on 25 November 2009, and a ruling was made on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant’s father returned to Denmark in November 2003. He was informed that he, who had been recognised as a refugee, had visited his country of origin. On 9 August 2005, three months before the applicant turned eighteen years old, she contacted the Danish Embassy in Nairobi with a view to returning to live with her mother and siblings in Denmark. An interview was conducted with the help of an English/Somali interpreter although it was stated that the applicant spoke Danish. On 21 December 2006 the Immigration Service found that the applicants residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. The Immigration Service also found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. On 1 October 2007 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. It stated among other things: “... The Ministry emphasises that there is no information available of any circumstances that would lead to [the applicant’s] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed’. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant. The applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. On 11 December 2007 the Immigration Service brought the case. before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), before which the case was decided on the documents submitted, without any parties being summoned. On 25 April 2008 it found against the. applicant. The applicant's parents had sent her voluntarily to Kenya to live with family for an indefinite period. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. 30 October 2008 the High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. By letter of 27 January 2010 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The applicant is four-limb deficient as a result of phocomelia due to thalidomide. She also suffers from problems with her kidneys. On 20 January 1995, in the course of civil proceedings in Lincoln County Court for recovery of a judgment debt, she refused to answer questions put to her concerning her financial position. She was committed to prison for seven days for contempt of court. The judge ordered that she should be taken directly to Wakefield Prison. Before leaving the court the applicant asked a court officer if she could take the battery charger for her wheelchair with her. She alleges that the officer told her that this would be considered a luxury item and that she would not be able to bring it.

The applicant alleged that on the evening of 21 January 1995 she was lifted onto the toilet by a female prison officer, but was then left sitting on the toilet for over three hours until she agreed to allow a male nursing officer to clean her and help her off the toilet. The Government denied that these incidents occurred. An agency nurse was employed to care for the applicant during the night of 22 to 23 January 1995. The entries in the nursing record for 22 January stated: “Says she finds bed uncomfortable and there is a risk of her developing bed sores, but she is not completely immobile and is able to shift her weight about the bed.”

The applicant alleged that on the evening of 21 January 1995 she was lifted onto the toilet by a female prison officer, but was then left sitting on the toilet for over three hours. The Government denied that these incidents occurred. An agency nurse was employed to care for the applicant during the night of 22 to 23 January 1995. The entries in the nursing record for 22 January stated: “Says she finds bed uncomfortable and there is a risk of her developing bed sores, but she is not completely immobile and is able to shift her weight about the bed. No problems with diet but fluid intake diminished due to her not liking water.”

Nurses who cared for the applicant during her detention kept a contemporaneous record, which stated for the night of 21 January 1995: “Impossible to toilet during the night. Have been into Adele's cell twice. Took over 1/2 hour to toilet her then could not get her back on the bed. Given analgesia and she is getting a great deal of pain through lying on a solid mattress. Very difficult to care for her with one nurse.” The Government denied that these incidents occurred. They pointed out that prior to her release the applicant made a complaint to the prison governor concerning the lack of adequate facilities, but containing no mention of the above events.

The applicant claimed to have suffered health problems as a result of her treatment in detention, but has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. She was granted legal aid, limited to obtaining evidence and seeking counsel's opinion as to merits and quantum. Her counsel referred to the difficulties which the applicant was likely to face in proving that she had suffered the ill-treatment which she alleged. Counsel advised that, in the light of this case-law and the difficulties of proof which she faced, the applicant had a limited prospect of success in her claim. Even if successful, damages were not likely to exceed 3,000 pounds sterling. The applicant's legal aid certificate was discharged on 13 May.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33394/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her committal to prison and her treatment in detention violated Article 3 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 September 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The applicant claims she was forced to sleep in her wheelchair since the bed was hard and would have caused pain in her hips. She also alleges that the emergency buttons and light switches were out of her reach, and that she was unable to use the toilet since it was higher than her wheelchair and therefore inaccessible. The custody record states that on arrival, at 7.20 p.m., the applicant informed the custody officer that she suffered from kidney trouble and a recurring ear infection but that she did not require any medication or to see a doctor at that time. At 7.50p.m. she declined a meal and a hot drink. At 8.50pm she said she was cold so the officer wrapped her in two blankets. When she was checked on again at 9.15pm she was still cold and had a headache caused by the cold. The applicant was taken to New Hall Women's Prison, Wakefield, where she was detained until the afternoon of 23 January 1995. She was not placed in a normal cell in New Hall, but was instead detained in the prison's health care centre. Her cell had a wider door for wheelchair access, handles for the disabled in the toilet recess and a hydraulic hospital bed. The applicant was examined by Dr Kidd, whose notes stated: “New reception. Thalidomide victim with numerous deformities including absent arms upper/lower with dislocating L shoulder and no use in R upper limb. Both lower limbs are absent with small feet.” A ‘continuous medical record’ on the applicant was kept during her detention. The first entry, dated 21 January 1995, stated: ‘I asked duty Governor, Mr Ellis, to give permission for a battery charger for Adele's wheelchair to be brought in if we could arrange it. He agreed to this and whilst here we pointed out the numerous problems staff may encounter with this inmate i.e. (1) Needs lifting in and out of bed and she says this is usually done by one person standing behind her with arms around her midriff then lifting her either onto the bed or onto her wheelchair. Because of recurrent urinary infections she should take two litres of fluid daily but usually has juice and doesn't like water, therefore will probably reduce her fluid intake.’ The Government denies that these incidents occurred. They point out that prior to her release the applicant made a complaint to the prison governor concerning the lack of adequate facilities. The applicant claimed that later that evening, a female nurse who was assisting her onto the toilet removed her bedclothes in the presence of two male prison nursing officers, thereby exposing her, naked from the chest down, to the male officers. It is unclear from the Government's submissions whether Senior Officer Tingle and Officer Bowman were nursing staff or whether they were prison officers without nursing qualifications. The remission provisions in sections 45 and 33 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 meant that the applicant had only to serve half the sentence imposed, namely, three and a half days. The applicant was collected from prison by a friend. She claimed to have suffered health problems for ten weeks as a result of her treatment in detention, but has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. She was granted legal aid, limited to obtaining evidence and seeking counsel's opinion as to merits and quantum. Her counsel referred to the difficulties which the applicant was likely to face in proving that she had suffered the ill-treatment which she alleged, and that, even if successful, damages were not likely to exceed 3,000 pounds sterling. In the light of this advice, the applicant's legal aid certificate was discharged on 13 May 1996.

The case involves a Mr and Mrs Hauser who were suspected of fraudulently using a credit card which did not belong to them. The applicant was suspected of having aided and abetted them by forging the signature on the credit card. The pair sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. The application was turned down on the grounds that the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. The case was finally settled in 1992 when a judge decided to discontinue the proceedings against the applicant and Mr andMrs Hauser and they were released from custody. The appeal was dismissed on the ground that the witnesses called by the public prosecutor did not have sufficiently clear memories.

Johannes Werner was arrested on 15 May 1991 for fraudulently using a credit card which did not belong to him. On 1 July 1991 the police also arrested the applicant, who was suspected of having aided and abetted Mr and Mrs Hauser by forging the signature on the credit card. On 3 July 1991 he was detained pending trial and on 19 July the applicant was released. On 24 February 1992 the investigating judge at the Vienna Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to discontinue the proceedings in the light of a graphologist’s finding that it was unlikely that the signatures on the payment slips for the purchases made with the stolen credit card were in Mr Werner's hand. In 1992 the Review Division (Ratskammer) refused their compensation claims.

The case involves a man suspected of using a stolen credit card to make purchases in Vienna. The man and his wife were detained pending trial, but later released. They sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. The court refused their compensation claims on the ground that the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. The case was settled in 1992, with the man released from detention and the woman released from the trial. The application for compensation was dismissed on the grounds that it was unlikely that the signatures on the payment slips for the purchases made with the stolen card were in Mr Werner’s hand.

Mr Werner and Mr and Mrs Hauser appealed against that decision to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) They asked the court to take further evidence and, in particular, to hear witnesses. No representative of the public prosecutor’s office attended the deliberations. On 29 October 1992 the Vienna court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It ruled that suspicion does not have to be wholly dispelled for compensation to be payable under section 2 (1) (b) of the Compensation (Criminal Proceedings) Act. The applicants have an inalienable and indefinite right to the use of wood (Einforstungsrecht) from certain plots of land now owned by the Republic of Austria and managed by the Austrian Federal Forestry Administration. In 1870 and 1876 the applicant's predecessors were granted the right to exchange their right to use the wood for ownership of the land. On 6 September 1978 the first applicant and Jakob Bachmayer, the second applicant's legal predecessor, requested this exchange. In 1985 the Salzburg Office of the Regional Governor in its capacity as Agricultural Authority (Amt der Landesregierung als Agrarbehörde) dismissed the request. On 30 April 1986, they filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) On 2 July 1986 the Supreme Land Reform Board dismissed the request. On 16 January 1991, the second applicant and Mr Jakob Bachmayer concluded a contract on the transfer of the rights of the latter to the second applicants. On 15 April 1992, after having held oral hearings in 1991 and 1992 the Regional Board, in a partial decision, dismissed the appeal against the Office of the Regional Governor of 27 June 1985 as regards “count 2” of the decision and also determined a new amount of compensation. On 21 February 1996 the applicants again requested a transfer of jurisdictions concerning their appeal against ‘count 1 lit.a’ and ‘lit.b’ The Austrian Federal Forestry Administration lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court on 31 January 2003. The Constitutional Court held that the legal provision under review was not in accordance with the Federal Constitution. On 7 November 2005 the Supreme Land Reform Board, quashed the Office of the Regional Governor's decision of 27 June 1985 and remitted the case back to that authority. The applicants filed a complaint against that decision. On 6 June 2006 the Constitutional court declined to deal with the applicants' complaint for lack of prospects of success and, upon their request, transferred the case to the Administrative Court. The case is still pending before that court and the applicants are seeking a review of the decision.

The fact that a prisoner is being released for educational or other purposes does not affect consideration of the merits of his application or remove the need for the normal criteria to be met. (2) Hearsay information may therefore afford a constable reasonable grounds to arrest, and such information may come from other officers. The applicants were born in Pakistan in 1985 and 1986 respectively and live in Oslo. In 1989 the applicants arrived in Norway with their mother and were in view of the children’s particular situation granted a residence permit on 28 February 1992. During the summer of 1992 the mother returned with the children to Pakistan, where the children first lived with their grandparents and then with their father and his wife. There they stayed until the turn of the year 1995‑1996, when the mother resettled in Norway. In the meantime, on 2 August 1995 the Directorate of Immigration had granted them a settlement permit, while being ignorant about their stay in Pakistan from 1992.

The first and second applicants, who are sister and brother, were born in Pakistan in 1985 and 1986 respectively and live in Oslo. In 1989 the applicants arrived in Norway with their mother and were in view of the children’s particular situation granted a residence permit on 28 February 1992. In 1996 the applicants’ father applied for family reunification. His application, which was refused, prompted an investigation by the immigration authorities which revealed that the applicants and their mother had lived in Pakistan from 1992 to 1996. On 23 January 1999 the Directorate of Immigration decided to withdraw the applicants' and their mothers’ settlement permit. Several successive requests for reconsideration were rejected. In May 2001 the children were apprehended with a view to being deported to Pakistan.

The applicants arrived in Norway with their mother in 1989. They were granted a residence permit on 28 February 1992 on the ground of strong humanitarian considerations. In August 1995 the Directorate of Immigration granted them a settlement permit, while being ignorant about their stay in Pakistan from 1992. In May 2001 the children were apprehended with a view to being deported to Pakistan. The police considered that it would be inappropriate to expel them without their mother who had disappeared around the turn of the year 2000‑2001. The applicants had no contacts with the mother until she was hospitalised in Norway in 2004. They lived with an uncle and aunt in Oslo during this period. On 24 November 2003 the second applicant was convicted for unprovoked aggravated physical assault.

In May 2005 the Immigration Appeals Board decided to expel him indefinitely, with reference to section 29(1)(c) of the 1988 Immigration Act, as he had been convicted for an offence that was punishable by more than three months’ imprisonment. The applicants alleged that their deportation from Norway to Pakistan would entail a violation of their rights under Article 8. The application was communicated to the Government on 7 June 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1).I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE were: The first and second applicants, who are sister and brother, were born in Pakistan in 1985 and 1986 respectively and live in Oslo. The children were granted a residence permit in Norway on the ground of strong humanitarian considerations. The children were apprehended with a view to being deported to Pakistan. The police considered that it would be inappropriate to expel them without their mother who had disappeared around the turn of the year 2000‑2001. The applicants had no contacts with their mother until she was hospitalised in Norway in 2004. During this period they lived with an uncle and aunt in Oslo. It was observed that when the settlement permit was revoked in 1999, the applicants had in reality resided unlawfully in Norway for three years. At that time they had close relatives in Pakistan, including their father, with whom they had lived for periods a few years before. Nor did the High Court find against the applicants. The application claims deportation would constitute a violation of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. The applicants argue that the decision of 13 October 2005 regarding the second applicant was disproportionate. The application was struck out of the Court’s list of cases on 6 February 2008. The Immigration Appeals Board rejected the applicants’ requests for modification of the decisions of 23 August 1999 revoking their settlement (and residence) permit and 31 May 2005 to expel him indefinitely from Norway. A Committee of three judges decided to strike the application from the Court's list of. cases (Article 37 § 1 of the convention) The application also asks for an interim measure to stay their deportation under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. Oslo City Court quashed the Immigration Appeals Board’s decision of 31 August 2007, disagreeing with its assessment that the applicants lacked special attachment to Norway. With the exception of May 2001, no active steps had been taken to implement the decision to expel the applicants and no attempts had been made to this effect pending the judicial proceedings, until the autumn of 2007. The City Court further observed that in Norway the applicants had close relatives – uncles and aunts – and had lived with these since 2001. The applicants had gone to school in Norway, had friends and acquaintances there and were mastering the Norwegian language, both oral and written. The applicants had not had contact with their father since 1996 and did not wish to have any contact with him. They were able to speak Urdu and to understand the language in oral form but could not read or write it. The State appealed to the Borgarting High Court, which overturned the City Court’s ruling by a judgment of 14 November 2008. The High Court found it clear that the refusal to grant residence permits constituted an interference with the applicants’ rights under paragraph 1 of Article 8 of the Convention. In considering whether the interference was justified under paragraph 2, the central question was whether the measure was ‘necessary in a democratic society’ The applicants had been dependent on the assistance of the Norwegian authorities to obtain passports until passing the age of majority in 2003 and 2004. The High Court found it hardly probable that the applicants had no contacts with their mother and had no knowledge of her whereabouts from 2001 until the summer of 2005. It was difficult to ascribe any responsibility to the applicants for not having taken any steps to leave the country while the mother had gone into hiding from the police. The applicants’ choice to stay in Norway had been something for which they ought to bear the risk and responsibility. The High Court, nonetheless, with doubt, arrived at the conclusion that the refusal of residence had not been unlawful as being contrary to Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It also observed that in the experience of the Immigration Appeals Board, it was rare that one was confronted with cases where the duration of the unlawful stay had been nearly as long as the present case. The applicants' strong attachment to Norway had been established during unlawful residence, that they still had links to their home place in Pakistan and that they as adults had relatively good possibilities for settling in Pakistan. On 5 September 1993 he had raped E.P., had beaten and strangled her, had forced her to swallow drugs, had burned her skin with cigarettes and had cut her vagina with a knife causing a deep laceration as well as opening the abdominal cavity. In assessing the penalty, the court considered as mitigating circumstances the applicant’s partial confession and that he had acted under the influence of alcohol and drugs. The applicant did not request to attend the hearings before the Supreme Court or the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) The Supreme Court, sitting in private, rejected as inadmissible the applicant’s plea of nullity. The applicant received a notification which stated that he, being detained, could only appear through his counsel and would not be brought to the court as the conditions of Section 296 § 3 [Section 294 § 5] of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung) were not fulfilled. On 18 December 1996, after having held a hearing in the absence of the applicant but in the presence of his defence counsel, dismissed the appeal against the sentence.

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 41516/10 and 75702/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two British nationals, Mr Charles Bernard O’Neill and Mr William Hugh Lauchlan (“the applicants”) were convicted for various sexual offences. Both applicants were placed on the Sexual Offenders’ Register. The applicants’ complaints concerning the length of their criminal proceedings were communicated to the Government on 13 November 2012 and 17 December 2012 respectively. The initial investigation was launched on 16 February 1998 when R.M. reported his ex-wife, A.M, missing. The applicants travelled to Spain without notification, thereby breaching the terms of their parole licence in contravention of the Sex Offenders Act 1997. The Scottish Executive subsequently revoked their licences. In 2004 they were arrested in Spain in connection with the apparent abduction of a 14 year old boy. They were returned to the United Kingdom, where they were recalled to prison to serve the unexpired portion of their licence periods. On 5 April 2005 a decision was made by the Procurator Fiscal to place both applicants on petition in relation to the murder of A.M. The applicants’ had subsequently killed her and disposed of her body. They pled guilty and on 4 April 2005 they were sentenced to a further three years’ imprisonment. The applicants were charged with the murder of A.M. and with concealing and disposing of her body in an attempt to pervert the course of justice. On 6 June 2005 the Crown Office provisionally fixed a preliminary hearing date for 12 September 2005. That hearing date was set aside as the first applicant lodged a “devolution minute’ (see paragraphs 51-52 below) relating to a potential violation of the reasonable time guarantee contained within Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 14 October 2005 the Sheriff Court held that the devolution minute had been raised prematurely as no indictment had been served. On 26 April 2006 the applicants were informed that there would be ‘no proceedings meantime’ Crown Counsel concluded that there had been a material change in the prospects of securing a conviction against both applicants on the murder charges contained in the 2005 petition. Central Scotland Police formed ‘Operation Aspen’, the objective of which was to look for evidence both of further sexual offending by the applicants, and of their involvement in the disappearance of A.M. The applicants were granted permission to appeal, but their appeal was refused on 5 June 2009. The High Court found that the Crown had acted properly in investigating and reviewing the evidence between 1997 and 2008; that the expiry of the section 65 time-limit had come about through a positive decision rather than through inadvertence. The applicants were convicted of murder and attempting to pervert the course of justice. They were sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, with a tariff of thirty years for the first applicant and twenty-six years for second applicant. Both applicants unsuccessfully sought to appeal against conviction and sentence. The applicants’ trials took place between 19 April 2010 and 13 May 2010. The first applicant also argued that the murder charge against him should be dismissed for reason of delay. However, the court refused to dismiss the charge, finding, inter alia, that proceedings had begun on 5 April 2005; that the “reasonable time” permitted by Article 6 had not been exceeded; and that there was no other compelling reason why it would be unfair to proceed. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. The first applicant lodged a Note of Appeal on 2 September 2010, containing numerous grounds and sub-grounds on a wide range of issues regarding all the charges. The sifting judges granted him leave to appeal against his sentence for murder, but not against his conviction. The applicants subsequently applied under section 107(8) of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 (“the 1995 Act”) for leave to reinstate grounds which the sifts judges had found to be unarguable, including those relating to the length of proceedings. The main issue before the Supreme Court was whether the applicants could be said to have been “charged” on 17 September 1998 or whether the appropriate “starting point” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 was 5 April 2005. Supreme Court observed that as the “fair trial’ guarantee under Article 6 was distinct from the ‘reasonable-time” guarantee it had to be approached separately. Court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the first applicant’s appeal against conviction and sentence on 27 March 2014, and the second applicant's appeal on 19 June 2014. The case was heard by the Supreme Court in London and concluded on 6 November 2013. The applicants were found not guilty of the alleged offence and convicted of two counts of perverting the course of justice.
