The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that there was no public hearing in the succession proceedings. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 26 June 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Court ruled that the case was not admissible and that the application was not part of the succession process.

The applicant was born in 1937 and lives in Mank/Austria. A.A., the applicant's brother, died on 1 December 1988. On 23 December 1998 the competent court was informed about A.'s death and, subsequently, appointed a notary public as court commissioner (Gerichtskommissär). On 22 and 23 February 1989 the applicant and eight other persons entitled to the estate of A. made conditional declarations of acceptance of succession (bedingte Erbserklärung) The applicant's sister M. argued that the farm was a hereditary one (Erbhof) within the meaning of the Agricultural Succession Act 1958.

The applicant was born in 1937 and lives in Mank/Austria. A.A., the applicant's brother, died on 1 December 1988. He had been a farmer and the owner of a farm. The applicant and eight other persons entitled to the estate of A. made conditional declarations of acceptance of succession (bedingte Erbserklärung) On 28 December 1989 the Ybbs District Court found that the farm did not qualify as a hereditary one because it could not provide a living for five adults as required under the applicable law. On 9 January 1990 the applicant appealed. On 18 October 1990 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeals and upheld the Regional Court's finding.

The applicant was born in 1937 and lives in Mank/Austria. He had been a farmer and the owner of a farm. The applicant's sister argued that the farm was a hereditary one (Erbhof) within the meaning of the Agricultural Succession Act 1958 (Anerbengesetz) A.A. died on 1 December 1988. On 2 October 1989 the applicant requested to be appointed as principal heir. The Ybbs District Court (Bezirksgericht) found on 28 December 1989 the farm did not qualify as hereditary.

Five parties appealed the decision in 1991. An estate curator was appointed and the succession proceedings were suspended. The applicant appealed and submitted a new private expert opinion. The case was dismissed by the District Court in 1994 and again by the Regional Court in 1995. In 1997 the applicant submitted a private expert opinions and requested to discuss it at an hearing. The District Court held a further hearing on 5 February 1996. The application was rejected on 12 August 1997. The farm was sold to a private company in 1998. The owner of the farm is now the owner of another hereditary farm, which he has been trying to sell for several years. He has also unsuccessfully tried to sell the other hereditary farm.

Five parties appealed the decision of the District Court on 17 October 1991. The Supreme Court dismissed an appeal on points of law and confirmed that the Agricultural Succession Act 1958 was applicable. As the parties of the hereditary proceedings did not reach an agreement, an estate curator (Verlassenschaftskurator) was appointed and the succession proceedings were suspended. The applicant appealed and submitted a new private expert opinion and requested to discuss it at an hearing in 1997. On 10 August 1995 the file was transmitted to the notary public. Thereafter, it obtained further expert reports and the applicant commented repeatedly on these reports and repeatedly requested further opinions.

The farm was ruled to be a hereditary one under the Agricultural Succession Act 1958. An estate curator (Verlassenschaftskurator) was appointed and the succession proceedings were suspended. The applicant appealed and submitted a new private expert opinion. The case was heard by the District Court, which dismissed the applicant's request to be appointed as principal heir in 1993. The District Court again dismissed the request and appointed M. as principal heirs in 1995. The application was dismissed in 1997 and the file was sent to the public notary public. The decision was quashed on 12 July 1995 and the case was reopened in 1996.

The applicant asked to hear further experts. The court-appointed expert commented on the private expert opinion. The applicant's appeal was dismissed on points of law on 10 June 1999. This decision was served on the applicant's lawyer on 14 July 1999. The application was rejected on the grounds that the court's expert had commented in detail on a private opinion submitted by the applicant. The appeal was also dismissed on the basis that the expert could not impugn the plausibility of the opinion of the court- appointed expert. The case was settled in the High Court of Justice of the Kingdom of Belgium. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant and the ruling was upheld in the Supreme Court.

The applicant asked to hear further experts. The court-appointed expert commented on the private expert opinion. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law on 14 July 1999. The applicant was named as principal heir in the will, but was not appointed as principal beneficiary.

The applicant asked to hear further experts. The court-appointed expert commented on the private expert opinion. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law on 10 June 1999. This decision was served on the applicant and his lawyer on 14 July 1999. The application was dismissed on the grounds that it did not meet the legal requirements to be a principal heir. The applicant was awarded £200,000 in damages. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights in London in 1998. The High Court of Justice ruled in favour of the applicant on 13 May 1998. It dismissed the appeal on 14 March 1999, saying that the applicant had not shown that his claim was founded in law. The appeal was dismissed again on 15 March 1999.

Four men were discharged from the armed forces for their sexual orientation. The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise” He concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. The primary decision was for him and the secondary judgment amounted to asking whether a reasonable Minister, on the material before him, could have reasonably made that primary judgment.

He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, ‘I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise’ The court concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. The primary decision was for him and the secondary judgment amounted to asking whether a reasonable Minister, on the material before him, could have reasonably made that primary judgment.

All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In none of the cases before him was it suggested that the applicants’ sexual orientation had in any way affected their ability to carry out their work or had any ill-effect on discipline. The Chamber declared the applications admissible and, while it retained the joinder of the present applications, it decided to disjoin them from the above-mentioned Smith and Grady cases. It was also decided to hold a hearing on the merits of the case. On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. Mr Lustig-Prean joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. He was involved in a steady relationship with a civilian partner for about 30 months prior to June 1994. The applicant admitted to his commanding officer that he was homosexual. He had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. He agreed to be interviewed by the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. For confidential support on suicide matters call the Samaritans on 08457 909090, visit a local Samaritans branch or click here for details. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. In 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. The applicant’s report dated 27 November 1992 noted that he displayed potential in a number of areas essential to good leadership. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. He was then called for interview by the service police. The applicant immediately confirmed his homosexuality, later clarifying that he first had “niggling doubts” about his sexual Orientation approximately two and a half years previously. The interview was suspended pending the search. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett”. That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) along with Ms Smith and Mr Grady obtained leave to apply for judicial review. Four homosexuals were discharged by the Ministry of Defence because of their sexual orientation. Lord Justice Simon Brown LJ dismissed the application for judicial review. He said the tide of history was against the MoD and the policy could not survive. He added that the court had to be scrupulous to ensure that no recognised ground of challenge was in truth available to an applicant before rejecting the application. He concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. The primary decision was for him. The secondary judgment of the court amounted to asking whether a reasonable Minister, on the material before him, could have reasonably made that primary judgment. Simon Brown LJ found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the forces. The applications had to be rejected “albeit with hesitation and regret”. The judge said that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’s obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. He said that, even where the most fundamental human rights were being restricted, “the threshold of unreasonableness is not lowered” In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. It was indicated that the case was likely to progress to the European courts. The applicants in the judicial review proceedings had argued that the MoD’s position was “bereft of factual evidence” but that this was not surprising since evidence was difficult to amass given that homosexuals were not permitted to serve. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment. The Master of the Rolls noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind. He considered that the greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. While the court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ He concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and, in particular, with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. It was important to highlight this point since Parliament had not given the domestic courts primary jurisdiction over human rights issues contained in the Convention. In December 1995 Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Those proceedings were adjourned pending the above-described application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In December 1997 Mr Beckett also issued proceedings claiming sexual discrimination Contrary to the 1975 Act. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial tribunal. The applicants’ Industrial Tribunal proceedings can be found on the Tribunal’s website.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13229/03) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 27 September 2005 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section. On 11 July 2006 a Chamber composed of the same judges delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of Article 5. The applicant and the Government each filed their observations on the merits. In addition, third-party comments were received jointly from the AIRE Centre and the European Council on Human Rights. The applicant, an Iraqi Kurd, was born in 1976 and now lives and works as a doctor in London. He fled the Kurdish Autonomous Region of Iraq when, in the course of his duties as a hospital doctor, he treated and facilitated the escape of three fellow members of the Iraqi Workers' Communist Party. He arrived at Heathrow Airport on 30 December 2000 and immediately claimed asylum. The immigration officer contacted the Oakington Reception Centre (“Oakington”, see paragraphs 23-25 below) but there was no immediate room there, so the applicant was granted “temporary admission” (see paragraphs 20-21 below) The applicant met at Oakington with a lawyer from the Refugee Legal Centre, who contacted the Home Office to enquire why the applicant was being detained and to request his release. When refused, the applicant applied for judicial review of the decision to detain him. The following day he was released and again granted temporary admission pending the determination of his appeal. On 14 January 2003 his appeal was allowed and he was granted asylum. The judicial review proceedings were heard at the Court of Appeal on 7 September 2001 (R.C. v. Saadi and others) (EWHC Admin 670) Collins J found that the Secretary of State had such a power to detain under the Immigration Act 1971 (see paragraph 19 below) Appeal court ruled in favour of detention of asylum-seeker. Lord Phillips of Worth Matravers, Master of the Rolls, gave the lead judgment. Court of Appeal unanimously overturned this judgment on 19 October 2001. Appeal ruled that the applicant had not been given adequate reasons for his detention. The average monthly number of applications from July to September 1999 was nearly 7,000. This was 60% higher than the previous year. Coping with huge numbers of Asylum-seekers posed heavy administrative problems. ‘No responsible government can simply shrug their shoulders and do nothing’ ... A short period of detention designed to ensure that the regime operates without dislocation. House of Lords unanimously dismissed the applicant’s appeal. Court of Appeal next considered whether the detention fell within the first limb of Article 5 § 1 (f), and held that the right to liberty was intended to preserve the sovereign power of member States to decide whether to allow aliens to enter their territories on any terms whatsoever. Detention of an alien would be covered by the sub-paragraph unless and until entry was authorised, subject to the proviso, derived from Chahal v. the United Kingdom (15 November 1996, Reports 1996-V), that the asylum or deportation procedure should not be prolonged unreasonably. Lord Slynn of Hadley: “In my view it is clear that detention to achieve a quick process of decision-making is not of itself necessarily and in all cases unlawful” The. power to detain is to ‘prevent’ unauthorised entry. In my opinion until the State has ‘authorised’ entry the entry is un authorised. The State has power to detained without violating Article 5 until the application has been considered and the entry ‘ authorised�’ ... There remains the issue whether, even if detention does fall within Article 5 (1) (f), ‘detention was unlawful on grounds of being a disproportionate response to the reasonable requirements of immigration control’ The need for highly structured and tightly managed arrangements, which would be disrupted by late[ness] or non-attendance of the applicant for interview, is apparent.

If they were to be required in each case, no covert listening would ever be realistic or possible,’ he added. ‘The weight of his loss of privacy is another matter which I may take into account.’ The applicant together with three others was convicted on 20 July 2000 of various robbery and firearms offences. Lord Woolf CJ said: “The complaints of the appellants with regard to the decision of the judge are not to the relevance of the contents of the tape. They were clearly highly relevant. ... On the evidence there were proper grounds for the arrests and ignoring the fact that the police were working to an overall plan, there was nothing improper about the purpose for which the arrests took place. ... This was a situation where thePolice were responding reasonably and proportionately to a very serious threat to the safety of the public and law and order" The Court of Appeal certified a question for consideration by the House of Lords concerning use of evidence obtained by an arrest for the purpose of eavesdropping on the defendant. eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mark William Grayson and John Barnham, on 20 May 2005 and 10 April 2006 respectively. Each applicant alleged that, in confiscation proceedings following his conviction for drugs offences, the fact that the legal burden of proof was on him to show that he did not have realisable assets equivalent to the benefit figure offended the basic principles of a fair procedure. The Court decided to examine the merits of each application at the same time as its admissibility. It also decided to join the applications. The judge found that the applicant had been the principal participant in the offence and must have contributed to a large extent to the purchase of the drugs. The judge was further satisfied that so large a consignment would not have represented the applicant’s first venture into drug trafficking and that he had financed the purchase with the proceeds of previous drug dealing. The final item of expenditure taken into account by the judge was GBP 70,000 which an associate of the applicant, who claimed to have an income of approximately GBP 40,000 a year, had paid for the applicant's legal fees. He concluded that the. applicant had benefited to the amount of GBP 1,230,748.69. Police had found realisable assets of GBP 236,000, including cash found on the applicant at the time of his arrest, a car and some business stock. The judge observed: “The fact that the police have traced a certain amount of property is not of itself a reason to find it is the only property available to the [applicant]. Also credibility is a real issue. This Defendant is cunning, devious and intelligent. Giving evidence he sought to mislead at every turn, wary that the truth would reveal assets he didn’t want to and that he had hidden assets prior to conviction. He has lied persistently and blatantly and his credibility is nil’ Court of Appeal referred to Phillips v. the United Kingdom, no. 41087/98, ECHR 2001-VII, and observed that: “In that case the court held that the reverse onus of proof in relation to the statutory assumption at the calculation of the benefit stage is fully Convention compliant” The second applicant (Mr Barnham) was convicted of two conspiracy charges involving plans to import large consignments of cannabis into the UK. The Court added that although the accountancy report raised a suggestion of possible double-counting by the prosecution, that was “irrelevant, since the judge’s order did not depend upon any calculation of realisable property” The judge ruled that the total benefit to the applicant was GBP 1,525,615. This sum included GBP 27,000 that the applicant had given to Murray to establish his trust; various amounts totalling GBP 59,000. The applicant claimed to have been entirely unsuccessful in his attempts at drug dealing and to have earned a living by singing in bars. His car, worth GBP 11,615, had also been confiscated by the Portuguese authorities. The defence submitted that there was no evidence capable of supporting a finding of assumed ‘hidden’ assets and such would lead to a risk of injustice. The judge made his ruling on 12 April 2002. Judge found that the applicant and his wife had lied about their activities and their sources of income. He made a confiscation order equal to the amount which he had assessed as the benefit, namely GBP 1,525,615, with five years, three months’ imprisonment if the applicant had not paid within 18 months. The applicant appealed against the judge’s ruling regarding his realisable assets, asserting that Article 6 of the 1994 Act was ‘contrary to the scheme laid down by the1994 Act’ The judge made a decision in favour of confiscating the assets and imposing a sentence of up to five years in prison. The Court of Appeal rejected the argument that there was a difference between cases where the prosecution had proved benefit by evidence and cases where it had used assumptions. Once the prosecution has established the benefit there is no requirement on it to provide a prima facie case. At the second stage the burden of proof shifts to a defendant to establish, if he can, his realisable assets to the satisfaction of the court. The expression ‘hidden assets’ is indicative of the fact that the prosecution can have no means of knowing how and where a defendant may have dealt with or disposed of the proceeds of his criminal activities. It is designed to enable the court to confiscate a criminal’s ill-gotten gains. The Court of Appeal refused to certify a point of law of general public importance for appeal to the House of Lords concerning Article 6 of the Convention. The case has been referred to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, as a matter of 'urgent concern' The case was referred to as a 'matter of public importance' by the European court of human rights. The court of appeal ruled that the appeal was not of 'general public importance', and referred the case back to the Court of appeal. The appeal was dismissed as being of no public importance, and the case was thrown out of court by the Supreme Court of Justice.

He complained that his trial was unfair because of the non-disclosure of the sources of the evidence of a Chief Superintendent without adequate counterbalancing measures. The application was communicated to the Government on 4 January 2012. The Irish Human Rights Commission, which had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party, made submissions to the Court. The applicant was born in 1978 and has a permanent address in Dublin. The Nissan Almera remained on the estate parked near the Transit van. One of the men walked away from the group while four of them got into the back of the van and one into the driver’s seat. The five men of the original eight who remained in the estate, and who were in the Ford Transit van, were arrested and charged with being members of an illegal organisation. During police investigations, the Nissan Micra car which had left Corke Abbey after dropping a man named O’Snodaigh was found to have false registration plates. The owner of the car was later identified as MB. The trial court later regarded the items as “ significant pieces of evidence” see § 11 below. The applicant was arrested under section 30 of the Offences against the State Act 1939, as amended (“the 1939 Act’). He was brought to the police station where he was questioned about membership, contrary to section 21 of the 1939 Act, of an unlawful organisation (the Irish Republican Army, “IRA”). The applicant did not make a statement and was released from custody. On 30 October 2002 he was arrested on suspicion that, on 10 October 2002, he was a member of the IRA. He and a co-accused (NB) were interviewed at length by police officers. Numerous questions were put to them concerning the events in Corke Abbey and the evidence gathered by the police. Chief Superintendent testified that he believed the applicant was a member of the IRA. He claimed privilege stating that disclosure would endanger lives and State security. The SCC found that, while it was unthinkable that information that would threaten lives or State security would be disclosed, the admission of PK’s evidence without any inquiry into its basis would unfairly balance the trial in favour of the prosecution. The accused, it held, was entitled to some enquiry into the basis of PK's testimony. The trial court considered the first strand, which comprised the evidence of a Chief Superintendent who testified that, on 10 October 2002, the applicant had been involved in unlawful activity at Corke Abbey. The Chief Superintendent asserted that the accused were members of the IRA. The Court conducted a review of those files considering this to be the most appropriate solution in the interests of justice. It found that there was nothing in the files that would assist the defence in proving the innocence of their clients. Later, in weighing PK’s evidence, the SCC confirmed that it had excluded any information to which it had become privy during its review of the files he had produced to the court. The SCC totally rejected a suggestion put to the Chief Superintendent PK, in cross-examination that his evidence was a fiction. It was difficult to imagine anyone better informed on the subject in the country. The trial court held that the demands of justice required that it should not convict solely on the basis of PK's evidence. The SCC considered that the above evidence showed that both accused were aware of, or acquiesced in, unlawful activities in Corke Abbey. However, it was of the view that those activities could equally be ascribed to persons engaged in organised crime as opposed to those engaged in subversive crime. Appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal (“CCA”) was refused leave to appeal. The CCA found no evidence that would have assisted the accused and the material examined constituted a good basis for the belief of the Chief Superintendent. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 11 December 1995. It originated in three applications (nos. 21627/93, 21826/93 and 21974/93) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 14 December 1992. The late Mr Laskey’s father and the two other applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President. Rights International, a New York-based non-governmental human rights organisation, was granted leave to submit written comments on specified aspects of the case. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. The applicants, with several other men, were charged with a series of offences, including assault and wounding, relating to sado-masochistic activities that had taken place over a ten-year period. The acts consisted in the main of maltreatment of the genitalia (with, for example, hot wax, sandpaper, fish hooks and needles) and ritualistic beatings. The activities took place at a number of locations, including rooms equipped as torture chambers. Video cameras were used to record events and the tapes copied and distributed amongst members of the group. Mr Laskey was sentenced to imprisonment for four years and six months. Mr Jaggard received two years’ imprisonment for aiding and abetting unlawful wounding - contrary to section 20 of the 1861 Act (see paragraph 25 below) - and a further twelve months' imprisonment for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, aiding and. abetting the same offence, and unlawful wounding. The trial judge commented that the unlawful conduct would be dealt with equally in the prosecution of heterosexuals or bisexuals if carried out by them. The homosexuality of the defendants is only the background against which the case must be viewed. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. The appeal, known as the case of R. v. Brown ([1993] 2 All England Law Reports 75), was dismissed by a majority of the House of Lords. Lord Templeman, in the majority, held after reviewing the case-law that: “... the authorities dealing with the intentional infliction of bodily harm do not establish that consent is a defence to a charge under the Act of 1861’” The question is whether the defence should be extended to the infliction Of bodily harm in the course of sado-masochistic encounters. The applicants argued that consent should provide a defence ... because it was said every person has a right to deal with his own body as he chooses. Lord Jauncey of Tullichettle found that: ‘In my view the line falls properly to be drawn between assault at common law and the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm created by section 47 of the 1861 Act’ He said: “I am not prepared to invent a defence of consent for sado-masochistic encounters which breed and glorify cruelty ... Society is entitled and bound to protect itself against a cult of violence. Pleasure derived from the infliction of pain is an evil thing. Cruelty is uncivilised.“ The Lord Chief Justice said that the decision on whether or not to ban the practice must now be taken. There is no suggestion that they and their associates are the only practitioners of homosexual sado-masochism in England and Wales. Wounds can easily become septic if not properly treated, the free flow of blood from a person who is HIV-positive or who has AIDS can infect another. An inflicter who is carried away by sexual excitement or by drink or drugs could very easily inflict pain and injury beyond the level to which the receiver had consented. The possibility of proselytisation and corruption of young men is a real danger even in the case of these appellants. The taking of video recordings of such activities suggests that secrecy may not be as strict as the appellants claimed to your Lordships. Lord Slynn of Hadley found that as the law stood adults were able to consent to acts done in private which did not result in serious bodily harm. He agreed that it was in the end a matter of policy in an area where social and moral factors were extremely important and where attitudes could change. It was however for the legislature to decide whether such conduct should be brought within the criminal law and not for the courts. All the applicants lost their jobs and Mr Jaggard required extensive psychiatric treatment. The case was settled out of court in a settlement which was agreed to by the Crown Prosecution Service and all those involved were ordered to pay compensation.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 June 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr W. Okresek, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs E. Schindler, Federal Ministry of Justice. The Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to hold the hearing at Garsten Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. The hearing list was distributed by the public prosecutor's office to the media, namely to the most important national and regional newspapers. The Government were unable to provide the list for the week of 29 January 1996, as these lists are not kept, but asserted that it would, in accordance with the usual practice, have indicated Garsten Prison. The applicant, assisted by counsel, pleaded not guilty. Neither the applicant nor his counsel complained about a lack of publicity at that time. Following the hearing, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of threatening behaviour and sentenced him to ten months' imprisonment. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe). He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison, to which only people with special permits, other than prison personnel, had access. The Court of Appeal had no doubts regarding the Regional Court's evaluation of the evidence and its establishment of the facts. It found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The appellate court also confirmed the legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. The hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. Had the prison governor been concerned that interested persons should not be granted access to the closed area, he would have be obliged to prohibit the conduct of the trial in that part of the prison. In any case, no such persons wishing to attend the trial had been present at the beginning of the hearing.

The President of the Court gave the lawyer in question leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. The applicant was a German national who was born in 1939. The relevant municipal authorities required him to pay a fire service levy (Feuerwehrabgabe) of 75 German marks (DM) for 1982. This decision was based on section 43 of the Land Fire Brigades Act, as amended on 27 November 1978. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig, Mr Vögtle, Mr Weitzel and Mr Olbrich. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1994. On 7 February 1994 the Commission produced various documents as requested by the Registrar on the President's instructions. The Administrative Court of the District of Constance dismissed the appeal in 1982. The case was referred to the Constitutional Court of Germany. The Constitutional Court ruled that the obligation for men to pay was compatible with the Constitution. The Administrative Court could not persuade it to reconsider its case-law. The court's decision was upheld on appeal in 1986. The appeal was dismissed on appeal again on September 6, 1998. The matter was referred back to the Federal Constitutional Court for review. The decision was made to reject the appeal on October 18, 1998, and the case was settled in favour of the Administrative Court on September 20, 1999. The Court of Appeals ruled in favor of the decision on September 18, 1999, and it was upheld in October, 2000. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the appeal for adjudication, on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. It noted, inter alia, that the court had already held, in its judgment of 17 October 1961, that there had been no violation of the principle of equal treatment. The fact that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to the male residents of a municipality still continued to be objectively justified on account of the risks inherent in service. Some fire brigade duties were performed by women and recently fire brigades for female volunteers had even been set up. The sole decisive factor is that there remain today objective reasons (Anknüpfungspunkte) on the basis of which the legislature is entitled to treat men and women differently.

The applicants had felt harassed in Kosovo because of their being Roma, but they had not been subjected to any persecution, allegedly due to their isolation. They applied for asylum and permanent residence permits on arrival. On 13 March 2008 the Migration Board (Migrationsverket) rejected their applications. The Board found that neither the general situation in Kosovo nor that in Serbia was such that it in itself constituted grounds for granting asylum. Also, the Board found the applicants were not to be considered as refugees or as in need of any other specific protection. In regard to the applicants’ Roma ethnicity, the board noted that the first applicant’s mother was Serb, that none of the family members spoke Romani or had any contact with other Roma. In Kosovo, they had lived in Serb areas and had only socialised with Serbs. The Board found that the medical certificate did not contain any diagnosis and that it therefore could not assess whether or not the applicant could receive appropriate medical care in Kosovo or Serbia. The Board noted that treatment for depression was offered both in Kosovo and Serbia. It further noted that the applicant’s health had not improved after he had received treatment in Sweden and that his condition would probably only improve if he were in a more secure and stable environment. The applicants submitted that they had been subjected to persecution in Kosovo due to their ethnicity and that this had caused their health problems. The Migration Court of Appeal quashed the lower court’s judgment and granted him a permanent residence permit. The other applicants were all in better health and should be granted a right to stay, according to the court's ruling. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 12 March 1999. It originated in an application (27052/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government”) lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant is represented by Ms Mary Cunneen of Liberty. The Government of the United UK are represented by their Agent, Mr Martin Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The Commission's request referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the United States recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46) The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 October 1999. The Court heard addresses by Mr Cranston and Mr Emmerson and also their replies to questions put by several of its members. The applicant was serving a prison sentence. The background to his conviction is as follows. On 30 June 1993 approximately three tonnes of cannabis resin was imported into the United Kingdom concealed in a consignment of frozen meat on a lorry travelling from Zeebrugge to Dover. There had been two previous importations of meat from the same consignor in May and early June 1993, both of which had been collected by a firm of hauliers called Davidsons. Six of the ten pallets of meat were still on the lorry in a frozen state, although the refrigerator motor was not operative. Four of the pallets, containing a large quantity of cannabis resin, had been opened and left to defrost in the unrefrigerated garage. The applicant told Customs officers that he worked as a haulage contractor and had not known that the meat contained cannabis. The prosecution made an ex parte application to the trial judge to withhold material in its possession on the grounds of public interest immunity. The trial judge examined the material in question and ruled that it should not be disclosed. The defence were not informed of the reasons for the judge's decision. Prosecution counsel provided the answer to questions 9(iii) and (vi), informing the defence that there had been no such observations and no ‘information received’ from an informant. The defence therefore applied to the trial judge for an order that the prosecution should provide the information requested. The application was heard on 24 January 1994, when prosecution counsel submitted: “I have refused and still refuse to answer the questions set out in ... paragraph 9” The position was upheld by the trialJudge who, in his ruling of 24 January1994, ruled that the ex parte application should not be the subject of any ex-parte application. The applicant did not give evidence at his trial. The defence case was that he had no knowledge of the cannabis hidden in the consignment and was acting as an innocent haulier of the goods. On 31 January 1994 the applicant was convicted of the offence charged and on 21 March 1994 he was sentenced to ten years' imprisonment. The Court of Appeal found that the Crown had not disclosed information that might have led to the applicant being able to trace those who had involved him in a smuggling enterprise. The applicant appealed to the Court of appeal, on the following grounds: “It was clear that not all unused material had been disclosed. ... It was plain from the course of the argument that the ex parte application had not dealt with the unused material’ The Court of Appeal declined to order the disclosure of either to the defence of Mr Jasper. The application was made, correctly, on the ground that if the matters which emerged during the ex parte hearing are relevant, or likely to have been relevant, to Mr Jasper, he should be permitted to have sight of the ruling and the transcript of the proceedings which took place on that occasion. We have read the record and it seems ... that the learned judge ... knew precisely the scope of the application and listened with the greatest possible care. He tested those matters, and he came to the conclusion that the ruling which he made was appropriate in all the circumstances.” Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal on 28 March 1995. First ground of appeal, namely the non-disclosure of relevant evidence, was rejected. Court continued: “This was a case of enormous strength so far as the prosecution were concerned. The appellant had been caught red handed with a huge amount of cannabis resin. He was exercising a proprietorial form of control over the packages’ contents. By opening them he was allowing what were ostensibly their sole contents to defreeze, with a risk (to put it no higher) of their becoming valueless.” It is difficult, if not impossible, to see what other inference than that he was indeed guilty of the offence charged any reasonable jury could have reached.

The applicant did not suggest that he was advised by his lawyer not to comment but said that he did not want to incriminate people in relation to stolen vehicles. He admits that he failed to mention any of the facts to which I have just referred, when he was interviewed and he says his reason for that, was that although well knowing that others had been arrested for the much more serious offence of armed robbery, as he had been, he didn't want to implicate them. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) The jury found the applicant guilty of the offences charged and he was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The judge noted that he was satisfied that Mr Adetoro was involved in the sixth robbery and ignored his assertion he was with Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson at the material time. He was a 'rather clever and determined liar' and his alibi 'fell apart' The judge was not prepared to place reliance on anything he said and made no finding in respect of Mr Sheareth's presence or absence in the circumstances of the fifth robbery. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the applicant's conviction to the Court of Appeal on the basis of the trial judge's direction to the jury. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicant’s silence was that he had no answer to the questions asked, or no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. The Court of appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trialJudge, the conviction was safe. The court found that the jury had rejected the applicant's defence and, in doing so, must also have rejected his explanation of why he failed to answer questions in the police interview. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction which, in the event, provided assistance to the jury in how to approach the question of adverse inferences. It concluded that: “The direction the judge gave could only have related to lies told by the appellant in court.” The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by him they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The appeal was dismissed because of the overwhelming evidence against the applicant. The case was described as 'a classic case of miscarriage of justice' by the Court of Appeal. The judge concluded that the correct direction would have tipped the balance in the applicant's favour. The Appeal Court dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2006, and the case was dismissed. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of England and Wales in November 2006, but the appeal was rejected by the Appeal Court on 6 June 2007. The conviction was quashed on 14 June 2007 and the appeal dismissed on 16 June 2007, and both appeals were dismissed.

The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in Altmünster. He became a member of the recognised religious community of the Jehovah’s Witnesses in Austria. He assumed the function of a preacher (Prediger) and, since 6 November 1997, an elder (Ältester) in the community in Gmunden. In September 2000 the Upper Austrian Military Authority (Militärkommando) ordered the applicant to undergo examinations as to his ability to perform military service. The applicant appealed against the order, claiming that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society.

In September 2000 the Upper Austrian Military Authority (Militärkommando) ordered the applicant to undergo examinations as to his ability to perform military service. The applicant appealed against the order, claiming that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 23 May 2003 the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) dismissed the complaint. It found that exemption from the obligation to do military service merely applied to members of recognised religious societies and could not be extended to registered religious communities.

The Court of Appeal, after an oral hearing on 4 July 1996, refused an application for appeal from Mr Justice Jowsit's decision. "There seems to be no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal," he says. "The decision would stand because the decision has to be made by the Board and could not be delegated to the independent tribunal," he adds. “There would have been no meaningful independent panel and the decision would have stood.“It would have meant that the decision was not made by an independent panel, and that the case would not have been heard by an impartial tribunal,” the judge adds. 'It seems to me that there is noarguable point,' he adds, ‘which would justify the appeal.’

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 24876/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two British nationals. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They complained that these measures also disclosed an interference with the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from the European Roma Rights Centre. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The applicants are gypsies by birth. They lived and travelled with their respective families in and around the area known as the Borough of Maidstone in Kent. From 1987, the Borough was a designated area pursuant to section 12 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 (see paragraphs 43-48 below) The applicants wished for their children to be brought up in a stable environment which would facilitate the continuity of their education. The applicants were refused a place on any local authorised site. They camped outside one official site for 5-6 weeks hoping to be offered a plot. No place was offered and court proceedings were brought against them by the Borough to secure their eviction from the land. The Government stated that the Borough has no knowledge or record of any request by the applicants for a pitch in 1982. They moved into the caravan occupied by the first applicant’s mother on a permitted gypsy site and sold their own caravan. The caravan was however small and conditions became intolerable. Having nowhere else to go, the applicants in or about 1983 reluctantly applied for permanent accommodation and accepted the offer of a council flat. The application was rejected on 11 December 1989. A public enquiry was held before a Planning Inspector on 26 March 1991. The Inspector refused their appeal on 24 April 1991 and the applicants were penalised in costs on the basis that it was identical to the previous application. The applicants conceded that the only action taken since the 1989 decision by or on behalf of the family to find another site or accommodation, was a telephone call … to the [Borough], on instructions, assured the family would be offered short-term housing. This is the position the family have faced for a long time.” The Inspector did not find the granting of permission for caravans for two gypsy families some 300-400 metres away along the same road could be regarded as a material difference. “On the contrary, in my opinion three gypsy caravan sites within some 600 m of the length of Lenham Road would amount to an overconcentration of caravan sites in these rural surroundings” No new gypsy sites have been opened in Maidstone since 1967. There is nowhere within the site at which a mobile home could be positioned without causing equally serious harm. The only way in which it could be made virtually invisible, …, would be to provide physical screening which would in itself be an intrusive feature in the countryside. This development seriously damages the appearance and character of the surroundings. There are still gypsy families parked on unauthorised sites in the Maidstone area, including [the applicants]… No new gypsies have been added to the area since 1967, and there has been no increase in the number of applications. The applicants were formally informed by the Borough that they were considered as intentionally homeless since they had terminated their council tenancy to move onto land not permitted for residential use. The applicants were told that there was a waiting list for places on official sites but that since they were intentionally homeless they could not put their names on it for 2 years. In March 1992, the applicants applied to the Borough for housing on the grounds of homelessness and that contrary to the policy of refusing registration within two years after a finding of intentional homelessness the Borough agreed to re-register them as homeless on condition that they paid their arrears of rent for the council tenancy. A third prosecution resulted in conviction and sentence was deferred to enable the applicants to move. The applicants returned to their land, where the children could resume their education at their previous school. The Government stated that the applicants’ names were placed on the waiting list at the end of 1992 but they removed their names from that list in January 1993. The applicants disputed that they removal their names. The Borough commenced its proceedings for an injunction by summons dated 22 December 1993. In February 1997, the applicants sold their land. They also sold their caravan at a substantial undervalue. They went to live temporarily in the caravan occupied by the second applicant’s brother, which involved a family of six sharing with aFamily of five. This became intolerable. The applicants suffered headaches, anxiety, claustrophobia and depression requiring them to seek medical treatment. They were both prescribed medication which did not however resolve their physical sense of confinement. The applicants bought a touring caravan, which they stationed on the land of the second applicant’s brother. They took every opportunity they could to travel in the traditional style during school holidays, attending traditional gypsy fairs to continue horse trading activities. They have bought another plot of land in Yalding, Kent, with the intention of resuming their traditional life. They intend to apply for planning permission for a new home in the spring of next year.

eval_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Norwegian nationals. The applicants alleged that their right under Article 8 of. the Convention to respect for private life had been breached by a Supreme Court judgment of 2 September 2008. The application was communicated to the Government, but it was decided to await the outcome of Von Hannover v. Germany (no. 2) [GC], nos. 40660/08 and 60641/08, ECHR 2012 and Axel Springer AG v Germany [GC] 7 February 2012. The applicants brought compensation proceedings against the magazine before Oslo District Court. The magazine appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett), which by judgment of 2 September 2008 found against the applicants, by three votes to two. Mr Justice U.S. gave the following reasons, which in the main were endorsed by the two other members of the majority: “I have concluded that the appeal should be allowed.” The provision in section 3-6 refers, at any rate primarily, to violation of section 390. In my view, there is no need to consider whether, as contended by [the applicants], the magazine should pay them. There is no reason for me to evaluate individual elements on the basis of whether or not they impinge on the concept of privacy. The article as a whole contains information about the couple and their child. The relationships within the family are clearly of a personal nature. There would have been no question of violation of privacy if consent to publication had been obtained. The couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. The next question is whether the article was unlawful. This question must be decided on the. basis of an overall evaluation of the article, cf. paragraph 64 of the Big Brother judgment with further references. European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case. The fundamental issue with respect to protection of privacy is whether the published article contributes to a debate of public interest. Both [applicants] are well-known figures, but neither of them has had a prominent role either in the public administration or in any other public body. The article in question clearly has a purely entertainment value. In the assessment of legality, protection under Article 8 is the most relevant principle to be weighed. The Court of Human Rights in the case of von Hannover and the subsequent judgment of the Supreme Court in the Big Brother case have premises that seem to go far in support of protection against the use of pictures and texts concerning an individual’s private life. A wedding is a public affirmation that two persons intend to live together, and has legal consequences in many different sectors of society. Information about a wedding does not in itself involve a violation of privacy if it is given in a neutral form and based on a reliable source, cf. paragraph 80 of the Big Sister judgment. The Court reiterates the fundamental importance of protecting private life from the point of view of the development of every human being's personality. Se og Hør ran several articles featuring photos taken from different sources together with speculation and gossip. The magazine also described the relationship between the parties during their life together, which was an invasion of their private life as a couple. The right to protection of privacy is no weaker for well-known cultural personalities than it is for others, despite the fact that their photos are published in magazines and newspapers and on the internet in connection with their professional lives. A wedding is a very significant personal experience for the bridal couple, an experience that includes their families, friends and other persons close to them. The wedding ceremony and celebrations are therefore clearly part of private and family life and thus should be protected. The photos were taken from a headland about 200-250 metres from the islet where the ceremony was being held. A 300- to 400-millimetre zoom lens was used. The situation would not have been any better if the photography had taken place somewhere closer, or from a place where the photographer and journalist could have been seen by the wedding party. This could have disturbed the whole wedding. Nor was the photographing in the nature of a breach of confidence, as it would have been if for example any of the participants had published personal photos taken during or in connection with the wedding. (53) The article contained a photo of [the second applicant] Mr Justice T. gave the following reasons which in the main were endorsed by the other member of the minority: “(58) I am substantially in agreement with the first-voting judge’s general interpretation of section 3-6 of the Damages Act and section 390 of the Penal Code. (59) I will first examine whether the subject of the article in Se og Hør can be considered to be ‘a personal matter’ in the meaning of section 390. However, when weighing the right to privacy against the principle of freedom of expression in this specific case, I have arrived at a different conclusion. No award of costs should therefore be made.” Wedding ceremonies have always been a subject of general interest. It is not unusual for the couple to wish to share their wedding and its arrangements only with those closest to them. The wedding party was held at a hotel on Tjøme, which in this context is clearly a private area. It follows from the von Hannover judgment that protection of privacy also applies to places to which the public has access. Se og Hør published in words and pictures a number of details relating to a personal matter. The couple's desire to hold a private wedding should be respected in the sense that the wedding ceremony should be regarded as a private matter within the meaning of section 390. The article included a description of the guests and the couple’s families, together with the names of well-known figures. The names of guests with children were also given, and pictures were shown of the children and their parents. I regard these as the personal touch that the bridal couple had wished to give their wedding and that in my view underlines the private nature of the wedding. Although the desire to entertain is in itself legitimate, its nature does not justify overriding the affected parties’ desire to protect their privacy. Well-known persons also have the right to respect for personal matters of the kind we are dealing with here. Se og Hør used a zoom lens to take close-up pictures of the bridal couple and their guests. The zoom lens enabled the journalist and the photographer to make it look as if they were actually at the event themselves, when in fact they were hidden from those who were being observed. The opposite parties have demanded that the amount decided by the Court of Appeal should be maintained. I have no objections to the amounts decided on. Since I know that I am in the minority, I will not formulate a final conclusion. (70) For these reasons I am of the opinion that the article cannot be justified on the basis of an assessment of legality.

According to this agreement, certain posts were upgraded and the salary scales were generally increased retroactively as from 1 January 1971. Clause 18, however, provided for an exception in this respect: “Officials who were members between 1 January and 12 March 1971 (or any part of this period) shall not be entitled to the increased wage benefits applicable under the agreement, unless the Collective Bargaining Office decides otherwise” Mr. Dahlström, who was upgraded under the new agreement, was affected for the whole period up to 12 March 1971. During these periods the applicants performed work for a lower salary than that paid to other employees who were in the same salary brackets but not members of SACO or SR. Their financial losses amounted to Kr. 300 and Kr. 1,000 respectively. Mr. Schmidt, following the conclusion of the collective agreement, gave notice to the Office that, through his special treatment in regard to wages, his right to organise had been violated. When the Office nevertheless refused him the benefit of retroactivity, SACo and SR brought an action against the State before the Labour Court. Employer’s duty to respect this right did not include any obligation in principle to pay equal wages to union and non-union employees or to members of different organisations. The mere fact that different wages were accorded to different groups of employees did not by itself lead to the conclusion that a measure violating Section 3 had been employed. No support had appeared for the idea that the State intended to induce members of SACO and SR to switch over to TCO-S and SF, the Court found. The Court assumed that the latter organisations would also have been refused retroactivity if they had organised industrial action during the process of negotiations. The reason why they were granted a special benefit had nothing to do with their position as non- union. The Court indicated that the plaintiffs’ view concerning the State’s. purpose in its treatment of non-union officials might have appeared more reasonable if it. had been possible to show that the large majority of. non- union officials were active within the main field of activity of SACO and SR. Conversely, it would be less reasonable to take notice of the treatment of the group of non. union officials if these could primarily be classified within the field of recruitment of SF and TCO-S. The uncertainty in regard to these circumstances argued, in the Court’S conclusion, in favour of the States declaration that its purpose did not extend beyond upholding the principle that a strike destroys retroactivity. The report contains a separate concurring opinion. The opinion says the differential treatment complained of was in the circumstances justified as an industrial relations policy. The report says there had been no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 para. 1 (art. 14+11-1). The report concludes that the treatment was justified by the circumstances and that it was not a violation of the law. It also says that there was no breach of Article 11 or Article 14 (Art. 11/11/1) in relation to the treatment of the patient. The case has been referred to the European Court of Human Rights for further action.

‘Under the Act a ‘proper’ inference is one relevant to ‘in determining whether the defendant is guilty’ We agree with the first proposition, but not the second,’ says the judge. ‘It’s proper to take into account the fact that the defendant may not have been able to make such an inference’ ‘The jury’ should not have had to be told of the defendant’’, the judge added. “The jury should have been allowed to make its own conclusion, and not be forced to do so.” “We’re not saying the jury should not make their own conclusion. ‘The only purpose of the Act is to encourage disclosure of the truth,’ says the judge. ‘It is not for the jury to decide whether or not the defendant is guilty.’ ‘The jury should not be required to make a decision that is not in accordance with the law’, he adds, ‘the jury should be able to make an informed decision’ The judge concludes that the jury should make an ‘accidental’ decision not to reach a verdict. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his trial for terrorism related offences was unfair because of the way the courts in Northern Ireland had approached the question of non-disclosure of prosecution papers to the defence on grounds of public interest immunity. On 17 March 2008 the President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The application was brought by Mr Clifford George McKeown (“the applicant”), a British national. The applicant claims that he was entrapped by a person known to him working with the police either for the purpose of incriminating him or his co-defendant. The application was made ex parte for an order preventing disclosure. In non-jury trials in Northern Ireland, such an application is made to a judge other than the trial judge. That judge is designated by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and is referred to as the ‘disclosure judge’ (see domestic law and practice below) The judge, in an ex tempore judgment, found that it was proper to hear the application by the disclosure judge. He stated that while this Court's case-law suggested that ex partes applications without any notice to the defence were problematic, the present case was an ex parta application with notice. In Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, ECHR 2000‑II, the disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. : “... the European Court has certainly not forbidden that procedure. ... No procedure exists to ensure that an assessment of the possible value to the defence of such material other than by the prosecutor or at his own expense” “ ... I have to consider, in the light of the defence. of entrapment advanced on behalf of the accused, whether the material which. is the subject of the application is such that it might be of assistance to the defense or. in any way undermines any part of the prosecution case” The judge ruled that none of the material which is the subject of the application before me is such that it might reasonably be expected to undermine the case for the prosecution or to assist the accused's defence. The judge then suggested that one way of proceeding would be to appoint special counsel who would be shown the material and remain throughout the trial. The trial judge indicated that he had not received the disclosure judge's ruling or the statement of reasons and did not intend to receive anything that had not been made available to the defence. A hearing took place on 1 August 2002 to allow the parties and counsel appearing for the Attorney-General made submissions as to whether it was appropriate either for special counsel to be appointed or for the trial judge himself to consider the undisclosed material. The trial judge heard submissions from the defence, prosecution and counsel for the Attorney-General. The latter argued that the question of disclosure should be referred back to the disclosure judge for his decision. Counsel for the applicant's co-accused also suggested that the trial judge recuse himself since he had seen the statement of reasons which had not been made available to the defence. The trial judge ruled that it was not appropriate for him to recusing himself. The matter came before the disclosureJudge on 13 September 2002. In an ex tempore judgment he ruled: “There is no further safeguard that I am aware of that would be of any assistance” The trial judge said there were two types of material involved. The first could not assist the applicant because it was adverse to him. The second related to police procedures, was general in nature and content, and did not relate directly to the applicant. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel... The present reality is that I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material, that is the material undisclosed to the trial judge, would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that's the position then the Crown should make the matter known to thetrial judge.” The trial judge rejected both applications. the defence of entrapment, further disclosure was required. The trial judge found that taking the circumstantial evidence and the inferences to be drawn from it, he was satisfied of the applicant's guilt of the two offences beyond reasonable doubt. On 12 November 2002 the applicant was convicted by the trial judge, without a jury, of two offences: possession of firearms and ammunition with intent, contrary to Article 17 of the Firearms (NI) Order 1981; and possession of articles for a purpose connected with terrorism. The applicant was sentenced to concurrent terms of imprisonment of twelve years and two years respectively. The applicant appealed against his conviction on both charges. On 28 October 2004, the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland unanimously dismissed the appeal. The non-disclosed material was not considered by the Court before it gave judgment. It considered the House of Lords ruling in R. v. H and C [2004] A.C. 134 (see paragraph 32 below) and reviewed this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis and Jasper, both cited above; Fitt v the United Kingdom [GC], no. 29777/96, ECHR 2000‑II; Edwards and Lewis v the. United Kingdom, nos. 39647/98 and 40461/98, 22 July 2003. The Court of Appeal found that the applicant's defence of entrapment was well known to the trial judge, the prosecution, and the disclosure judge and no other issue had been identified that might sound on the question of disclosure. The disclosure judge had been unable to envisage any circumstances in which the non-disclosed material could assist the defence either by enhancing the case that was being made for the applicant or by undermining or weakening the prosecution case. It agreed with the disclosureJudge that there had been no need for special counsel to be appointed and there was nothing to indicate that the material characterised as wholly irrelevant to the applicant’s defence might have suddenly become relevant. The Court of Appeal refused to certify a point of law of general importance. It also refused to grant leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The appeal was dismissed on 19 November 2004, and the case was settled in court in March 2005. The judge described the case as "a case of the law, not the law itself" and said it was a clear miscarriage of justice. He said the court should have considered the circumstances of the case and made its decision on the basis of the evidence given by the parties to the case. The court ruled that the matter was resolved in favour of the claimant. The case was decided in court and the appeal was thrown out.

The applicant and her husband applied repeatedly throughout the years for places on many of the local private and official sites in Surrey. Their applications proved unsuccessful as all the sites were full with long waiting lists. In March 1993, the applicant bought land known as 111A Almners Road, Runnymede. It was a portion of a garden in a Green Belt area where there was already some residential development. The applicant moved a mobile home onto the land and took up residence with her family. In June 1989, the Secretary of State issued a direction under section 9 of the 1968 Act directing that gypsies should be allowed to live on official sites. The High Court had granted a declaration that Surrey County Council was in breach of its duty under section 6 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968. The previous owner of 111A Almners Road, also a gypsy, had been refused planning permission in January 1993 to live on the land in a caravan on the basis that it conflicted with local and national planning policies. The Council considered that the stationing of a caravan would be detrimental to the character of the Green Belt. The applicant was advised that there was a special concession for granting planning permission to gypsies in Green Belt areas under Circular 28/77. She took over the appeal from the previous owner. An Inspector appointed by the Department of Environment heard evidence and representations from the applicant and the Council. By a letter dated 3 June 1993, the Inspector dismissed the appeal. The appeals site lies within the south west sector of the Metropolitan Green Belt. This section is described as containing valuable green wedges which thrust inwards to the Thames west of Molesey. Lyne is a small settlement located within one of these wedges. I consider that the development subject to the appeals conflicts with the second and third objectives of government green belt policy listed in PPG2. … In light of this I conclude that the use of the land for a residential caravan site for a mobile home and associated operational development is not appropriate to this part of the Met Green Belt’s green belt. … The development is significantly different to the character of the touring caravans that are parked in nearby gardens. There is no need to change the name of the site as it is already in the public domain. The site is in the same area as the rest of the council, it is just that the name has been changed. It is a good idea to keep the name the same as it was when it was first established. There is no reason why the name should change. The name should remain the same, it does not need to be changed. The only reason to change it is if the new name is not as good as the old one. It doesn't mean that there is a reason not to keep it as the original name. It means that there isn't a reason for changing the name. We don't want to change anything.
