They found that a high degree of judicial scrutiny was required before finding exceptional circumstances to justify the imposition of a confiscation order outside the six-month time-limit. They noted that on 29 June 2000, defence counsel for the second applicant and the co-accused Mr. E. had requested an early hearing at the Crown Court. However, the earliest date that the trial judge would be available was the week beginning 30 October 2000. That date was pencilled in, even though it was “more than four months away’. The trial judge had also “candidly acknowledged more than once” that there were no exceptional circumstances. The House of Lords observed that the core problem before it was whether, as a matter of statutory construction, failure to comply with a statutory time-limit would have the effect of invalidating an act. The fact that Parliament cast statutory requirements in imperative form without expressly specifying the consequences had caused a great deal of litigation over the preceding 130 years. In London and Clydeside Estates Ltd v. Aberdeen District Council [1980] 1 WLR 182, 189E-190C, Lord Hailsham had emphasised that it was within the courts’ inherently discretionary jurisdiction to determine the nature of a particular statutory requirement. The prime purpose behind the statutory provision for confiscation orders was to recover any financial benefit that an offender might have obtained from his criminal conduct. The prejudice to the applicants was not significant and was outweighed by the countervailing public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation for what were no more than bona fide errors in the judicial process. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 9 July 1997. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. Liberty, a non-governmental organisation based in London, was granted leave to submit written comments on the case. No observations were submitted. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1998. The applicants are all British citizens, born in 1941, 1948, 1947 and 1932 respectively. The background to their complaints to the Convention institutions is constituted by the enactment and implementation of legislative measures designed to limit the rights of the applicants. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Goudie, Mr Morris, Mr MacLeod, Mr Banks and Mr Steele. The application is brought by Mr Mobin Ahmed, Mr Dennis Perrin and Mr Ray Bentley. The history of the enactment of the relevant measures as well as their purport and scope are described in Section B below. The impact of the measures on the applicants, all persons considered holders of politically restricted posts within the meaning of the applicable legislation, is described in sections C and D. The adoption of the Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 is referred to as the “Widdicombe Committee’s Report”. The Committee firmly endorsed the continuation of the tradition of politically impartial local government officers having regard in particular to the roles of senior officers as managers, advisers and arbitrators in the day-to-day functioning of local government. Local government has traditionally been based on the same public service tradition as central government. There must continue to be a system of permanent and politically neutral officers appointed on the basis of merit. The Widdicombe Committee recommended that senior officers discharge their functions in a manner which was impartial from both a subjective and an objective point of view. The Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 (“the Regulations”) were made under section 1(5) of the Act on 4 April 1990. They were laid before Parliament the following day and came into force on 1 May 1990. The Regulations applied to all persons holding a politically restricted post. This term covers three broad categories of local government officials. The Regulations apply to local government officials in three categories. An officer in the second and third categories could apply to have his or her post removed from the list of posts to which the Regulations applied. The first applicant, Mr Ahmed, was a solicitor employed by the London Borough of Hackney. The second applicant was Principal Valuer with the Devon County Council. Mr Ahmed was adopted as Labour candidate for election in 1990, but was obliged to withdraw his candidature as a result of the Regulations. The Council confirmed that Mr Ahmed had not attended committees during the previous twelve months, but stated that he would be involved in giving advice to committees in future, and would attend on a more regular basis. Mr Perrin's post required him to give regular advice to the Council’s committees, including strategy advice on key estate management issues, and to speak to the media. His application for exemption was refused on 20 March 1990. As a result of the Regulations, Mr Perrin had to give up his position as Vice-Chair and Property Officer of the Exeter Constituency Labour Party. He also had to refrain from supporting and assisting Labour candidates in Exeter City Council elections, including his wife, who was a candidate in May 1990 and May 1991. Mr Bentley's post was classified as politically sensitive and appropriately subject to political restrictions under section 2(3) of the Act. Mr Bentley applied for exemption from political restrictions. The application was dismissed on 20 December 1991. Mr Brough can no longer act as Parliamentary Chairman of his party in Harrow East. He is prevented from speaking at public meetings on issues such as housing and the health service. The judge, Mr Justice Hutchison, considered that he was bound by the recent decision of the House of Lords in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Brind and Others. The applicants and NALGO (the predecessor of UNISON, the trade union of which the applicants are members) applied for and were granted leave to apply for judicial review of the Regulations. Judge referred to an affidavit submitted by Mr Simcock, a senior civil servant at the Department of the Environment. He explained how the Widdicombe Committee had been set up in 1985 to inquire into local authority practices and procedures with particular reference to the respective roles of elected members and officers. Judge continued: “... I preface my summary by pointing out that some of [the applicants’ complaints] reflect the applicant’s root and branch opposition to the whole concept of restricting the political activities of local government employees” NALGO was involved in the making of the Regulations, in which the judge said there was no pressing social need for the Regulations. The Regulations go too far in prohibiting conduct undertaken with apparent intention, etc., or likely to create the impression of support, etc. They should, at most, have proscribed actual political activities. The width of the language used means that many non-party political activities, including trade unions and charitable activities, are prohibited. The terms are imposed on existing employees, who entered into their contracts of employment on a different basis. The restrictions may have an adverse effect on recruitment and lead to resignations by skilled staff. The arguments summarised in (c) and (d) are to the effect that the Regulations are uncertain and incapable of consistent and fair application. The DTP had twenty MPs, the minimum number to be able to form a parliamentary group, and was able to do so. The applicant argued that independent candidates should not be allowed to campaign on national radio and television. The application was dismissed on the basis of Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298 on Elections. The High Electoral Council pointed out that this provision could only be modified by a fresh legislative amendment. The applicant said that the large number of independent candidates standing in the 22 July 2007 elections had stemmed from the 10% electoral threshold imposed during the parliamentary elections. He said that this phenomenon stemmed from dissatisfaction felt by most people with the performance of the political parties, whether in power or in opposition. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 14 July 2007.

By a faxed letter of 20 May 2008, the Registry was informed of the death of Ahmet Oğuz Serçinoghlu. His second wife and five children declared their intention to pursue the application. Following the death of their father, the applicants, as his heirs, appealed to the Court of Cassation on 31 March 2003. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26589/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the respondent State had failed to take steps to protect the right to life of their relative Mr Şevket Epözdemir (“the deceased”) The deceased was a lawyer and the chairman of the Tatvan provincial branch of a pro-Kurdish political party, the Democracy Party (‘DEP’) The applicants submitted that between August and December 1993, DEP party buildings were bombed and ten of its members and administrators were killed. Şevket Epözdemir left his house to go to his office, which was nearby. When he failed to arrive the family became concerned and contacted the authorities. His body was found by soldiers in a ditch at the side of a road which connected the town of Tatvan to the city of Bitlis. He was blindfolded and there was a gunshot wound on his face. The criminal investigation into his disappearance is currently under way. The case is being investigated by the Turkish National Court of Justice, which has opened a criminal case into the death of his wife, who went to the police station to ask them to find her husband. Doctors established that the cause of death was cerebrovascular haemorrhagic shock caused by the gunshot wound. The applicants sent letters to the offices of the Van and Tatvan prosecutors and asked to be provided with information regarding the steps taken in the investigation over the course of the previous ten years. The Tatvan prosecutor opened an investigation file into the killing and informed the Ministry of Justice. The Van prosecutor’s office decided that it had no jurisdiction ratione loci to investigate the incident and forwarded the applicants’ letter (mentioned in the preceding paragraph) to the prosecutor in Tatvan. The Güroymak prosecutor took a decision of non-jurisdiction ratione materiae. The applicants argued that the perpetrators of the killing had not been found, despite the fact that more than one year had elapsed since the incident. They argued that States were responsible for protecting their citizens’ lives and that in the event that they failed to do so, they had a duty to find and punish the perpetrators. The Van Administrative Court decided to award compensation to the applicants, in accordance with Article 125 of the Constitution (see paragraphs 32-34 below). It held that when carrying out their duties the public authorities had an obligation to take the necessary measures. The compensation proceedings were decided on 16 December 1997. The applicants’ relative, Şevket Epözdemir, had never requested protection from the authorities. The Ministry of the Interior appealed, arguing that it had not failed in that obligation because the reason for the killing and the identity of its perpetrators had not yet been established. The applicants lodged an appeal with the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision. The court ruled that it was not possible to award compensation to the family on the basis of the State’s “absolute liability” because the sole fact that the deceased had been a “member of society” was not sufficient. It added that for the public authorities to be said to have failed in their obligation, it was necessary to establish that they had either not performed their duties at all, or failed to perform them in a timely manner. The appeal lodged by the applicants was rejected by the Supreme Administrative Court on 17 April 2003. The applicants maintained that the authorities had failed to take the necessary steps to prevent the attack on their relative and to find the perpetrators. The Ministry was therefore responsible for the pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage arising from the failures on its part. The final decision was served on the applicants on 3 January 2006. A request made by the applicant for the decision to be rectified was also rejected, on 14 November 2005. The appeal was rejected and the request to rectify the decision was rejected on 17 November 2003. A decision to rectified the decision on 14 January 2006 was served.

The applicants were taken into police custody at the Mersin Security Headquarters for car theft. They were allegedly ill-treated by police officers, who stripped them naked, beat them and subjected them to electric shocks. They lodged a complaint with the public prosecutor against the police officers (S.D. and I.A.) who had interrogated them and against the doctor who drew up their medical report. The court found the officers guilty of ill-treatment during the performance of their duties under Article 245 of the former Criminal Code, and sentenced them to imprisonment, which was converted to a fine. For treatment to be qualified as torture under domestic law, the victims needed to have been charged with a particular crime, whereas the applicants had only been suspects and were later released without charge.

The applicant was born in 1973 and has lived in Vienna since 1999. She comes from a traditional family of practising Muslims and considers it her religious duty to wear the Islamic headscarf. The applicant lodged an application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. The disciplinary measures taken against the applicant include a warning, a suspension and a written examination on public health. The head of a university in Turkey was banned from wearing the headscarf. The ban was imposed in 1998 by the University of Bursa. The headteacher says the ban is in accordance with the European Convention on Human Rights. She was banned because she was wearing a head scarf. The university says that the ban does not apply to those who are not wearing a hat or covering their faces with a scarf, such as a scarf or a headpiece, or to people who are under 18 years of age. The school says that it will continue to ban the headwear if it is required to do so for security reasons. The student was allowed to wear the scarf for the rest of the school year. The applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health, again for the same reason. The application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998 was dismissed. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress in order to maintain order. That regulatory power had to be exercised in accordance with the relevant legislation and the judgments of the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Administrative Court. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for one semester for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. She appealed to the Istanbul Administrative Court for an order quashing the decision to suspend her. Following the entry into force of Law no. 4584 of 28 June 2000, the applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the disciplinary penalties and their effects. On 28 September 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court held that the aforementioned legislation made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the applicant’s appeal on points of law against the judgment of 30 November 1999. In the meantime the applicant had enrolled at Vienna University, where she pursued her university education.

Franz Weber, a Swiss journalist, lives at Clarens, in the Canton of Vaud. In 1980 the applicant and one of the associations he runs, Helvetia Nostra, lodged a complaint alleging defamation against R.M., who had written a letter published in the letters column of the newspaper L’Est vaudois. In order to establish the truth of his allegations, R.m. requested Mr Weber to produce a number of documents relating to his and his associations’ financial position. Mr Weber refused all conciliation. In November 1980 the investigating judge ordered disclosure of the Helveti Nostra association’s and the Franz Weber Foundation's articles and accounts for the previous two financial years. On 22 January 1981, having still not received them, he ordered their sequestration, but on 13 April 1981 he had to renew the order.

R.M. Weber forwarded Helvetia Nostra’s accounts in a sealed envelope but not those of the Foundation. Two subsequent sequestration orders were not executed. The applicant was dissatisfied with the way in which the investigating judge was proceeding. On 1 March 1982 he lodged a criminal complaint alleging misuse of official authority and coercion. The investigating judge of the Canton of Vaud refused to take any action. Mr Weber challenged the Cantonal Court en bloc. He was charged with defamation (Article 173 of the Criminal Code) and was committed for trial at the Vevey district police court. He appealed against the order committing him for trial, but the Indictment Division (tribunal d’accusation) dismissed the appeal.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 12 April 1989 and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation (“the Government’s) on 3 July 1989. It originated in an application (no. 11034/84) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr Franz Weber, on 15 May 1984. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6§ 1 and Article 10. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Boillat and Mr Vautier for the Government, by Mr Trechsel for the Commission and by Mr Schaller for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant and one of the associations he runs, Helvetia Nostra, lodged a complaint alleging defamation against R.M., who had written a letter published in the letters column of the newspaper L’Est vaudois under the headline ‘Franz Weber is fooling you’. The list of municipal taxpayers is not published. It is easy to hide behind that sort of censorship and live by devious means. May everyone have the courage to tell Helvetia Nostra (there’s a fine name to fleece you with!) that we have had enough of playing into the hands of people who sponge off us and whose behaviour borders on the criminal. ...’‘’I’m not a criminal’. I’ve never done anything wrong.’ ’’'‘I have never been a criminal. I haven’t ever done anything illegal’ The applicant had already divulged the first three items of information at a press conference in Berne on 11 May 1981, during which he denounced “the plot hatched against him by the Vaud authorities in order to intimidate him” He also stated that he had lodged a challenge and a complaint against the investigating judge. On 27 April 1982 the President of the Cassation Division imposed a fine of 300 Swiss francs on him, together with a probationary period of a year for the purposes of deletion of the fine from the cantonal register. He based his decision on the following grounds: “II. Mr Weber relied on Article 6 (art. 6) of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and impugned the procedure’. It is of little importance that the matter which was to be kept confidential was known to a limited or indefinite number of people because confidentiality had already been breached by a third party or by the same person. The actus reus of the offence punishable under Article 185 CC is therefore made out. This offence is punishable even if it has been committed inadvertently (s. 4 of the Vaud Criminal Justice Act, s. 6 of the Minor Offences Act). In the instant case it is plain that Mr Weber acted deliberately. His submission based on a kind of necessity is devoid of merit since it was open to him to appeal to the Indictment Division against the orders for the sequestration of his accounts. Disclosure that the first complaint had been lodged, because this was punishable as defamation, does not amount to an offence. The disclosure of the orders for production and sequestration of the accounts in the file does amount to information about an investigation. It remains to be considered whether one can talk of disclosure, given that the matters had already been made public at an earlier press conference. The applicant cannot rely on common knowledge when that knowledge is due to an earlier disclosure that he himself has made. ...“ Finally, the Criminal Cassation Division set aside of its own motion the entry of the fine in the cantonal register.” The applicant maintained that Article 185 of the Vaud Code of Criminal Procedure (Vaud CCP) violates in the abstract, and in the specific case, freedom of expression. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 16 November 1983. It noted that such restrictions are permissible where they are necessary in a democratic society, in particular for maintaining the authority and impartiality of the judiciary. The rule enacted in Article 185 Vaud CCP clearly conforms to these principles. A weighing of the competing interests at stake leads to the same conclusions. The prohibition against communicating information about an investigation until its completion and the penalties attaching to the offence are undoubtedly consistent with the proportionality principle. The public’s interest in being informed by this means cannot outweigh the interest in ensuring that the judicial system can function as smoothly and impartially. The fine was convertible into ten days’ imprisonment under Article 12 of the Vaud Order on the recovery of fines and their conversion into imprisonment. The possibility of conversion into a custodial sentence makes no difference, since conversion is possible only in the event of the appellant’s refusing to pay the fine out of sheer unwillingness. The safeguards provided for in Article 6 § 1 (art. 6-1) ECHR were therefore not applicable in the instant case.“ The applicant paid the fine in January 1985. at barristers, and in that instance their disciplinary nature is not in doubt,” the court said.

Manfred Jacubowski was editor-in-chief of a news agency run by a commercial company. He instituted two different sets of proceedings. In the first (A) he sought to challenge his dismissal and in the second (B) he claimed the right to reply to a press release issued by his employer. At almost the same time, he became involved in a third set of proceedings (C) brought against him under the Unfair Competition Act of 7 June 1909. The Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) held on 11 October 1988 that he had been validly dismissed on 28 October 1984. According to the court, the distribution of the circular and cuttings was to be regarded as such a serious breach of Mr Jacubowsky’s duty of loyalty that it was not possible for the employer to continue his contract.

It originated in an application (no. 15088/89) against Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mr Manfred Jacubowski, on 11 April 1989. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 November 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig, Mr von Mühlendahl, Mr Frowein and Mr Meilicke, and also replies to its questions. Jacubowski was editor-in-chief of a news agency run by a commercial company, the Deutsche Depeschendienst GmbH, of which he was a founder member and manager. This company filed a petition in bankruptcy (Eröffnung des Konkursverfahrens) on 31 March 1983. In the first proceedings he sought to challenge his dismissal and in the second he claimed the right to reply to a press release issued by his employer. The Cologne Court of Appeal found that Mr Jacubowski had been validly dismissed on 28 October 1984. The court ruled that the distribution of the circular and cuttings was to be regarded as such a serious breach of Mr JacUBowski’s duty of loyalty that it was not possible for the applicant to continue his contract. The circular contained no reference to the allegations against the applicant. It could not be inferred from the circular that its main aim was to defend the applicant's reputation and honour. Such behaviour on the part of a leading employee was unacceptable and therefore not covered by the constitutional right to freedom of expression. Manfred Jacubowski sued his former employer, the D.B.D., for mismanaging the company. He had been dismissed without notice on account of his business incompetence. The courts rejected his applications on the ground they had no prospects of success. The Cologne Court of Appeal reversed the Regional Court’s judgment and ordered the agency to accede to his request, which it did a month later. In the reply then published the applicant answered in detail the allegations made in the press release. Only the timely intervention of the former finance and accounting director, K., the current director, prevented more serious harm being done, so that today the agency is once again on a sound financial footing. On 25 September 1984, Mr Jacubowski had sent 13 articles from newspapers with large circulations to forty newspaper publishers and newspaper, radio and television journalists. The articles gave critical accounts of his dismissal, the circumstances surrounding it and the ddp’s activities in general. They reported in particular that the dDP’S financial position had worsened again since the bankruptcy in April 1983. Some of its clients were preparing to dispense with its services, mainly because of their poor standard and the lack of certain technical facilities. On 29 January 1986 the Düsseldorf Regional Court refused the application on the ground that E. had no legal interest (rechtliches Interesse) The court held that in his circular the respondent had repeated in his own name the allegations made in the attached articles. Admittedly, he had sought to correct assertions made about him in the press release that were possibly false. The judgment was based on section 1 of the 1909 Act, which provides: “Any person who, in the course of business commits, for purposes of competition, acts contrary to accepted moral standards may be enjoined from further engaging in those acts and held liable for damages’” The court went on to hold that he would have to “compensate the [E. company] for all the damage that the acts [in question] ha[d] caused and [would] cause the [ddp]’ The court found that the respondent had a 'competitive intention' behind his actions. The court said that he 'unnecessarily handicapped the [ddp] as a competitor' The court concluded that even true statements may only be used to disparage a competitor where the person making them has sufficient reason to link his own competitive position with disparagement of the competitor and provided that the criticism does not in nature or degree exceed what is necessary (Federal Court of Justice in GRUR), adding that 'it is not apparent what else the respondent could have meant when he wrote that he wished to discuss ‘not only the past but also future developments in the German “news market”’ Mr Jacubowski had needlessly handicapped (behinderte unnötig) a competitor and accordingly infringed section 1 of the 1909 Act. It does not appear that there was any such reason to disparage the [ddp] by taking up the unfavourable comments on its activities in the Horizont article. On 4 October 1988 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the complaint for adjudication on the ground that it was unfounded. It noted, firstly, that the prohibition in issue related solely to the applicant’s chosen method of circulating his information. The information was, moreover, of a business nature, but this did not mean that it ceased to be an opinion whose expression was protected. In principle, freedom of expression takes precedence over rights (Rechtsgüter) protected by ordinary laws in so far as the statement is part of the ongoing discussion of questions of public importance. In the light of these facts, the distribution of the applicant’s circular can hardly be regarded as an attempt to influence public opinion. Rather it was designed almost exclusively to promote his private business interests and to secure or improve his competitive position in the news market. It follows ... that the prejudice caused to the complainants by the distribution. of the circular was disproportionate to the applicant's aim, stated in it, of clarifying his. relationship with the ddp and ‘current developments at the agency’ Relying on Article 10 (art. 10) of the Convention, he complained of a breach of his right to freedom of expression. The Commission declared the application (no. 15088/89) admissible on 3 December 1991. In its report of 7 January 1993, it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 10. The full text of the Commission’s opinion is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. It is published under the heading of ‘The European Convention on Human Rights’ and is available on the Internet at: http://www.human rights.org.uk/.

The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1997. Mr Tejedor García, who was born in 1948, now lives in Saragossa. At the material time, he was an officer in the national police force and lived at Mataró (Barcelona) The facts underlying the procedure in issue were described in the judgment of the SaragOSSa Audiencia Provincial of 6 November 1991. Mr Thór Vilhjálmsson replaced, as President of the Chamber, Mr Ryssdal who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case, and Mr I. Foighel, substitute judge. Manuel Tejedor García, who was dressed in plain clothing, did not consider the documents satisfactory and, showing his police identification, fired a shot into the ceiling of the café. He then kicked Mr Leonel Pajucides in the testicles after throwing the latter’s identity card to the floor saying that it was ‘shit’ Pointing his revolver at the two Africans, he forced them to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them to the guardia civil barracks, where, finally, he handed them over to the officers on duty. These events provoked the indignation and disapproval of the people present who gathered round the police officer and his prisoners. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. The investigating judge sent the case file to the Saragossa Audiencia Provincial. On 18 September 1989 the ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. It requested the court to declare that the applicant was innocent, and to investigate the responsibility of the two officers who had arrested him. On 10 September 1990 the investigating judge, having regard to the contradictory evidence as to the assault and the offer of drugs to the applicant, considered that no offence had been made out. In an annotation of 7 November 1990 the registrar attested that the public prosecutor had returned the case file and lodged an application for the decision to be set aside (recurso de reforma) or, in the alternative, an appeal (see paragraph 16 below), dated 13 September 1990. On the following day, the decision was served on Mr Gallego. However, no annotation appears on the file attesting service on the publicProsecutor. In a decision (auto) of 4 December 1990 the investigating judge rejected MrGallego’s observations and held that the application had been made in time. As to the merits he stated that it would be better to test the evidence at an adversarial On 12 February 1991 the investigating judge made a final discontinuance order (Articles 637 no. 2 and 790 no. 6 of the CCP) in respect of the two guardia civil officers accused by the ANPU. Mr Tejedor García appointed Mr Marco as his barrister (abogado) and Mr Gallego as his solicitor (procurador) The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 28 May 1993 the Supreme Court found that there was nothing in the case file to show when it had been sent to the public prosecutor or when the publicProsecutor had been served with the decision. The Constitutional Court ruled that the application was not in breach of the law. The court found that the appeal had been made on the basis of a legal interpretation of the case. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was not a constitutional issue. The decision was made on two grounds: (a) The application was intended to be admissible; and (b) The interpretation was not compatible with the original intent of the application, which was to be made on a legal basis. The case was rejected on all three grounds, and the appeal was rejected. The ruling was upheld by the Supreme Court of the Republic of South Africa on 6 June 1994.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9154/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr H. Meyer-Mews, a lawyer practising in Bremen. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs K. Behr, Regierungsdirektorin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court advised the parties on 14 January 2014 that it would continue processing the application under the name Schatschaschwili v. Germany. The crimes were committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006 and in Göttingen on 3 February 2007. The applicant was sentenced to nine years and six months in prison for the crimes. The court found it established that the applicant, acting jointly with an unidentified accomplice and according to a previously agreed plan, entered by force into a Kassel apartment and robbed its occupants. The men were aware that the apartment was used for prostitution and expected its two female occupants to keep valuables and cash in there. The applicants also robbed another apartment located in GöTtingen in February 2007, acting in accordance with a plan previously set up among the gang. The applicant and a further accomplice gained access to O. and P.’s apartment pretending to be potential clients. Once inside the apartment B. produced a knife that he had carried along in his jacket. Fearing for her life O. opened the safe from which B. removed EUR 300 and also handed over the contents of her wallet in the amount of EUR 250. B. left the apartment at around 8.30 p.m. taking the money. The applicant jumped after her but abandoned the chase after some minutes when passers-by appeared nearby on the street. He then called the co-accused waiting in front of the women's apartment on his mobile phone and gave him an account of the events. The Regional Court based its finding of facts regarding the first crime committed in Kassel on the statements made by the victims L. and I. on the occasion of their police interrogations as well as in the course of the subsequent trial. Both witnesses had identified the applicant without any hesitation as the perpetrator who had carried the gun when presented with his photo. The Regional Court found L and I’s testimonies to be consistent and credible and noted that they were supported by the statements of the police officers who had attended the crime scene and had interviewed the victims. The records of O. and P.’'s interrogations by the police and the investigating judge will be read out at the trial and be admitted as evidence in the proceedings. The Regional Court specified that O. and P. had been summoned to appear before the Regional Court on 24 August 2007, the third day of the trial. They both had refused to attend the hearing relying on medical certificates dated 9 August 2007 that indicated their unstable post‑traumatic emotional and psychological condition. The Regional Court asked for the witnesses to be heard by a court in Latvia and the hearing to be transmitted by voice and image (audiovisuelle Vernehmung) However, a witness hearing scheduled by the competent Latvian court for 13 February 2008 was cancelled shortly before by the presiding judge on the ground that the witnesses had demonstrated that they were still suffering from post-traumatic disorders. The Regional Court concluded that it was impossible to have the witnesses examined in the foreseeable future. The court was not prevented from admitting O. and P.’s pre-trial statements as evidence in the proceedings. The Regional Court held that notwithstanding the resulting restrictions for the defence, the trial as a whole had been fair and had complied with the requirements of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. The investigating judge had excluded the applicant from the hearing in accordance with Article 168 (c) ofThe Code of Criminal Procedure since he had been concerned that the witnesses would be afraid of telling the truth in the presence of the accused. In the Regional Court’s opinion the records of O. and P.’‘s interrogations at the investigative stage showed that they had given detailed and coherent descriptions of the circumstances of the crime. Minor contradictions in their statements could be explained by their concern not to disclose their illegal residence status and activities to the authorities. The court observed that the witnesses’ attention during the incident had been focussed on the further perpetrator carrying the knife and that the applicant himself had only stayed a short period of time in the apartment. This explained why the witnesses had not pressed charges immediately after the events and why the police had only been informed of the incident on 12 February 2007. Their inability to identify the applicant also showed that, as opposed to the defence's allegations, they had not testified with a view to incriminating him. O. and P.’s description of the events also coincided with their friend L.�'s recollection of her conversations with O. and. P. following the crime. In addition, the police officers and the investigating judge had all testified at trial that they had found the witnesses to be credible. The Regional Court noted that since neither the defence nor the court itself had had an opportunity to observe the main witnesses’ demeanour at trial or by means of an audio-visual examination. The court further emphasised that when taking into account the testimonies given by the witnesses' neighbour E. and their friendL. it had paid special attention to the fact that their statements constituted hearsay evidence. The applicant and the co-accused had denied any participation in the robbery as such or any premeditated criminal activity in this respect. However, their own statements at trial had at least confirmed that one of them had visited the apartment at Göttingen on the evening before the crime. The applicant had testified that he and B. had come to the apartment with a view to making use of the women’s services as prostitutes. He further had conceded that he had followed P. when she escaped over the balcony in order to prevent her from calling the neighbours or the police since he had been afraid of getting problems in view of his criminal record. In 2008 the Federal Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded. The Prosecutor General argued that the proceedings had been fair and there had been no reason to exclude the witness statements of O. and P. as evidence. The applicant complained of a violation of his right to be heard (Anhörungsrüge) on the ground that no hearing had been held in the appeal proceedings and that the decision rejecting his appeal did not provide any reasons. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint against the decisions of the Federal court of Justice dated 30 October and 9 December 2008 for examination without providing reasons. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court first by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain and then by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 12952/87) against Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by six Spanish nationals on 5 May 1987. The object of the application and the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J. M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Mr Ryssdal had assumed the office of President of the Chamber and consulted the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicants on the organisation of the proceedings. On 20 November the Government appointed a new ad hoc judge, Mr Dámaso Ruiz-Jarabo Colomer, a judge who is on secondment as head of the private office of the president of the General Council of the Judiciary. On 27 November 1992 the President directed that the oral proceedings should open on 27 January 1993. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Chamber decided under Rule 51 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The RUMASA group of five brothers and one sister sued the Government for the expropriation of their shares in the company. The Government claimed they were the rightful owners of the shares. The case was heard by the Constitutional Court, which ruled in favour of the applicants. The court heard evidence from the Government, the Commission, the applicants and the lawyers for both groups. The State was to take immediate possession of the property through the intermediary of the Directorate General for National Assets (Article 2) The Court decided that the Government had the right to expropriate the shares of the RUM ASA group, including those of the parent company, including that of the applicant. The application was dismissed on appeal. Law no. 7/1983 of 29 June 1983, published a day later in the Official State Gazette (Boletín Oficial del Estado), replaced the legislative decree. The aim of these measures was to protect the public interest because, in order to finance the group’s companies, its banks had taken risks considered to be disproportionate in relation to their solvency. Six members of the court expressed the view that the expropriation procedure followed was contrary to the Constitution. The Constitutional Court dismissed the deputies’ appeal by a judgment of 2 December 1983, adopted with the President's casting vote, in a dissenting opinion. The first applicant had requested Court no. 18 to refer to the Constitutional Court a question on the conformity of Articles 1 and 2 of Law no. 7/1983 with Articles 14, 24 and 33 of the Constitution. On 21 September the Counsel for the State applied for the joinder of the two sets of proceedings. The court held hearings on 18 June and 17 September 1984. In the opinion of the first-instance court, the decision on the merits of the dispute depended on the validity of the provisions in issue. The Constitutional Court found the question admissible on 17 October 1984; it then gave notice of the question to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the Government and the Attorney General. José María Ruiz-Mateos challenged two judges for lack of impartiality. The Constitutional Court dismissed the challenge on the ground that the judges lacked locus standi. By a judgment of 19 December 1986, it held that Articles 1 and 2 of Law no. 7/1983 were compatible with Article 24 of the Constitution. It found that legislative expropriation - even by means of a special statute concerning a specific case - was not contrary to the Constitution, as it was always open to them to contest the measure in the administrative courts and to ask those courts to refer a question to the Constitutional Court on the constitutional conformity of such action. Two judges expressed the view, in a dissenting opinion, that the expropriation procedure used had deprived the applicants of their right of access to the courts. The hearing was initially set down for 21 October, but was adjourned at the request of the applicants’ lawyer, who was unable to attend. The applicants sought a stay of the proceedings until the European Commission and Court of Human Rights had had an opportunity to rule on their application to Strasbourg. After having received their comments, the Audiencia provincial referred the question to the Constitutional Court on 9 July 1989. The latter court declared it admissible on 31 October 1989, then communicated it to the institutions. However, the Court may declare the question inadmissible, in a decision stating its reasons, after hearing only the Attorney General, when the procedural requirements are not satisfied or when the question is manifestly ill-founded.” “The applicants lodged their application with the Commission on 5 May 1987. They alleged in the first place that their case had not been given a fair hearing conducted within a reasonable time by an impartial tribunal. The applicants complained of their right of access to the courts to challenge the public interest justification for the expropriation and the necessity of the immediate transfer of their property (Articles 6 para. 1 and 13 of the Convention) (art. 6-1, art. 13). She had significant psychological difficulties, but did not associate those with the abuse. The applicants are the sons of the late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased”) who died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at the age of 71 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. Dr U., a German national, had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. He had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon but also formally qualified as GP. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Two hours after U. had left, Mr Gray’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed that Mr Gray had died. On Sunday 17 February 2008 TCN suspended U from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany. U. was suspended from the British medical register on an interim basis. He explained that when treating the deceased he had committed a grave mistake with fatal outcome that had resulted from the confusion between the drugs pethidine and diamorphine. On the day of the incident he had further been overtired following his journey from Germany to the United Kingdom and had found himself in a tremendous stress situation. The application was brought by a German national, Mr Christof Stollenwerk (“the applicant”), on 9 February 2012. The applicant was found guilty of smuggling drugs into Germany and trafficking. He was sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment. On the same day, in a separate decision, the District Court ordered the continuation of the applicant’s detention. On 13 December 2010 he lodged an appeal against the judgment. On 28 January 2011 the Düsseldorf Chief Public Prosecutor’S Office (Generalstaatsanwaltschaft – “the prosecution authorities”) submitted written observations to the Court of Appeal, requesting the dismissal of the appeal of 5 January 2011. On 25 February 2011 the Court. of Appeal dismissed the request for a subsequent hearing as inadmissible, finding that the applicant's right to be heard had not been violated. The German Court of Appeal has ruled that there was no need for the decision. The decision was made by the court after an appeal to the German Supreme Court had been rejected. The court ruled that the decision had been made before the appeal had been heard. The appeal was made because the decision was not based on facts that the court had known at the time of the appeal. The Court's decision was a result of an appeals process that had already taken place, and was not the result of the court's failure to find out the facts of the case before it. The case is being appealed, but the decision is expected to be made later this year, if it is successful.

It originated in an application (no. 22714/93) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Alfred Worm, on 28 July 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Geus, Mr Masser and Mr Cede and also replies to its questions. The applicant, Mr Alfred Worm, is a journalist. He was born in 1945 and lives in Vienna. At the time the applicant was working for Profil, an Austrian periodical dealing mostly with politics. For several years he investigated into and reported on the case of Mr Hannes Androsch, a former Vice-Chancellor and Minister of Finance, who was involved in certain criminal proceedings. In 1991 the Vienna Regional Criminal Court (Landesgericht für Strafsachen), sitting as a court of two professional judges and two lay judges, conducted criminal proceedings against Mr Androsh concerning charges of tax evasion. Hannes Androsch was convicted of having evaded taxes between 1973 and 1981. He was sentenced to a fine of 1.8 million Austrian schillings (ATS). The atmosphere during the trial was glacial. ‘Above all, there were to be no mistakes during the proceedings. The case was to be handled with common prudence, properly and to the best of our knowledge and belief – but not with kid gloves!’ – Mr Heinz Tschernutter, tax investigator and witness. On the day before the trial Die Presse dropped the bombshell that was meant to shake all Austria. Lawyer Herbert Schachter was quoted as saying: ‘I’m sure that Dr Androsh will present his case in an impressive manner.’ The public prosecutor, Matousek, is able to find his way around in the dark generated by the ‘international legal adviser's’ murky financial deals. Judge Zeilinger knows the file inside out, as was clear from each of his questions. ‘You, my dear Public Prosecutor ...’ in a tone as if to say ‘you wretched worm!’ Androsch underestimates the judiciary. Once again. The accused mistook the excessively polite and markedly accommodating manner of the presiding judge for weakness. He has also known the public prosecutor for years and yet still doesn't know him properly. The alleged tax evasion was perhaps ‘long-term’ but by no means ‘ingenious and sophisticated’ It has been known since 1980 that Androsch evaded taxes. The tax officials Walter Handerek, Heinz Tschernutter and Gerhard Berner, who reopened the file between 1985 and 1988, were treated by defending counsel Herbert Schachter as though they were the accused. It is both symptomatic and revealing that he told the trial court again and again that ‘seven inspections’ had been carried out and on each occasion had found in his favour. It was very unfair that just the eighth inspection should shatter the ideal world of his illusory innocence. Everyone except him is to blame for this. He has become so completely immersed in the role of innocent victim that he cannot subjectively conceive of ever having been the guilty party. The flow of funds into and out of the seven accounts containing money not declared to the tax authorities allows of no other interpretation than that Androsch was evading taxes. His defence in court was disgraceful; after so many years one would at least have expected properly constructed arguments. Each time Judge Zeilinger asked him a specific question he either took refuge in lapses of memory or blamed his ‘adoptive father’ He even trotted out the late Sir Arthur Stein, the explorer of the Silk Road, from whom he claims to have received a legacy. The court kept trying very gently to bring the defendant back down to earth from his long-winded waffling. And each time he replied ‘I can't say. After all, I do have other things to do' Judge Zeilinger had prepared for this trial keenly and diligently. By citing facts he kept forcing Androsch into corners from which he could only escape by taking refuge in memory lapses. In many major trials the sinner has been given a fair chance to the very end. The judicial system has uncovered serious matters. The defendant has shown no humility to date, not even for a second. But he now has a few weeks to consider whether it is consonant with the principles of a State based on the rule of law for a Finance Minister and his family to have at their disposal accounts containing millions in undeclared funds. It is now for him to display greatness. The article, unlike court reports of the scandal press, analysed the conduct of the presiding judge, the public prosecutor, defence counsel and in particular the accused, Mr Androsch. The court found that it was clear for every reader, who was vaguely familiar with the issue, that the applicant, who had been working for Profil for many years, had intensively dealt with the so-called “Causa AndrosCh” and had frequently reported on it. The applicant's way of writing and the wording used were not capable of influencing these proceedings. It had not been established that the. applicant had acted with the intention of influencing the outcome of the proceedings, in particular as it appeared. that he was convinced that Mr Andrusch would in any event be convicted. The Court of Appeal also contested the Regional Court's assumption that everybody, including the lay judges, knew the applicant's long-standing commitment in the Androsch case. It observed that “the objective element of the offence defined in section 23 of the Media Act is constituted not only by unfavourable comment on evidence but also by favourable comment”. The full text of the judgment was served on the applicant on 25 March 1993. The court convicted the applicant of having exercised prohibited influence on criminal proceedings and imposed on him forty day-fines of ATS 1,200 each, that is ATS 48,000, or twenty days' imprisonment in default of payment. The court found that the applicant's expertise and involvement in the subject matter rather reinforced the impression that he had written the article with the intention of influencing the outcome of the proceedings. From the beginning he had been convinced that Mr Androsch had committed tax evasion. In the article in issue he had not only criticised Mr Androsch's statement but had also anticipated the outcome. The judgment ended as follows: “Even the quotation of the answer given by Mr Heinz Tschernutter placed at the top of the article – ‘Above all, there were to be no mistakes during the proceedings’ – gives the average reader the impression the court was being advised and urged to follow the same approach.”

The Kurdish government says it is acting to protect the public and the country's security. It says the PKK is a terrorist organisation that needs to be brought to justice. The U.S. State Department says it supports the PKK's right to express its views on political and social issues but opposes its use of force to impose the ban.

The group has called on other groups to do the same, calling for the ban to be lifted in the name of the Kurdish people. The Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) called for the lifting of a ban on its activities. The ban was imposed in 2003 to prevent the group from funding terrorism. The court said that the PKK had flouted the ban in another way by raising funds for the PKK through illegal means. The case was settled in the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which ruled in favor of the PKK's right to raise money for the fight against terrorism.

All investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation. The parties, their friends and relatives, their lawyers, the latter’s associates, consultants and staff, and any experts and witnesses are also bound by the law. However, disclosure to friends or relatives by the parties or their lawyer is not punishable. The reason for the confidentiality of judicial investigations is the need to protect the interests of the criminal proceedings by anticipating risks of collusion and the danger of evidence being tampered with or destroyed. The interest of the accused must not be disregarded, particularly vis-à-vis the presumption of innocence and, more broadly, the accused's personal relations and interests.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56925/08) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fine imposed on him in criminal proceedings for having published information covered by the secrecy of criminal investigations had violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 1 July 2014 a Chamber of that Section delivered its judgment (see A.B. v. Switzerland, no.56925-08, 1 July 14), in which it declared the application admissible and held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 10. M.B. had been remanded in custody after an incident on 8 July 2003 in which he had rammed his car into pedestrians, before throwing himself off the Lausanne Bridge. The incident, in which three people had died and eight others had been injured, had caused much emotion and controversy in Switzerland. The article in question concerned a set of criminal proceedings against M.B., a motorist who was being held in custody at the time of the incident. The Court heard addresses by Mr Poncet, Mr Schürmann and Mr Hoffmann and replies to questions put by judges. The application was brought by a journalist by profession. The article was accompanied by several photographs of letters which M.B. had sent to the investigating judge. The article also included a brief summary entitled ‘He lost his marbles...’ (“Il a perdu la boule...”) It appears from the file that the applicant’s article was not the only piece to have been published on the Lausanne Bridge tragedy.M.B., did not lodge a complaint against the applicant for his article in the Tribune de Genève on 14 August 2003. The authorities responsible for the criminal investigation had themselves decided to inform the press of certain aspects of the investigation, which had led to the publication of an article. M.B. was sentenced to one month’s imprisonment, suspended for one year. The Lausanne Police Court replaced the prison sentence with a fine of 4,000 Swiss francs (CHF) (approximately 2,667 euros) The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. His appeal was dismissed on 30 January 2006 by the Criminal Court of Cassation of the Canton of Vaud. In April 2008, the Federal Court dismissed the appeals. Its decision was served on the applicant on 9 May 2008. The relevant passages from the decision follow. “In short, the appellant submits that his conviction for a breach of Article 293 of the Criminal Code is contrary to federal law. He does, on the other hand, submit that having received that information in good faith without obtaining it unlawfully, he had the duty as a professional journalist to publish it’ Anyone who makes public documents, investigations or deliberations of an authority which are secret by law or by virtue of a decision taken by that authority, acting within its powers, will be punished by a fine. The court may decide not to impose any penalties if the secret thus made public is of minor importance. According to case-law, this provision proceeds from a formal conception of secrecy. In its Stoll v. Switzerland judgment of 10 December 2007, the European Court of Human Rights confirmed that this formal conception was not contrary to Article 10 ECHR inasmuch as it did not prevent publication of the documents in question. In order to exclude the application of paragraph 3, the court must first of all examine the reasons for classifying the information as secret. In pursuance of Article 184 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Canton of Vaud, all investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation itself as well as all non-public decisions and investigative measures. The law also specifies that the following are bound by secrecy vis-à-vis anyone who does not have access to the case file: the judges and judicial staff, and also the parties, their friends and relatives, their lawyers, the latter’s associates, consultants and staff. However, disclosure to friends or relatives by the parties or their lawyer is not punishable (see Article 185a CPP/VD). The aim is to maintain the authority and impartiality of the judiciary in accordance with the wording of Article 10 of the ECHR. This is the inescapable conclusion as regards the records of interviews of the accused. It would be inadmissible to allow such documents to be analysed in the public sphere, before the conclusion of the investigation and before the trial. The letters sent by the accused to the investigating judge focused on practical problems and criticisms of his lawyer (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 7). We might point out here that it appears from the impugned publication that it is not the first time that such a thing has happened. The appellant submits that he had the professional duty (under former Article 32 of the Criminal Code) as a journalist to publish the information in question because of what he describes as the obvious interest in the ‘Lausanne Bridge’ case for the population of French-speaking Switzerland. He considers that in the light of European case-law, the basic assumption should be that publication is justified in principle unless there is a pressing social need to maintain secrecy. In the instant case the information published by the appellant, in so far as it concerned the content of the records of his interviews and his correspondence with the investigating judge, cannot be described as a secret of minor importance. The cantonal court found that while the accident of 8 July 2003, the circumstances of which were undoubtedly unusual, had triggered a great deal of public emotion, it had nevertheless, in legal terms, been simply a road accident with fatal consequences. It is true that the ‘Lausanne Bridge case’ attracted extensive media coverage (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 8, to which the cantonal judgment refers) However, this circumstance alone, alongside the unusual nature of the accident, is insufficient to substantiate a major public interest in publishing the confidential information in question. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute a public interest. The same applies to the appellant’s requests to the investigating judge in relation to his choice of defence lawyer. Public-law appeal, is binding on this court (see section 277 bis of the Federal Criminal Procedure Act) 8.2.1. The appellant fails to demonstrate the ‘obvious’ interest to the general public of the information published. The headline of the article already lacked objectivity. It suggested that the case had already been tried in the author’s view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a reckless driver. The mode of publication can play a more important role in the context of safeguarding freedom of expression. The cantonal court concluded that this factor did not indicate that the public interest in receiving information prevailed. The manner in which he quoted the excerpts from the records of interviews and reproduced the letters sent by the defendant to the judge pointed to the motives of the author of the impugned article. Readers of this highly biased publication would have formed an opinion and subjectively prejudged the future action to be taken by the courts regarding this case. The appellant did not explicitly criticise the amount of the fine imposed on him. Nor did he challenge the refusal to grant him a probationary period after which the fine would be struck out (former Article 49, point 4) under Swiss law. The fine does not exceed half the amount of the appellant’s monthly income at the material time (see Police Court judgment, point 1, p. 5), and there is nothing to suggest that his freelance status at the time of the first-instance judgment led to any significant drop in his earnings. The sanction for the offence with which the appellant is charged did not prevent him from expressing his views, since it was imposed after the article had been published. It is unclear, in view of the nature of the offence charged (the least serious in the classification set out in the Swiss Criminal Code), how the sanction imposed on the applicant could be regarded as a form of censorship.

Both sought a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b) The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. There appeared before the Court: O. Jacot-Guillarmod, Head of the Department of International Affairs, Federal Department of Justice, Agent, Mr. P. Zappelli, Cantonal Judge, Canton of Fribourg, and Mr. B. Münger. Mr. Vandenberghe, Delegate of the Commission. Mr P. Rechsteiner, avocat, Counsel. Mr J. De Meyer, substitute judge, was replaced by Mr. Ryssdal. The Court decided to inspect the impugned paintings by Josef Felix Müller. The first applicant, Josef Felix Müller, a painter born in 1955, lives in St. Gall. The other nine applicants are: Charles Descloux, art critic, born in 1939 and living in Fribourg. The artists were meant to make free use of the space allocated to them. Their works, which they created on the spot from early August 1981 onwards, were to have been removed when the exhibition ended on 18 October 1981. The exhibition, entitled ‘Fri-Art 81’, was held as part of the celebrations of the 500th anniversary of the Canton of Friburg’s entry into the Swiss Confederation. Josef Felix Müller produced three large paintings entitled “Drei Nächte, drei Bilder’ (“Three Nights, Three Pictures’) They were on show when the exhibition began on 21 August 1981. The prosecutor thought that one of the three pictures also infringed freedom of religious belief and worship within the meaning of Article 261 of the Criminal Code. The court sentenced each of them to a fine of 300 Swiss francs (SF) for publishing obscene material (Article 204) but acquitted them on the charge of infringing freedom of religion (Article 261) It also ordered that the confiscated paintings should be deposited in the Art and History Museum of the Canton of Fribourg for safekeeping. The court pointed out that “the law [did] not define obscenity for the purposes of Article 204 CC [Criminal Code]’ The overall impression is of persons giving free rein to licentiousness and even perversion. The subjects - sodomy, fellatio, bestiality, the erect penis - are obviously morally offensive to the vast majority of the population. The artistic merit of the three works exhibited in Fribourg is admittedly less obvious than is supposed by the witness Ammann. The court will not order the destruction of theThree works. sthalle in Basle as to Josef Felix Müller’s artistic qualities. Müller's works seized in Fribourg appear rather scamped. The court concurs with the relevant findings of the Federal Court in the Rey judgment. The Art and History Museum of the Canton of Friburg meets the requirements for preventing any further breach of Article 204 of the Criminal Code. The three confiscated paintings will be deposited there and will be available to a few serious specialists capable of taking an exclusively artistic or cultural interest in them.“All the applicants appealed on points of law on 24 February 1982; in particular, they challenged the trial court’s interpretation as regards the obscenity of the relevant paintings’ Josef Felix Müller’s paintings aroused “repugnance and disgust’ One of the paintings contains no fewer than eight erect members. All the persons depicted are entirely naked and one of them is engaging simultaneously in various sexual practices with two other males and an animal. Even the animals’ tongues (especially in the smallest painting) are more suggestive, in shape and aspect, of erect male organs than of tongues. The court is likewise unconvinced by the appellants’ contention that the paintings are symbolical. What counts is their face value, their effect on the observer, not some abstraction utterly unconnected with the visible image. Not much of the argument in the appeal was directed to the issues of intention or of awareness of obscenity, nor indeed could it have been. The important thing is not the artist’s meaning or purported meaning but the objective effect of the image on the observer. It should be possible to show in an exhibition pictures which, if they were displayed in the market-place, would fall foul of Article 204. Similar pictures by Josef Felix Müller, moreover, had been exhibited in Basle in February 1982 and it had not occurred to anyone to regard them as being obscene. As the trial court pointed out, the defendants at the very least acted recklessly. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 26 January 1983. Josef Felix Müller would certainly not show his paintings in Fribourg in the near future. On the other hand, they could be shown without any difficulty elsewhere, as was proved by his exhibition in Basle in February 1982. It was consequently out of all proportion to deprive him of them. The paintings in issue show an orgy of unnatural sexual practices (sodomy, bestiality, petting), which is crudely depicted in large format. They are liable grossly to offend the sense of sexual propriety of persons of ordinary sensitivity. The artistic licence relied on by the appellant cannot in any way alter that conclusion in the instant case. Josef Felix Müller had three of his paintings confiscated in 1982. The Cantonal Court found that the paintings were obscene. The Federal Court found them to be inadmissible as they had not first been heard by the cantonal courts. The paintings were put on display in an exhibition open to the public which had been advertised on posters and in the press. There was no condition of admission to ‘Fri-Art 81’, such as an age-limit.“ The overall impression created by Müller’s paintings is such as to be morally offensive to a person of normal sensitivity.” ‘A work of art is not obscene, however, if the artist contrives to present subjects of a sexual nature in an artistic form such that their offensiveness is toned down' Confiscation is a preventive measure in rem. Confiscation remains however the rule. It should be departed from only where a more lenient order achieves the desired aim. The Federal Court has, moreover, held that a measure should not remain in force where the circumstances justifying it cease to obtain. The court preferred a morelenient measure which achieved the aim of security, whilst complying with the principle of proportionality. In this case, where the applicant has availed himself of the possibility of applying for the return of the paintings. ‘almost eight years later’. “Almost eight years after”. ’The court’s decision was ‘a reasoned decision’ and ‘contradicts’ the argument that the confiscation was an act of war. Josef Felix Müller recovered his paintings in March 1988. The artist is entitled to have his works returned to him. There is no reason to believe that he will use the three paintings in future to offend other people’s moral sensibilities. Since then he has become known for more ‘demanding’ works, to use the terms of the art critic who gave evidence in 1982. Having achieved a certain repute, he may find it unnecessary to shock by resorting to vulgarity. ...“ It is not necessary to attach any obligations to this decision. If J.F. Müller decided to exhibit the three painting again elsewhere, he knows that he would be running the risk of further action by the courts’.

Guy Ankerl sued the landlord, Chrysanthemum SA, for refusing to let him his flat. The Canton of Geneva Court of Justice dismissed his appeal. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. The Federal Court upheld the Canton's decision. The appeal was heard by the Supreme Court of France, which heard the case in 1991. The case was settled in the Supreme court of France and was heard in Paris in 1995. It was decided that there was no legal relationship between the parties. The lower court ruled that the landlord was entitled to raise his ownership against the subtenant. The appeals court upheld the original decision and the appeal was dismissed.

Mr Meftah was charged with using a vehicle registration document that had been obtained illegally and handling a stolen vehicle. He was remanded in custody from 16 April to 18 May 1992. The applicants were born in 1960, 1950 and 1938 and live at Irigny, at Colombes and in Paris respectively. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 February 2002 (Rule 59 § 2) The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial on the merits. The Court heard addresses by Mr Rio, Mr Abraham and Mr Cotte, and also their replies to questions put by some of the judges. The case of Mr Adoud was heard at the Mâcon Criminal Court. The applicant was found guilty of exceeding the speed limit by at least 40 k.p.h. He was sentenced to eight months' imprisonment and a fine of 10,000 French francs (FRF) The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation. By a judgment of 17 January 1996 the Courtof Cassation dismissed the appeal. The case was heard again at the Dijon Criminal Court in February 1995. The judge found the applicant guilty and imposed a suspended sentence of eight months’ imprisonment. The appeal was dismissed on 6 August 1996.

The case relates to a wall in Neuilly-sur-Seine, France. The applicant had built the wall without first obtaining planning permission. He was sentenced to a fine of 8,000 French francs (FRF), payment of which was suspended. The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of the Nanterre Criminal Court. The Court of Cassation dismissed Mr Vacher's appeal on the grounds that no ground of appeal had been filed in support of his appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the basis that the findings of fact, which cannot be appealed against, justify both the classification of the offence and the sentence.

Mr Gérard Vacher, a French national, is a company director and lives at Neuilly-sur-Seine. On 9 February 1990 the Nanterre Criminal Court sentenced the applicant to a fine of 8,000 French francs (FRF), payment of which was suspended. On 23 May 1991, following an appeal brought by Mr Vacher on 16 February 1990 and a subsequent cross-appeal by the prosecution, the Versailles Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of the court below.

He was sentenced to a fine of 8,000 French francs (FRF), payment of which was suspended, and ordered to alter the wall so it complied with regulations. On 19 June 1991 the case file for the appeal was registered by the Court of Cassation registry. On 14 August 1991 the applicant filed a pleading in support of his appeal. On 3 September 1991 the chief registrar of the court sent Mr Vacher the following letter: “Further to your letter, I have to inform you that the Criminal Division of the Court Of Cassation delivered a judgment on 6 August 1991 dismissing your appeal.“ The judgment in question, which was served on the applicant on 30 October 1995, was based on the following ground: � “No ground of appeal has been filed in support. of the appeal; the judgment appealed against is in the proper form and the findings of fact, which cannot be appealed against, justify both the classification of the offence and the sentence.’

Between 1974 and 1990 the applicant was convicted of sexual offences including attempted rape, sexual abuse of children, sexual assault, attempted sexual assault and dangerous assault. He spent some eleven years in prison before being released on probation. He has now been detained in Aachen Prison for four years and nine months. The court found that owing to his criminal tendencies, it was very likely that the applicant would commit further serious sexual offences comparable to those he was found guilty of on release. Therefore, his preventive detention was necessary. He served his prison sentence until 17 January 1995 and was then held in preventive detention until 29 March 1995, when the preventive detention order was suspended on probation and the applicant released.
