The applicant has been in preventive detention in Aachen Prison since 26 May 2000. He was ordered to be detained by the Cologne Regional Court of 14 February 1990 and the Cologne Court of Appeal of 11 November 1996. He argued his detention violated Article 5 of the Convention and Article 67d of the Criminal Code. He is currently serving a full prison sentence imposed in the judgment of 11 Nov 1996 until 25 May 2000 and has been on probation since May 2002. The decision of the Aachens Regional Court in July 2003 was upheld by the Federal Constitutional court in February 2004. It said that preventive detention under Article 66 of the Criminal Code, which was to be qualified as a measure of correction and prevention and not as a penalty, neither violated the Convention nor the Basic Law. The applicant was released from preventive detention on probation on 26 May 2000.

The decision of the Cologne Court of Appeal, endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, dismissed the applicant's appeal on 10 September 2003. It added that preventive Detention under Article 66 of the Criminal Code was to be qualified as a measure of correction and prevention and not as a penalty.

The first placement in preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty. The court also held that the provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot) These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal Code in its version in force since January 1998. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive Detention was abolished. The Court also ruled that the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period was not compatible with the Basic Law.

The Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading judgment concerning the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period. The court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal code in its version in force since 2001. The judge said that the provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot). The court ruled that the former maximum duration of a first period of preventive Detention was abolished.

Article 67d of the Criminal Code was amended by the Combating of Sexual Offences and Other Dangerous Offences Act of 26 January 1998, which entered into force on 31 January 1998. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions on the retrospective prolongation of preventive detention were incompatible with the Basic Law as they failed to comply with the constitutional protection of legitimate expectations guaranteed in a State governed by the rule of law. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the. Criminal Code in its version in force since. 1998. Relevant case-law of the Federal. Constitutional Court of Germany is cited as a source of the case.

The Federal Constitutional Court ordered that all provisions declared incompatible with the Basic Law remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. In its reasoning, the Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention made by this Court in its judgment in the case of M. v. Germany.

The Federal Constitutional Court ordered that all provisions declared incompatible with the Basic Law remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. In relation to detainees whose preventive detention had been prolonged or ordered retrospectively, the courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences and if, additionally, they suffered from a mental disorder. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality.

The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway, the L 52. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The Administrative Court dismissed the first request as irrelevant to the case. Administrative Court said the complaint was not based on any reasonable overall plan. The Regional Court considered that the applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. The court would have to decide at the next periodic review whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations in the conditions of his detention and had not been considered as no longer posing a threat to the public. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. The original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and that only the excerpts were still available. The Munich general public prosecutor confirmed the decision of the public prosecutor’s office of 4 August 2009 to discontinue the investigation. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. The Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2, 19, 4 and 103 of the German Basic Law (Gürzingerzwingungsverfahren) The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. In its decision the Constitutional Court referred to the case-law concerning the procedural obligation of Article 2 of the Convention.

The right to freedom to move people and property also includes freedom of speech, as well as the right not to interfere with the right of others to hold opinions. The Agricultural Authority ordered the Federal Forestry Administration to provide the applicant with a certain quantity of timber within four weeks. The applicant appealed against this decision, claiming that a fixed annual supply of timber should be granted irrespective of the need to maintain the cabins. On 25 August 1994 and 25 January 1995 hearings were held. On 6 February 1995 the Agricultural Authority issued a decision, by which it amended the regulatory deed of 1868 and determined the provision of timber. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) on 30 May 1996. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of sufficient prospects of success and remitted the case to the Administrative Court. The applicant, a Muslim, decided, on her own initiative, to wear the niqab in accordance with her religious beliefs. She argued that the provision in question expressly targeted the Islamic veil, which she wore, and that the resulting ban constituted an interference with her rights. She contended that the interference did not pursue a legitimate aim as the principle of secularism was not a constitutional principle and there could therefore be a breach of Article 14 of the Convention. The case was heard by the Conseil d’État and the verdict was handed down in September 2013. The decision was made to uphold the ban on the wearing of the burqa.

Dr Herbert Wille was the President of the Liechtenstein Administrative Court. His comments were published in the 17 February issue of the Lebanese Volksblatt. He was asked to explain his views on the role of the Constitutional Court. Wille said that he did not consider himself to be bound by the Constitution. He said that the court could be appealed to in the event of a disagreement between the Prince and the people. He added that he considered the government’s attitude to be 'incredibly arrogant' and that he had lost his confidence in the government. He later regained his confidence after a compromise was reached between the government and the Diet.

He still does not consider himself to be bound by the constitution, he writes. He says he has lost confidence in the government after the report was published in the Volksblatt in February 1995. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49151/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a Rom of Spanish nationality, complained about a refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension, following the death of her husband. She alleged that there had been a violation of Article 14 of the. Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 12 of. the Convention. The Court heard addresses by Mr Blasco Lozano, Ms Queipo de Llano López-Cózar and Mr S. Sánchez Lorente, Counsel. The applicant was born in 1956 and lives in Madrid. She and her husband were married in November 1971 according to their community’s own rites. The marriage was solemnised in accordance with Roma customs and cultural traditions and was recognised by that community. The applicant had six children, who were registered in the family record book issued to the couple by the Spanish civil registration authorities on 11 August 1983. In a decision of 27 March 2001, the INSS refused to grant her one on the following ground: “[she was] not and [had] never been the wife of the deceased prior to the date of death” The applicant filed a claim with the Labour Court. In a judgment dated 30 May 2002 of Labour Court no. 12 of Madrid, she was granted an entitlement to receive a survivor’s pension with a base rate of 903.29 euros per month. Her Roma marriage thus being recognised as having civil effects. Article 61 of the Civil Code provides that marriage has civil effects from the time it is solemnised but that it must be registered in the Civil Register if those effects are to be recognised. The argument relied upon against the applicant is solely the non-recognition of the civil effects of her marriage to the insured person (a working man of Spanish nationality) The INSS refused to grant the applicant a survivor’s pension because the marriage between the widow and the deceased is not recognised. The refusal by the INSS reveals discriminatory treatment on grounds of ethnic affiliation in breach of Article 14 of the Spanish Constitution and Directive 2000/43/EC. The Madrid Higher Court of Justice quashed the impugned judgment, giving the following reasons: “... It should be noted that the principle of equality and non-discrimination is based on the idea that equal situations should be treated equally” The INSS appealed the decision, and the High Court quashed it on 7 November 2002. In Spain there are statutory norms governing marriage. An ethnic group is merely a group which is differentiated on grounds of race. The morality of the rite or its conformity with public order are not called into question, but only its capacity to produce erga omnes obligations. Section 174 of the LGSS requires that a person be the spouse of the deceased in order to benefit from the survivor’s pension, and the notion of spouse has been interpreted strictly according to an established constitutional and ordinary case-law. A couple living together de facto as husband and wife and many others who, in reality, are not married under the applicable law, are excluded from the benefit of that pension. The court ruled that 'discrimination by absence of differentiation' did not arise from Article 14 of the Spanish Constitution. The court rejected the idea that the recognition of the civil effects of a marital relationship created by certain specific religious rites, but not one that has been solemnised according to Roma rites and customs, may entail directly or indirectly, the alleged ethnic discrimination. ... To sum up, in view of the fact that the law establishes a general possibility – neutral from a racial and ethnic point of view – of marrying in the civil form, and that the legislature, the courts must reject the idea of discrimination on social grounds. in the case of the surviving spouse. A dissenting opinion was appended to the judgment. It referred to judgment no. 199/2004, in which the Constitutional Court had found a violation of the right to equality in a case concerning the widower of a civil servant. The two claimants had applied for a survivor’s pension on the basis of what they considered to be a marital relationship, albeit that it had not been registered civilly. The dissenting judge concluded as follows: “It is disproportionate for the Spanish State, which took into consideration the applicant and her Roma family by issuing them with a family record book, granting them large-family status, affording health-care assistance to her and her six children and collecting the corresponding contributions from her Roma husband for nineteen years, three months and eight days, now to refuse to recognise her.” The applicant was granted a survivor’s pension with effect from 1 January 2007, as the partner of M.D. the Roma marriage. The relevant provisions of the Spanish Constitution are as follows: Article 14 “Spaniards shall be equal before the law; they may not be discriminated against in any way on account of birth, race, sex, religion, opinion or any other condition or personal or social circumstance” Article 16 “1. Freedom of ideas, religion and worship shall be guaranteed to individuals and communities without any restrictions on its expression other than those necessary for the maintenance of public order as protected by law.” The relevant provisions of the Civil Code, in its current version, read as follows: Article 44 “A man and a woman shall have the right to enter into marriage’ Article 49 “Any Spanish national is entitled to marry in Spain or abroad: before a magistrate, a mayor or a public servant designated by the present Code. ” “In the religious form provided for by law. [Any Spanishnational] may also marry abroad in accordance with the formalities required by the law in the place where the marriage is solemnised.” � “When the death of one of the partners has occurred before the entry into force of the present Law, the survivor will be entitled to the benefits provided for in the first paragraph’ Law no. 40/2007 of 4 December 2007 on social security measures, amending the LGSS, reads as follows: Third transitional amendment “Exceptionally, a survivor’s pension shall be granted where the death of the insured person occurred before the entry into force of the present Act, subject to fulfilment of the following conditions’” The recognition of the pension entitlement will take effect from 1 January 2007. Marriages solemnised according to the rites of those religious denominations are therefore recognised by the General Social Security Act. ‘The beneficiary has no recognised entitlement to receive a contributory pension from the social security. ...’ The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities, opened for signature on 1 February 1995, contains the following provisions in particular. Article 1 “The protection of national minorities and of the rights and freedoms of persons belonging to those minorities forms an integral part of the international protection of human rights, and as such falls within the scope of international cooperation” Article 4 “1. The Parties undertake to guarantee to persons. belonging to national minorities the right of equality before the law and of equal protection of the law’ Article 5 “In this respect, any discrimination based on belonging to a national minority shall be prohibited.” Spain signed the Convention on the day that it was opened for signature and ratified it on 1 September 1995. It came into force in respect of Spain on 1 February 1998. The Convention states that: “The Government shall refrain from policies or practices aimed at assimilation of persons belonging to national minorities against their will and shall protect these persons from any action aimed at such assimilation.” Spain ratified the Convention in September 1995 and signed it on the first day it was open for signature. Spain's membership of the Convention was approved by the European Parliament on September 23, 1995, and ratified by the Spanish Senate on September 26, 1995.

Ms Eliane van Glabeke (“the applicant”) was compulsorily admitted to Lommelet de Saint-André Psychiatric Hospital, where she was injected with unknown substances. The Government submitted that the applicant had been “picked up” on the public highway by a police officer who had asked for her to be admitted to hospital. They added that her admission had been ordered on the basis of two medical certificates issued by different doctors to the effect that she required hospital treatment. The parties have been unable to establish the date on which the letter was received. On 22 April 2002 State Counsel's Office decided to take no further action on that application as it was devoid of purpose. On 28 March 2002 Afcap in turn applied to the President of the Lille tribunal de grande instance for the immediate discharge of her daughter. The application was denied. The parties have not yet been able to reach an agreement over the issue of the daughter's immediate discharge. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2034/07) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding him guilty of serious insult against the King of Spain amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to freedom of expression. The Court examined the information available to it, it decided that no hearing was necessary. The case was decided not to hold a public hearing as the applicant had not asked for it. The application was lodged by Mr Arnaldo Otegi Mondragon (“the applicant”), on 5 January 2007. The applicant, as spokesperson for the Sozialista Abertzaleak parliamentary group, outlined his group’s political response to the situation concerning the newspaper Euskaldunon Egunkaria. He said that inaugurating a project with the King of the Spaniards, who was the Supreme Head of the Civil Guard (Guardia Civil) and the Commander-in-Chief of the Spanish armed forces, was absolutely pitiful. He added that the King was in charge of those who had tortured the persons detained in connection with the operation. On 7 April 2003 the public prosecutor lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for “serious insult against the King” The High Court of Justice found the applicant not guilty of the charges against him. The court found that his remarks had been ‘clearly offensive, improper, unjust, ignominious and divorced from reality’ The applicant, as a politician, had sought to express political criticism in the context of freedom of expression, one of the foundations of the rule of law and democracy. The Constitution does not guarantee the right to freedom of. expression solely in relation to certain points of view that are considered correct, but in. relation to all ideas, subject to the limits which it lays down, the court found. The applicant argued that there was no insult or attempt to dishonour in saying that the Civil Guard had tortured the persons detained in connection with the closure of the. newspaper Euskaldunon Egunkaria. The public prosecutor lodged an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. He argued that the law protected the honour of the King as a specific individual possessed of personal dignity. In the view of the public prosecutor, it was clear that the King had been performing official duties and that he was a figure in the public eye. That did not deprive him of the right to respect for his honour, he said. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the lower court, making several references to the Court’s case-law. It sentenced the applicant to one year's imprisonment, suspended his right to stand for election for the duration of the sentence and ordered him to pay a fine. The Supreme Court considered the impugned remarks to have been value judgments rather than statements of fact. The judge agreed with the Basque Country High Court of Justice that the remarks had not targeted the King’s private life or his personal honour but had been directed solely at his institutional role as Commander-in-Chief of the Spanish armed forces. The applicant had not claimed that the King was responsible for actual acts of torture, only that he was strictly liable as Head of the State apparatus. In view of the seriousness of the insulting comments and the fact that the applicant had deliberately expressed them in public, the Supreme Court sentenced him to one year's imprisonment. The Supreme Court’s judgment had incorrectly weighed the competing interests at stake. The statements in question had not been disproportionate in the context in which they had been uttered. The Constitutional Court noted at the outset that the right to freedom of expression did not encompass a right to proffer insults. It pointed out in that connection that the Constitution did not prohibit the use of hurtful expressions in all circumstances. The right to free speech did not protect vexatious expressions which, regardless of their veracity, were offensive and ignominious and were not pertinent for the purpose of conveying the opinions or information in question. The finding was all the more valid with regard to the King, who, by virtue of Article 56 § 3 of the Constitution, was “not liable” and was a “symbol of the unity and permanence of the democracy’ The applicant was imprisoned on 8 June 2007 after the Supreme Court upheld a judgment of the Audiencia Nacional of 27 April 2006 sentencing him to fifteen months’ imprisonment for publicly defending terrorism. In a decision (auto) of 15 May 2006, the Basque Country High Court of Justice ordered that enforcement of the applicant’s sentence be stayed for three years. According to the Government, his sentence was remitted on 16 July 2009. He is currently in pre-trial detention in connection with other criminal proceedings and is due to appear in court on 20 July. The Constitutional Court held that the remarks had expressed open contempt for the King and the institution he embodied, affecting the essential core of his dignity.

The accused in custody does not have an enforceable right to attend hearings in an appeal on a point of law. If he has not chosen a lawyer and is not brought to the hearing, the President of the court having jurisdiction will appoint one for him if he so requests. An accused who is at liberty may appear in person or be represented by a lawyer at the appeal hearing (Article 350 para. 2). According to the case-law of the Federal Court, defence counsel can be assigned to him only under Article 140 para.2. In all other cases the court has to hold a hearing before taking its decision (Article 349 para. 5). Article 350 para. 1 requires that the accused and his lawyer be informed of the date and place of the hearing. If it is not possible to contact the former, notification to the latter is sufficient. The appellant is heard first and the last address to the court is always made by the accused (Article 351).3. “Common defence counsel” (gemeinschaftliche Verteidigung) (art. 6-1, 6-3-c) of the Convention. The Government stated that this interpretation has since been accepted by all the Criminal Chambers of the Federal Court. The 1st Criminal Chamber followed these precedents in its judgment of 29 November 1977. Karl Obermeier was formerly employed by a private insurance company. He was suspended from his duties by his employer without giving reasons. He alleged that the measure was designed to penalise him for having instituted legal proceedings against the company and was therefore unjustified. On 23 April 1981 the Linz Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s claims. The company appealed on points of law. On 25 November 1981 the Regional Court allowed the appeal as regards the part of the judgment concerning the revocation of the suspension. It considered that by virtue of clause 32 of the collective agreement for insurance employees, suspension of an employee was subject to certain conditions and that the first-instance court should have ascertained whether they were satisfied.

Karl Obermeier was formerly employed by a private insurance company in Austria. He was suspended from his duties by his employer on 10 March 1978. Mr Obermeier instituted proceedings in the Vienna Labour Court. On 23 April 1981 the Linz Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s claims. The company appealed on points of law. On 25 November 1981 the. Linz Regional Court (Landesgericht) allowed the appeal as regards the part of the. judgment concerning the revocation of the suspension. The court dismissed the remainder of the appeal, finding that. a declaratory judgment may bear only on the existence of a legal. relationship (Rechtsverhältnis) and not on the validity of a. legal measure (Reachtshandlung) such as the suspension of an employee.

The Provincial Governor for Upper Austria confirmed the Board’s decision on 16 October 1981. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was brought by Mr Herwig C. Emmer-Reissig, a lawyer practising in Klosterneuburg and the owner of a parcel of land in Königstetten, which is designated as “forest” land in the zoning plan. He requested it to hear representatives of the District Farmer's Association (DFA, Bezirksbauernkammer) and the Austrian beekeeper association (ABA, Österreichischer Imkerbund) The Regional Government quashed the municipality's decision on 10 January 2001 and referred the case back to the municipal council. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court on 12 March 2002 and requested an oral hearing. The Administrative Court rejected the complaint as inadmissible for non-exhaustion of administrative remedies, as the applicant had failed to file an objection against the decision of 29 January 2002. The applicant's objection of 12 March 2003 was dismissed by the Lower Austria Regional Government on 22 July 2002. It found that, despite its request for a detailed business plan, the applicant failed to provide one. Accordingly, the alleged need for a shed for the so-called agricultural enterprise had not been made out. The application was rejected on 16 September 2003.

The Agency has the capacity to contract, to acquire and to dispose of movable and immovable property, and to be a party to legal proceedings. It has the duty to waive this immunity in all cases where reliance upon it would impede the course of justice and it can be waived without prejudicing the interests of the agency. Appeals Board will hear disputes between ESA staff and others. Board may rescind any decision against which there has been an appeal. Agreement was concluded between government of the Federal Republic of Germany and ESRO for the purpose of establishing a European Space Operations Centre, including the European Space Data Centre. Articles 1 to 4 of the Agreement concern the site for construction of the ESOC buildings and related matters. If the terms of employment of a staff member of the Organisation are not governed by the Organisation’s staff regulations, then they shall be subject to German laws and regulations. The Agreement concerning ESOC contains general provisions. Article 6 provides as follows: “1. Subject to the provisions of the Protocol on Privileges and Immunities of the. Organisation and of any complementary Agreement between the Federal. Republic of. Germany and the Organisation according to Article 30 of that Protocol” The application was made on 24 November 1994. The Commission declared the application admissible on 24 February 1997. In its report of 2 December 1997 the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the two separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government asked “for the applications to be rejected as inadmissible, or as an alternative for a finding that the Federal Republic of Germany has not violated Article 6’. The applicants invited the Court to hold that their rights pursuant to Article 6 had been violated and to award them just satisfaction under former Article 50.”

The case against her was dropped in May 1986, but she was still suspended from her position as chairperson of the Wilhelmshaven/Friesland local branch of the party.

The “indictment’ of 22 November 1983 specified eleven public, political activities that the applicant had engaged in for the DKP. The proceedings were stayed in order to widen the investigations to include further instances of the applicant's political activity that had come to light in the meantime. In a supplementary ‘indictments“ of 5 February 1986 Mrs Vogt was accused of also failing to comply with her duties as a civil servant. She was still a member of the “Executive Committee’ (Vorstand) of the Bremen/North Lower Saxony regional branch (Bezirksorganisation) at the time of her arrest.

It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and also, in the case of the Commission's request, of Article 14. Mrs Dorothea Vogt, a German national born in 1949, lives in Jever in the Land of Lower Saxony. She studied literature and languages at the University of Marburg/Lahn for six years, during which time she became a member of the German Communist Party. In June 1977 she sat the second State examination to become a secondary-school teacher (zweite Staatsprüfung für das Lehramt an Gymnasien) and obtained a post from 1 August 1977 as a teacher. On 1 February 1979 she was appointed a permanent civil servant (Beamtin auf Lebenszeit) The applicant had engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980. She had stood as a DKP candidate in the 1982 elections to the Parliament (Landtag) of the Land of Lower Saxony. Mrs Vogt was accused of also failing to comply with her duties as a civil servant in that she had been a member of the “Executive Committee“ of the Bremen/North Lower Saxonies regional branch. She was also accused of taking part in and addressing the 7th party congress, held from 6 to 8 January 1984 in Nuremberg, as Chairperson of the Wilhelmshaven/Friesland local branch of the party. From October 1986 Mrs Vogt was paid only 60 per cent of her salary (Dienstbezüge) The applicant, who by her own account has been a member of the DKP since 1972, argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany and in its external relations and her combat against neo-fascism were in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. The DKP, whose aims had always been wrongly alleged (but never proven) to be anti- constitutional, has never been proven to have taken such a stance. Disciplinary proceedings against civil servants on account of their political activities on behalf of a party that had not been banned breached International Labour Organisation (ILO) Convention No. 111 concerning discrimination in respect of employment and occupation. It also violated Article 10 (art. 10) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Disciplinary Division held that the applicant had failed to comply with her duty of political loyalty and ordered her dismissal as a disciplinary measure. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. The DKP's aims, as described in the Mannheim programme of 21 October 1978 (see paragraph 22 below), were clearly opposed to the free democratic constitutional system of the Federal Republic of Germany. The applicant was dismissed for having betrayed the relationship of trust between herself and her employer. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. It did so in recognition of the fact that apart from her breach of the duty of loyalty Mrs VogT had always performed her duties unexceptionably and enthusiastically and needed some income to be protected from immediate hardship. The fact that she had done her work satisfactorily for many years and that she was held in high regard by her pupils and their parents alike was immaterial. The applicant lodged an appeal against the above judgment with the Lower Saxony Disciplinary Court, reiterating her previous arguments (see paragraph 18 above). The court ruled that the DKP's political aims were incompatible with the constitutional system. The party aimed to establish a regime similar to that existing in the communist countries around 1980. Article 48 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the corresponding legislation of the Land of Lower Saxony securing the right to take office as a member of parliament did not set limits on the duty of political loyalty. The European Court of Human Rights had ruled that a decision by a competent authority relating to admission to the civil service did not amount to an interference with freedom of expression. The same approach applied in cases where a person had already been appointed to a permanent civil service post. Mrs Vogt's conduct had been unlawful. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. This did not mean that her conduct was not culpable. to achieve some of the DKP’s short-term objectives such as reducing unemployment, promoting peace and eliminating so-called Berufsverbote (prohibitions on pursuing various occupations) The court referred to the following observations made by the Federal Administrative Court (Bundesverwaltungsgericht) Political loyalty entailed a duty for civil servants to dissociate themselves unequivocally from groups which criticised or cast aspersions on the State and the existing constitutional system. For as long as the DKP had not abandoned its anti-constitutional aims, civil servants' duty of political loyalty prevented them from actively working for it. The court added that such a breach of duty was especially serious in the case of a teacher, who was supposed to teach the children entrusted to her care the fundamental values of the Constitution. Parents, who because of compulsory education had to send their children to State schools, were entitled to expect the State to rely on its servants' loyalty to the Constitution, the court said. The Federal Constitutional Court said Mrs Vogt had breached her duties as a civil servant. The court said that a more lenient disciplinary measure aimed at persuading her to abandon her political activities within the DKP was bound to fail. The Federal Constitutional Court invited the Federal Parliament, the Federal Council (Bundesrat) and the Federal Government to submit their written observations on the constitutional complaint. The court held that the contested interpretation of Section 539 of the Social Security Act did not violate the applicant's constitutional rights. The applicant alleged that he was the victim of a violation of his right to respect for private and family life, as guaranteed by Article 8. The Turkish Government did not avail themselves of their right to intervene in the proceedings. The application was assigned to the second Section of the Court (Rules 25 § 1 and 52 § 1) The case was decided on 22 April 2010. It was decided that the Chamber would rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. In a decision of 2 June 2003 the Aliens Department for the Canton of Neuchâtel ordered the applicant’s administrative removal for an indefinite duration. His appeals against that decision were dismissed. On 20 October 2004 the applicant was deported to Turkey. After returning to Switzerland illegally in May or June 2005, he was arrested and taken into custody on 1 July 2005. In a judgment of 22 May 2008, which became final on 22 August, the First Section of the Court unanimously declared admissible the complaint under Article 8 and found that there had been a violation of that provision. On that basis, it held that Switzerland had to pay the applicant the sums of 3,000 euros (EUR) for non-pecuniary damage and EUR 4,650 for the costs and expenses he had incurred ‘in the domestic proceedings and before the Court’ The Court notes that the criminal activities in question were spread over a wide period (from 1994 to 2004) and that the two suspended sentences of 12 November 1997 and 10 November 1999 were activated in view of the further offences committed by the applicant. The Court observes that some of the conduct attributed to the applicant dated back to his adolescence and some to a relatively young age. The total duration of his prison sentences (eighteen and a half months in all) is thus far from negligible. It is undeniable that the convictions for wounding weigh heavily against him. Concerning the weapons offence, however, it appears to have been constituted merely by the possession of a tear-gas canister. In the light of comparable cases, the applicant’s convictions should be assessed for what they really are. The Court notes that the applicant, who was born on 18 December 1980, arrived in Switzerland on 21 September 1986, before the age of six. He had thus spent more than seventeen and a half years in Switzerland. Similarly, the domestic courts noted that he had not shown any awareness of his criminal activities and had refused to follow his psychotherapy. Whilst there is some debate between parties as to his professional integration in Switzerland, the Federal Court noted that his parents and brothers, one of whom had Swiss nationality, lived in the country. The Court does not feel obliged to settle this question. The applicant argued that his illness, having involved suicide attempts, could not be adequately treated in Turkey. The basic rule of the common law is that the jurisdiction of the criminal courts in the United Kingdom is confined to crimes committed within the territory of each court. An exception is provided by section 9 of the 1861 Act, which gives jurisdiction to British courts in respect of alleged murders and manslaughters committed by British citizens anywhere in the world. The Offences against the Person Act 1861 gives British courts jurisdiction in all crimes committed by a British citizen outside of the UK. The applicant's mother and her four siblings jointly inherited two estates in Stockholm. The ownership of the estates was over the years partly transferred to other members of the family. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35179/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) In May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The applicant owned a number of houses on the land managed by the applicant’s mother – which formed part of Marum 1:8. The applicant applied for a building permit to the Österåker Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) on 9 September 1987. The committee granted a permit for the building of a new house further away from the shore. The new house was built in 1988. In 1989 practically all the other joint owners of the two estates brought proceedings against the applicant in the District Court (tingsrätten) of Södra Roslag. The court stated that it was the applicant who owned the house and that she had built it without the necessary consent. The applicant sought to have the joint ownership of the two estates dissolved and individual plots assigned to the family members. The case had to be referred back by the Court of Appeal to the REFA for re-examination as the latter had made procedural errors. Subsequently, by a decision of 1 December 1995, the Real Estate Court allowed the creation of four individual plots on Marum 1:8. The Central Office of the National Land Survey (Lantmäteriverket) gave its opinion in the division proceedings. On 7 March 1996 the Office ordered the applicant to remove the house before 3 April 1996 or risk having it demolished at her own expense. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She claimed that she had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself in accordance with the District Court’s judgment of 10 May 1990. She stated she had started to dismantle the house but was not able to complete the work before 3 June 1996. She also requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. It appears from the court that the applicant was ordered to complete her appeal by 12 midnight on 5 June 1996 but did not receive the decision until the evening of 5 June as she was at the site of the house in issue. The house in issue was therefore demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. However, this claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996, referring to Chapter 3, section 21, of the Enforcement Code (Utsökningsbalken) The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. On 22 November 1996 the Real Estate Court gave judgment in the division proceedings. It decided that Marum 1:8 should be divided into six individual plots and one common plot. In this respect, the real estate court agreed with the opinion given by the Central Office of the National Land Survey on 14 March 1996. The applicant and her sister brought removal proceedings against several other joint owners of Marum 1:6 and 1:8. The District Court rejected the claims, finding that the buildings had been erected before 1991. The court also decided that further litigation in this respect should not be paid for through public legal aid. Following an appeal, the declaratory judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 26 February 1998. No further appeal was lodged and the appellate court’s judgment consequently acquired legal force. . On 14 April 2000 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Building Committee granted the applicant building permits for the reconstruction of the demolished house and the construction of two smaller outbuildings.

The decision was based on four grounds: the duty of assiduity, school rules, the Conseil d'Etat and a memorandum on pupils' safety during school activities. The appeal panel found that the applicant had breached all four grounds and that she had been expelled for failing to participate actively in physical education and sports classes. The applicant indicated that she would like to appeal the decision. The case was heard by an appeal panel and the decision was upheld in March 1999.

She sought 3,907 euros (650,000 pesetas) for the damage she had sustained and the cost of installing double glazing. The Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal admissible and invited the applicant, the representative of state council’s office and the Valencia City council to submit their observations. It further submitted that the appeal was confined to the decision of the Valencia High Court of Justice. The authorities were obliged to exercise their power when the breach of the fundamental rights attained a certain level of gravity, the second judge said, adding that the authorities had a duty to act when there was evidence of a causal link between their failure to act and the alleged violation.

A forged identity card bearing the applicant’s photo was discovered, together with a sawn-off shotgun. The employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawn off shotgun. On 30 September 1996 the investigating judge substituted for the charge of false imprisonment with voluntary release (an intermediate offence (délit) and made a partial discharge order. On 20 January 1997 the applicant requested that a bailiff be called on to record officially that his detention had become unlawful as the last order extending it had expired at midnight on 19 January 1997. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Créteil public prosecutor alleging arbitrary detention but had received no reply. The applicant made an application to the Indictment Division for his immediate release on the ground that he was being detained arbitrarily. In a judgment of 19 August 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that on 19 January 1995 a warrant of commitment was issued in respect of [the applicant], who was under investigation for offences including armed robbery. On expiry of its validity a year later, the investigating judge extended the detention three times for four months, the final extension taking effect on 19 September 1996” On 10 September 1997, the Indictment Division directed that the applicant be committed for trial at the Yvelines Assize Court charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment and other connected lesser offences. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 18 December 1997. In a judgment delivered on the same day on the civil claims the applicant was ordered to pay the civil party FRF 50,000 in damages. The initial warrant of commitment remained effective, in accordance with Article 181, second paragraph, of the Code, after the transfer order was issued and so remains until a decision on indictment is taken.

Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The costs of the proceedings are paid after the final ruling on the guilt of the accused. An accused person may never be required to make any advance payment on these costs. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. The text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that while Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) exempts an accused from paying in advance for the expenses incurred by the use of an interpreter, it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person.

The Code of Criminal Procedure states that the accused shall bear the costs of such part of the proceedings as concerned the act that gave rise to the conviction. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention specifies that “everyone charged with a criminal offence has the (right) ... to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court“ This text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Some courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear costs in question for all time and in all cases.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in the framework of terrorist activity, killing two members of the State security police force (‘CRS’) on 10 November 1992. In February 2007 the Sentence enforcement division of the Paris Court of Appeal released him on licence from 14 February 2007 to 14 February 2014, ordering to follow a seven-year programme of assistance and supervision. The applicant took part in a peaceful demonstration outside Agen Prison in support of Basque detainees being held there. The media reported on that demonstration. The Paris Sentence Enforcement Court delivered a judgment on 14 May 2008 imposing additional special obligations on the applicant. The latter judgment was quashed by judgment of the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation on 10 June 2009. The Public Prosecutor’s Office requested that the sentence enforcement judge of the Regional Court of Paris add both the aforementioned obligations in 2010. The applicant must continue, in accordance with his means, to pay into the Guarantee Fund for the compensation of victims of terrorism; and refraining from possessing or carrying a weapon. Philippe Bidart was sentenced to five years in prison in 2007. He was also banned from promoting Basque separatism and supporting detainees charged with terrorist acts. The Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the obligation in question ‘merely prohibited commenting on or condoning the offences committed’ The Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on points of law lodged by the applicant, on the grounds that the judgment had properly applied Article 132-45 [16] of the Penal Code. The appeal was dismissed on 30 March 2011 by the Criminal division of the court of cassation. It is understood that Mr Bidart will be released from prison on licence in early 2013.

The breathalyser test had shown an alcohol level of 0.63 mg/l in his breath. The applicant appealed, repeating his argument as regards the alleged imprecision of the breathalyer test. The Upper Austria Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) allowed the applicant’s appeal in part. In its decision of 17 June 2002 it found that an alcohol levels in the applicant's breath of. 0.59mg/l could be considered to have been confirmed.

The applicant argued that allowance should be made for 5% inaccuracy in the result of the breathalyser test. This would lead to an established alcohol level of less than 0.60 mg/l and his conduct would therefore constitute a less serious offence under Sections 5(1) and 99(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act. In its decision of 17 June 2002 it found that an alcohol level in the applicant’s breath of 0.59mg/l could be considered to have been confirmed, since allowance had to be made. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,162 on him with seventeen days’ imprisonment in the event of default.

The decision was served on the applicant on 24 July 2002. He did not lodge a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) within the statutory six-week time-limit. The Federal Minister for Traffic, Innovation and Technology lodged an official complaint (Amtsbeschwerde) against that decision. On 18 February 2005 the Administrative Court quashed the Independent Administrative Panel’s decision of 17 June 2002 and referred the case back to it. It found that the decision had applied the law incorrectly, since there was no ground to make allowance for inaccuracy in the breathalyser test. The applicant asserted that it would violate the requirements of a fair trial if the quashing of the decision following his official complaint had any negative consequences for him.

The Independent Administrative Panel convicted the applicant under sections 5(1) and 99(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act, which provides for a fine of between EUR 581 and EUR 3,633. It reduced the fine to EUR 1,000 with fourteen days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The Federal Minister for Traffic, Innovation and Technology lodged an official complaint (Amtsbeschwerde) against that decision, on the ground that it contained an error of law. On 18 February 2005 the Administrative Court, following the official complaint, quashed the decision of 17 June 2002 and referred the case back to it. It found that the decision had applied the law incorrectly.

The Independent Administrative Panel considered that the question about possible inaccuracy of the breathalyser test was not a matter of law. There was documentary evidence, and also evidence from an expert on weights and measurements, that for this particular type of breath analyser 5% inaccuracy could not be ruled out. The Federal Minister for Traffic, Innovation and Technology lodged an official complaint (Amtsbeschwerde) against that decision. The Administrative Court, following the official complaint, quashed the decision of 17 June 2002 and referred the case back to it. It found that the decision had applied the law incorrectly, since there was no ground to make allowance for inaccuracy.

The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court, claiming several violations of Article 6 of the Convention. He alleged that the proceedings had been unreasonably lengthy and that he had no remedy in this respect. The applicant also complained that he did not have a review by a higher tribunal as required by Article 2 of Protocol No. 7. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. On a request by the applicant on 21 July 2005 it transferred the case to the Administrative Court. On 23 May 2006 the administrative court dismissed the complaint as being unfounded. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 21 June 2006.

The Constitutional Court refused to hear the case in 2005, citing the length of the proceedings as the reason. It was finally dismissed in August 2006, but the case was re-submitted to the Constitutional Court again in August 2007. The court ruled that the case could not be heard because the proceedings had already been adjourned more than a year. The decision was made to issue a new complaint, and the case is now before the Court of Appeal again, this time with the case being referred back to the original complaint. The appeal was rejected again on 12 November 2007, and again in April 2008.

The decision was that the case could not be heard because of the length of the proceedings. The complaint was dismissed again on 10 October 2008. The trial was then adjourned until 10 November 2009. The final hearing was held on 14 August 2009. It was the first time the case had been heard by a full panel. The Court of Appeal made its decision in favor of the complaint on 13 October 2009.

Judge G. did not make any further comment on the matter after the jury was seated. He is therefore satisfied that the jury members were not disqualified from the trial. Jury member reported to police as a witness and told police about her observations in close connection to the day of the explosion. Her observations are of such a nature that it can be questioned whether she is impartial in this case. After this, W. withdrew from the jury and the hearing continued with the remaining 10 jury members. The question here is whether W.'s presence as a member of the jury during the first four days of the hearing may have influenced the jury's verdict. The High Court agrees with the High Court that W. was prejudiced. But it does not find that the jury member may, by having possibly stated her observations to the other members of the Jury, have influenced them so that they are disqualified. Jury members will regularly be told by the presiding judge that, when deciding on the question of guilt, they must only place emphasis on what is stated as evidence in court. There is no corresponding barrier to the jury members discussing the case among themselves – even continuously during the court hearing. I refer to the fact that W. was at no time called as a witness in the case, by either the prosecuting authority or the defendants. The prosecutor has stated to the Supreme Court that the observations she had told to the police on 10 July 1997 – including about parts of the vehicle in question's licence number – were clarified early on as being of no importance to the further investigation.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71932/12) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin II Regulation would subject him to inhuman and degrading treatment. The Court decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to expel the applicant to Hungary until further notice. It further requested the Hungarian Government to provide information regarding the status of the applicant’s asylum proceedings, as well as the reception conditions for unaccompanied minor asylum-seekers. The applicant left Afghanistan with two other refugees via the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and Serbia. Allegedly, the Hungarian authorities did not give any consideration to the fact that he was a minor. The Traiskirchen Federal Asylum Office (Bundes­asylamt) rejected the applicant’s asylum request in December 2011. On 11 January 2012 the Asylum Court quashed that decision on the grounds that the facts had not been established exhaustively. It stated that the Asylum Office had failed to update its country information regarding the risk of refoulement of asylum‑seekers from Hungary to Serbia. Furthermore, the decision had not established the legal framework under the Dublin II Regulation. On 28 February 2012 the Asylum Office again rejected the applicant’s asylum request and ordered his expulsion to Hungary under the Dublin II Regulation. Hungary expelled asylum-seekers to Serbia, if their first asylum proceedings were terminated and there was no obstacle under the non-refoulement rule. A person lodging a subsequent asylum request was not allowed to remain in Hungary. Hungary did not practise refoulement to Serbia and did not have a list of safe third countries. In most cases Serbia was considered to be a safe third country. It was in any event possible to lodge an appeal against the expulsion order itself and the judge's discretion could award the proceedings suspensive effect. The Hungarian authorities did not consider itself legally obliged to make use of the sovereignty clause. Hungary's asylum proceedings in Hungary had been discontinued on 24 October 2011. At that time, the applicant was still a minor. Hungarian authorities stated that unaccompanied minor asylum-seekers were usually immediately assigned a guardian, except when the applicant would reach the age of majority before the decision on the merits was made. If he was returned to Hungary, an asylum request would be considered a subsequent request which would not have automatic suspensive effect if there were no new circumstances supporting his application but there was a safe third country which he could be returned to. The Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court and requested the Austrian Government to stay the applicant’s transfer to Hungary until further notice. The Austrian Government complied with this request. The applicant was placed in a children’s home in Fót, where care and education were provided to them according to their age. It was very unlikely that a guardian would be appointed for him upon his return. The Court notes that on 1 January 2014 Regulation (EU) No 604/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council (“the Dublin III Regulation’) entered into force. However, at the time of the decision by the Austrian authorities to expel the applicant to Hungary, the Dublin II Regulation was the applicable legal basis. The aim is to avoid multiple applications and to guarantee that each asylum-seeker's case is dealt with by a single member State. Under the Dublin II Regulation, the member State responsible for examining an asylum application of an unaccompanied minor shall be that where a member of his or her family is legally present. In the absence of a family member, theMember State responsible is that where the minor has lodged an application for asylum. The applicant drove a car through a village. Police officers required him to stop by giving a sign with a red light. The applicant disregarded their sign and drove on, obliging the police officers to step aside. He was charged with resisting the exercise of official authority. On 12 December 1997 the Ried im Innkreis Regional Court acquitted the applicant of the above charge. As neither party appealed, the judgment became final and the applicant was fined 4,000 Austrian schillings (approximately 290 euros) and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. The case was dismissed by the Independent Administrative Panel on 15 December 1998.

The case was referred to the Administrative Court by decision of 17 August 2000. The case was referred to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) by decision of 17 August 2000. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint as the fine imposed did not exceed 726 euros and the case did not raise an important legal issue. The decision was served on the applicant and his counsel on 31 January 2003. The court's decision was published in full on 24 January 2004. It is available for download from the German version of this website.

The case involved the applicant's conviction under the Road Traffic Act for refusing to comply with. police officers' request to stop. The Constitutional Court dismissed his argument that his conviction violated the ne bis in idem principle. The Administrative Court accepted his complaint and issued a fine of 726 euros. The decision was served on the applicant and his counsel on 31 January 2003. The case did not raise an important legal issue and the fine imposed did not exceed 726 euro. The judge found that the offences at issue differed in their constituent elements and they were distinct. The applicant was acquitted of resisting the exercise of official authority as it had not been shown that he had driven towards the police officers and thus threatened them with bodily harm.

The Government, in their observations, requested the Court to give a separate decision on the admissibility of the application. The Court has found no reasons to discontinue the application of Article 29 § 3. As neither party appealed, the judgment became final. The application was brought by an Austrian national, Mr Roland Schutte (“the applicant”), on 23 May 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Postlmayr, a lawyer practising in Mattighofen. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador F. Trauttmansdorff. The applicant was charged with failure to comply with a request to stop for the purpose of a traffic control contrary to Section 97 § 5 of the Road Traffic Act (Straßenverkehrsordnung). The applicant submitted his defence on 4 February 1998, asserting in particular that the conduct of proceedings for the said traffic offence violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. The applicant was acquitted of the offence of resisting the exercise of official authority in respect of the same act. Upon the applicant's appeal, the Upper Austria Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) held a hearing on 17 September 1998. The case was referred to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) by decision of 17 August 2000. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint as the fine imposed did not exceed 726 euros and the case did not raise an important legal issue. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 31 January 2003. The case was heard by the Independent Administrative Panel on 23 May 2002. The hearing was adjourned until 31 December 2003, when the decision was handed over to the applicant. It found that the single act constituting more than one offence was not contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (30 July 1998)

In an expert report of 16 April 1993 the Ministry of Justice’‘s Institute of Forensic Medicine in Cartagena indicated that gas concentrations in houses near the plants exceeded the permitted limit. It considered that there was a relationship of cause and effect between this clinical picture and the levels of gas.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 8 December 1993. It originated in an application (no. 16798/90) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Spanish national. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). On 10 January 1994 the lawyer was given leave by the President to use the Spanish language in the Proceedings. Government (‘the Government’), the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38) appeared before the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 June 1994. The Court heard addresses by them and also their replies to questions from two of its members. The plant began to operate in July 1988 without the licence (licencia) from the municipal authorities required by Regulation 6 of the 1961 regulations on activities classified as causing nuisance and being unhealthy, noxious and dangerous. On 23 November 1994 it declined to accept observations submitted out of time by counsel for the applicant on 13 October 1994. The application was brought by Mrs López Ostra, a resident of Lorca, Murcia, Spain. She was concerned about the nuisance and risks caused by the waste-treatment plant. She requested the court to order temporary or permanent cessation of its activities. The application for protection of fundamental rights was rejected by the Court of Audiencia Territorial. The court heard that the plant had not been granted a licence to operate. The applicant and her family returned to their flat and lived there until February 1992 (see paragraph 21 below). The application was heard by the court of audiencia territorial and the decision was made on 9 September 1988. Mrs López Ostra lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court (Tribunal Supremo - see paragraph 25 below in fine) She maintained that the plant was a source of polluting fumes, pestilential and irritant smells and repetitive noise that had caused both her daughter and herself health problems. The court took evidence from several witnesses offered by the applicant and instructed the regional Environment and Nature Agency to give an opinion on the plant’s operating conditions and location. In a report of 19 January 1989 the agency noted that at the time of its expert's visit on 17 January the plant's sole activity was the treatment of waste water contaminated with chromium. Mrs López Ostra lodged an appeal (recurso de amparo) with the Constitutional Court, alleging violations of Article 15. The court ruled that the appeal was inadmissible on the ground that it was manifestly ill-founded. In 1990 two sisters-in-law brought proceedings against the municipality of Lorca and SACURSA in the Administrative Division of the Murcia High Court (Tribunal Superior de Justicia) alleging that the plant was operating unlawfully. On 18 September 1991 the court, noting that the nuisance had continued after 9 September 1988 and that the company had not obtained a licence, suspended the plant. The judge ordered a number of expert opinions as to the seriousness of the nuisance caused by the waste-treatment plant and its effects on the health of those living nearby. An initial report of 13 October 1992 by a scientist from the University of Murcia stated that hydrogen sulphide (a colourless gas, soluble in water, with a characteristic rotten-egg smell) had been detected on the site. The discharge of effluent containing sulphur into a river was said to be unacceptable. In a report of 27 October 1992 the National Toxicology Institute stated that the levels of the gas probably exceeded the permitted limits but did not pose any danger to people living close to the plant. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court. The judge confirmed the order of 15 November 1991 and the plant was temporarily closed. Mrs López Ostra and her family were rehoused in a flat in the centre of Lorca, for which the municipality paid the rent. The applicant and her husband bought a house in a different part of town on 23 February 1993. On 1 February 1992 Mrs Lázquez Ostra was diagnosed with anorexia. On 17 January 1992 she was admitted to hospital with an enlarged lung. On 24 January 1992 the judge confirmed that the plant had been temporarily closed and that no further action was to be taken. On 27 October 1993 the judge. confirmed that no more action would be taken against the plant and that the order to close it had been confirmed.

The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Graz. The Graz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), sitting in private, dismissed the appeal and upheld the Regional Court's decision.

It considered that, given the applicant's criminal record, there was a risk that he might commit another offence similar to the one of which he was suspected (Tatbegehungsgefahr) The court stated that the applicant had nine previous convictions, mainly for property-related offences, but recently also for violent crimes. The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Graz. On 6 May 2000 the Graz Regional Criminal Court ordered the applicant's pre-trial detention on suspicion of attempted sexual coercion. The court based the suspicion against the applicant on the statement of the victim, who had identified the applicant in an identity parade. The applicant had nine previous convictions, mainly for property-related offences, but recently also for violent crimes. He lodged an appeal against this decision. The Graz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), sitting in private, dismissed the appeal and upheld the Regional Court's decision. He appealed against the decision again on 2 August 2000.

In 2000 the Graz Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the bill of indictment and the appeals against the Regional Court's decisions of 19 July 2000 and 2 August 2000. The applicant lodged a fundamental rights complaint (Grundrechtsbeschwerde) with the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) against this decision. He submitted that there was no strong suspicion against him and that there were no reasons to maintain the detention on remand. He was convicted of attempted sexual coercion and sentenced to two years' imprisonment. The Supreme Court rejected his plea of nullity on 8 March 2001.

The applicant was sentenced to two years' imprisonment in Graz in 2000. He appealed the conviction, but the Graz Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal. The Supreme Court dismissed the complaint, but allowed one lodged by the public prosecutor and increased the term of imprisonment to 2 years and six months. The applicant was convicted of attempted sexual coercion by the Regional Court on 24 October 2000. The conviction was upheld by the Supreme Court on 8 March 2001. The appeal was dismissed again on 8 May 2001 and the applicant was jailed for two years and four months. He was released on 28 July 2002. He is now serving his sentence in a Vienna prison.

The case was decided in favor of the applicant. Graz Regional Court ordered that the applicant's pre-trial detention should continue. The applicant appealed against this decision. The Graz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), sitting in private, dismissed the appeal and upheld the Regional Court's decision. On 18 September 2000 the applicant lodged a fundamental rights complaint (G). He stressed that there were no reasons to maintain his pre- trial detention. He submitted that there was no reasonable suspicion against him as the testimony of the only witness for the prosecution had been contradictory. He also argued that there had been no doubt about the credibility of the witness and there was therefore a reasonable suspicion. On 24 October 2000 the Regional Court, sitting with two professional and two lay judges, convicted the applicant of attempted sexual coercion and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment. On 8 March 2001 the Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal by the applicant, but allowed one lodged by the public prosecutor and increased the term of imprisonment from two years and six months to four years and two months. The appeal was rejected on 28 March 2001. The case was heard at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg. The ECHR ruled that there was no reason to keep the applicant on remand and that he should be released. The ECHR also ruled that the case should be dismissed because there were no grounds for detention.

The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Pozuelo de Alarcón (Madrid) The applicant cohabited with another man in a homosexual relationship from 1990 until the latter’s death on 2 July 2002. The applicant claimed social security allowances as a surviving spouse, under section 174 (1) of the General Social Security Act. On 22 September 2003 the National Institute of Social Security (Instituto Nacional de la Seguridad Social, hereafter referred to as ‘INSS’) refused to grant the applicant a survivor’S pension on the ground that since he had not been married to the deceased person, he could not legally be considered as his surviving spouse.

The case involves a man who cohabited with a man for many years before the latter’s death. The applicant claimed social security allowances as a surviving spouse under section 174 (1) of the General Social Security Act. The National Institute of Social Security refused to grant the applicant a survivor's pension on the ground that since he had not been married to the deceased person, he could not legally be considered as his surviving spouse. In a judgment of 14 November 2005 the Social Tribunal ruled for the applicant. The case was heard by the Madrid Social Tribunal no. 33 (“the Social Tribunal”). The ruling applies to same-sex marriage irrespective of the sex of its members.

The applicant lived with another man in a homosexual relationship from 1990 until the latter’s death on 2 July 2002. On 19 September 2003 the applicant claimed social security allowances as a surviving spouse, arguing that he had cohabited with his deceased partner for many years. On 1 July 2005 Law no. 13/2005 amending the provisions of the Civil Code with respect to the right to enter into marriage was passed. Two days later it entered into force. This law legalised same-sex marriage in Spain. In accordance with its first additional provision all legal and regulatory provisions making reference to marriage should be understood as applicable to all marriages irrespective of the sex of its members (see paragraph 35 below)

Social Tribunal observed that the issue at stake was whether the applicant, as the surviving partner of a same-sex relationship that ended (following his partner’s death) before the entry into force of Law no. 13/2005, had the right to a survivor's pension. Social Tribunal reiterated that, according to the well-established domestic case-law, surviving partners of unmarried couples were not entitled to a pension under section 174 of the General Social Security Act. The Social Tribunal held in this regard that: “From now onwards all references to marriage established in the law shall be understood as applying also to marriage celebrated between two persons of the same sex’
