The Social Tribunal held in this regard that: “This is a wide-ranging provision which affects all the other provisions of the legal system making reference to marriage. From now onwards all references to marriage established in the law shall be understood as applying also to marriage celebrated between two persons of the same sex.” The ruling was upheld by the High Court.

The case involved a same-sex couple whose relationship ended following the death of the partner. The tribunal ruled that the couple had not married to prevent them receiving a survivor’s pension. The ruling was made in the light of the newly enacted Law no. 13/2005, which was already in force and deemed constitutional by the tribunal. The Social Tribunal held in this regard that: “This is a wide-ranging provision which affects all the other provisions of the legal system making reference to marriage. From now onwards all references to marriage established in the law shall be understood as applying also to marriage celebrated between two persons of the same sex.”

Law no. 30/1981 of 7 July 1981 amending the provisions of the Civil Code pertaining to marriage and the procedure to be followed for cases of annulment, judicial separation and divorce. Social Tribunal stressed that such a provision was included in order to provide a solution for those cohabiting couples consisting of a man and a woman who could not have married under the legislation in force until that time, and thus did not qualify for a survivor’s pension. Law no. 13/2005 was aimed at protecting the rights of those who couldn’t marry on account of their sexual orientation. The Social Tribunal considered nonetheless that treating these two groups differently would not be in harmony with the strong egalitarian intention expressed by Parliament.

The INSS and the Treasury General of Social Security appealed against that judgment. The administration argued that the governing principle was that of non-retroactivity of laws. But the Tribunal ruled that this general principle was not absolute and that it did not apply where there was a specific rule giving retroactive effect to laws more favourable to the citizens, as is true of the instant case. The Tribunal relied on the constitutive effects of Law no. 13/2005 which created new rights and was effective only from the date it entered into force.

It was for Parliament to establish the characteristics of the legal transition, either by introducing retroactivity clauses or by restricting the application of the new legislation.

Prisoners are divided into broadly defined categories, or groups of people, according to the nature or the length of their sentences. As a result they are regarded as having acquired a distinctive status which attaches itself to them personally for the purposes of the regime. It must be accepted, as Lord Bingham points out, that a personal characteristic cannot be defined by the differential treatment of which a person complains. Mr Clift had already been sentenced, and he had already acquired the status which that sentence gave him before the Order was made that denied prisoners in his group the right to release on the recommendation of the Parole Board. Mr Clift's case raises whether the distinguishing feature or characteristic which enables persons or a group of persons to be singled out for separate treatment must have been identified as a personal characteristic before it is used for this purpose by the discriminator. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35637/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the relevant provisions of the Civil Code relating to custody and their application by the courts had discriminated against him as the father of a child born out of wedlock. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs.Neither party filed further observations on the merits of the case. By a decision of 25 September 2008 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant requested that the opinion of an expert in child psychology be taken. K.’s mother agreed to that request. The Youth Office (Jugendamt) expressed the view that both parents were capable of exercising custody. The judge then proceeded to discuss the factual and legal issues with the parties. The parties then concluded an agreement to the effect that. pending a decision on custody, K. would spend three days with his mother and three. days with the applicant. The opinion was based on interviews. which the expert had conducted with K.'s mother and the applicant and his. partner. A second expert, Dr J.-W., submitted his opinion to the Court on 17 April 2002. The District Court ordered a third expert, Dr B., to submit a decisive expert opinion on the question whether K’s mother was capable of exercising custody. Dr B. found that both parents were in principle capable of taking care of K. The mother had some issues as regards her own personality development and a somewhat limited capacity to cope with everyday life. The applicant could provide a more stable environment and a more coherent style of upbringing. It was recommended that the applicant be given extensive access rights, in that K. should stay with him from Friday to Sunday every second weekend, spend two weeks with him in summer and one week during the Christmas period. Under Article 166 of the Civil Code the mother of a child born out of wedlock had sole custody. A transfer of custody was only to be ordered if the child’s best interests were at risk. In the present case the applicant would have had to prove that the mother was unable to take care of him. The applicant had failed to adduce proof to the contrary. The application of different criteria when the parents of a. child born from wedlock separated lacked reasonable justification. The court ruled that its decision was immediately enforceable with the consequence that the agreement of 12 March 2002 was no longer effective. The case was dismissed on 24 February 2003. Regional Court found that the proceedings before the District Court had not suffered from any procedural defects. The Regional Court did not see any reason to request the Constitutional Court to rule on the constitutionality of the relevant provisions of the Civil Code. The applicant had not claimed to have cohabited with K.’s mother. On the contrary he had co‑habited. with another woman, U., who had meanwhile become his wife. A distinction between children born in wedlock and children born out of wedlock was not discriminatory as long as it was objectively justified. The Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) dismissed the applicant's extraordinary appeal on points of law. The relevant provisions of the Civil Code in the version in force at the material time read as follows. Article 166 “The mother shall have sole custody of an illegitimate child.” Article 167 “Whenever the parents of a child live in a common household, they may agree that both parents will have custody in the future. The court shall uphold the agreement if it serves the interests of the child’s well-being.’ Article 177 “(1) If the marriage of the parents. of a minor legitimate child is dissolved or annulled, the. court may withdraw all or part of the custodial rights in respect of the. child ...” Both parents must submit an agreement to the court regarding the parent with whom the child is to stay primarily. This parent must always be put in charge of all custodial matters. The court must approve the agreement of the parents, if it serves the interests of the child. The main elements referred to as a basis for allowing joint parental authority for unmarried parents are the establishment of paternity and the parents’ agreement to exercise joint authority. The solutions in the Member States vary as regards the attribution of joint parental. authority for children born out of wedlock in the event no agreement between the parents can be reached in this respect. In some Member States such as the Czech Republic and Luxembourg, the domestic courts have interpreted the applicable provisions so as to allow joint parental authority only with the consent of the parents. In Hungary, Ireland and Monaco the laws appear to provide for a joint exercise of parental authority even without the parents’ consent. All Member States emphasise the importance of the child’s best interest in decisions regarding the attribution of custody. The majority provide for paternal participation in custody if the parents were not married to each other, either irrespective of the mother's will or at least by court order following an evaluation of a child's interests.”

The order of preventive detention by the sentencing court may be ordered in addition to the penalty for an intentional offence.

The order for execution of the placement in preventive detention must show that the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. The perpetrator must previously have served a prison sentence or must have been detained pursuant to a measure of correction and prevention for at least two years. The court responsible for the execution of sentences must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person's preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. If that is not the case, it suspends on probation the execution. of the preventive detention order; supervision of the person’s conduct (Führungsaufsicht) commences with suspension.

A comprehensive assessment of the perpetrator and his acts must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. Judicial review and duration of preventive detention are part of Article 67e of the Criminal Code. If a person has spent ten years in preventive detention, the court shall declare the measure terminated (only) if there is no danger that the detainee will commit a new offence. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3).

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a German national, Mr Martin Schummer (“the applicant”), on 10 July 2004 and 4 September 2007 respectively. The applicant alleged in both applications, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a maximum period of ten years breached the prohibition of retrospective punishment under Article 7. The applications were adjourned in 2007 pending the outcome of the case of M. v. Germany, no. 19359/04. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the two applications at issue be resumed. The applicant was convicted of two counts of rape and abduction and of one count of attempted rape and deprivation of liberty committed in 1984. He served his full prison sentence in Freiburg Prison. He was then placed in preventive detention, executed in that same prison, for the first time on 27 June 1989. He had thus served ten years in preventive Detention by 26 June 1999. On 11 December 2001, in judicial review proceedings under Article 67e of the Criminal Code, the court refused to suspend the applicant's preventive detention and grant probation. The judge ruled that there was still a risk that the applicant, owing to his criminal tendencies, might commit serious offences. In 1992 the detention authorities had proposed certain relaxations in the conditions of the applicant's detention, but the applicant had refused to cooperate. In his report of 12 April 1999 the neurologic expert had found that the applicant still suffered from the said personality disorder. In any event, his release could only be taken into consideration after his conditions of detention had been relaxed, combined with a successful social-therapeutic treatment. The decision of the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal, fully endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The Federal Constitutional Court lodged a constitutional complaint against the decisions ordering his continued preventive detention even on completion of the ten‑year period. The applicant's constitutional complaint was dismissed as ill-founded. The Freiburg Regional Court refused to suspend the applicant's preventive detention and grant probation under Article 67d § 3 of the Criminal Code. The Karlsruhe Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 11 December 2006. The court of appeal endorsed the Regional Court's view that there was still a risk that the applicant, if released, might commit serious offences resulting in considerable psychological or physical harm to the victims. The applicant had refused a request to have his case heard by the Federal Constitutional Court. The second set of proceedings (application no. 42225/07) took place at the Federal Court of Justice in Berlin. The case was brought by an ex-convict who had been held in preventive detention for 10 years. He argued that he had been treated as an object of State action in disregard of his human dignity. The Freiburg Regional Court decided that he was still liable to commit serious offences if released. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (file no. 2 BvR 157/07). It found that the complaint was inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. The Karlsruhe Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case to the Freiburger Regional Court. The decision of the Regional Court was upheld on 31 August 2009. Court had not sufficiently established the facts on which it had based its decision and had failed to hear the medical expert, who had submitted a report in writing on its request, also in person at the hearing. Court of Appeal, referring to a leading decision of the Federal Court of Justice of 12 May 2010 (see paragraph 41 below), argued that it was possible to interpret the Criminal Code so as to comply with the Convention as interpreted by this Court in the case of M. v. Germany. It found that in relation to preventive detention the application of a new statutory provision retrospectively to the detriment of the person concerned was prohibited. The applicant was released on 10 September 2010 and has been submitted to constant surveillance by five police officers since then. The German Criminal Code distinguishes between penalties and measures of correction and prevention. The purpose of such measures is to rehabilitate dangerous offenders or to protect the public from them. They must, however, be proportionate to the gravity of the offences committed by, or to be expected from, the defendants as well as to their dangerousness. The Court's judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) makes the distinction between these measures and penalties. The provisions relevant to the present case can be summarised as follows: The order of preventive detention by the sentencing court can be reviewed by the Court. The court may order his preventive detention under certain circumstances in addition to his prison sentence. The order for execution of the placement in preventive detention must show that the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. The court responsible for the execution of sentences must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person's preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. A comprehensive assessment of the perpetrator and his acts must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, notably those which seriously harm their victims physically or mentally. If that is not the case, it suspends on probation the Execution of the preventive detention order. The maximum duration of preventive detention in Germany is at least two years, subject to fixed time-limits. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The application of the Court's findings in the M. v. Germany case by the domestic courts by the German courts has been terminated. Court decisions concerning orders of. preventive detention had to be based on the law in force at the time of the offence. Some Courts of Appeal have found that the abolition of the maximum period of ten years laid down in Article 67d. § 1 of the Criminal Code in its version in force before 31 January 1998 could not be effected retrospectively and. therefore still applied to preventive detention ordered in relation to offences committed prior to that date. On the contrary, several Courts of Appeal considered that the Court's findings in the case of M. v. Germany could not be applied at present by the domestic courts responsible for the execution of sentences as the Criminal Code as it stood did not permit its interpretation in compliance with Articles 5 and 7 of the Convention. It was therefore for the legislator to execute the court's judgment in the M. case. Several of these cases subsequently submitted such cases to the Federal Court of Justice for a preliminary ruling under a new provision of the Court Organisation Act in force since 30 July 2010, which is aimed at securing a uniform case-law of the German courts on that issue.

The application was made on behalf of and in the name of the applicant's children. The applicant argued that the grandparents were setting the children against him and obstructing the exercise of his contact rights. The case was decided by the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint against the decisions of the District Court and Court of appeal. The application was dismissed on the ground that the determination of contact arrangements between the father and the children was already the subject of the still pending proceedings under file no. 5 F 272/98. The appeal was dismissed as inadmissible on the grounds that the power of representation was part of the right to custody which had been transferred solely to the mother. The District Court in Düsseldorf rejected the application on 22 March 2001. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal since there was nothing to establish that contact with their grandparents was contrary to the children's wellbeing. There was no evidence that the grandparents had obstructed contact between the children and their father or had damaged their relationship. The applicant's request for legal aid for the appellate proceedings was rejected on 17 May 2002.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23279/14) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the retrospective prolongation of his preventive detention breached his right to liberty. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 June 2014. The Government was represented by two of their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens and Mrs K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The Court finds in favour of the applicant and upholds the detention of Mr Karl-Heinz Bergmann in the Rosdorf preventive detention centre. The Regional Court. found that between 7 July 1985 and 3 October 1985, the applicant had stabbed a. nineteen-year-old female cyclist in the back in a life-threatening manner for sexual gratification. Also stabbed a male cyclist he had mistaken for a woman twice in the. back and at the temple, again for sex. The Regional Court decided to order the applicant’s preventive detention under Article 66. § 2 of the Criminal Code. It considered that as a result of his personality disorder, the. applicant had a propensity to commit serious offences which seriously harmed the victims both physically. and mentally. Public security could therefore be better safeguarded by placing the applicant in preventive detention. The Lüneburg Regional Court ordered the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention at regular intervals. The Regional Court further ordered the Rosdorf Prison authorities to offer the applicant, within three months of the date on which its decision became final, a specific anti-hormonal therapy with medication aimed at reducing his sadistic fantasies and his libido. The court had consulted the Celle Prison authorities and the prosecution and had heard the applicant in person as well as his counsel, who represented him throughout the proceedings. It noted that at the time of his last offence on 3 October 1985, the applicant's first placement in preventive detention could not exceed ten years. The applicant therefore fell within the category of detainees whose preventive detention had been prolonged retrospectively, as defined by the Federal Constitutional Court in its judgment of 4 May 2011. The Regional Court found that, as required by section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code, there was still a very high risk that, owing to specific circumstances relating to his personality and his conduct, the applicant would if released commit the most serious sexually motivated violent offences. The Regional Court considered that the prolongation of the preventive detention of the applicant, who had been detained for almost thirty years, was still proportionate in view of the considerable threat he posed to the public. It noted in that context that the applicant’s detention in a supervised residence, which it had suggested in its previous decision, was not possible in practice. The applicant lodged an appeal against the Regional Court’s decision. He argued, in particular, that his preventive detention, a penalty which had been prolonged retrospectively, failed to comply with the Convention. The Court of Appeal held that the applicant was suffering from a mental disorder as defined in section 1(1) of the Therapy Detention Act. The application was dismissed on 2 September 2013. The decision of the Celle Court of. Appeal confirmed that the requirements laid down in section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory. Act to the Criminal Code for ordering the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention had been met. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court against the decisions of the Lüneburg Regional Court and the Celle Court of Appeal. He claimed that the order for the continuation of his preventive detention violated his constitutional right to liberty, read in conjunction with the protection of legitimate expectations guaranteed in a State governed by the rule of law. The decision of the Federal. Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file. no. 2 BvR 2182/13) The decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 7 November 2013. The application was brought by a former member of the German parliament. The applicant was held in preventive detention in a wing of Celle Prison. He had participated in group therapy sessions run by a doctor and in a social skills training course. He stopped attending the group for addicts and refused to take medication to reduce his libido for fear of side effects. Since 2 June 2013 the applicant has been detained in the new Rosdorf centre for mental health. The conditions of the applicant’s preventive detention before the period of detention at issue are outlined below. The applicant was transferred with his consent to a wing in the prison on 20 February 2012. The aim was to improve the available treatment options in the light of the duty to differentiate preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment. The conception of preventive detention in the centre was developed in order to comply with the constitutional requirement to differentiate between preventive detention and imprisonment. Detainees are placed in apartment units measuring some 23 square metres containing two furnished rooms and a bathroom. With the exception of detainees posing a particular security risk, the detainees can move freely within the preventive detention building and on its outdoor premises. They may furnish and paint their rooms, to which they have their own keys. The rooms are equipped with a controlled access to the internet including e-mail, telephone, television, CD and DVD player and radio. The outdoor premises, measuring some 1,600 square metres, can be used for sports, recreation or gardening. The applicant has refused regular and repeated offers to start a treatment with medication to reduce his libido, for fear of side effects. In December 2014 he showed willing for the first time to take up such treatment. He proved reliable during leave from the detention centre under escort on a number of occasions. He did not take part in any structured leisure activities and spent most of his day alone watching television. He declined repeated invitations totake part in group sessions of the treatment programme for offenders. Thus, as from August 2014 the applicant no longer participated in any therapy measures. His treatment plan (A. Vollzugsplan) is then drawn up.

The applicant company is the owner and publisher of the weekly newspaper Falter. On 2 May 2005 the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court acquitted H.P., a security officer at the Traiskirchen Reception Centre, of a charge of raping K., an asylum seeker from Cameroon. The reasoning of the judgment contained the following passage: “The statement made by witness K. during her examination [recorded on video tape in a separate room – kontradiktorische Einvernahme] allows inferences to be drawn with regard to the statement by the accused [P.] that the witness might have become involved with him.”

The case takes on a political dimension because it exposes conditions in the Traiskirchen Reception Centre. The applicant company is the owner and publisher of the weekly newspaper Falter. The asylum seeker had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon, kicked by them in the abdomen and placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ for having demonstrated on behalf of her son. She had survived her escape on a container ship, during which she ‘nearly went mad’ and ‘no longer knew whether it was night or day outside’ One year later only the victim is still before the courts. The chronicling of a judicial scandal.

At the hearings, the Agent of the Government made several documents available to the court. On 6 February, the agent and the applicant's lawyer supplemented in writing their answers to certain questions put to them at the hearing. Mr. Buchholz was born in 1918 and lives in Hamburg. From February 1949 onwards he worked for the dry-cleaning firm of J. H. Dependorf KG. He was mainly employed as a driver until the end of 1963 and thereafter as, in particular, controller of branch establishments. On 28 June 1974, he was given notice that he was dismissed with effect from 31 December of the same year as a result of rationalisation measures. The Hamburg Labour Court delivered judgment on 8 January 1975 immediately after hearing the final submissions of the parties. It held that neither the notice of 28 June 1974 nor the extraordinary notice of 30 September 1974 had terminated the applicant’s contract. Court of Appeal on 13 March 1975. In their submission, the accusations made by Mr. Buchholz constituted a “serious reason’ warranting the extraordinary notice of 30 September 1974. Sidney Elmer Golder was serving a 15-year sentence for robbery with violence in 1969. A prison officer who had taken part and been injured in quelling the disturbance, identified Golder as one of his assailants. Golder wrote to his Member of Parliament and a Chief Constable about the incident, but the prison governor stopped these letters because Golder had not raised the subject-matter through authorised channels beforehand. He was later charged with assaulting a prison officer causing bodily harm and sentenced to two years' imprisonment. The case was settled in the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom in 1971, which ordered a retrial of the case.

Sidney Elmer Golder was convicted in 1965 of robbery with violence and was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. In 1969, he was serving his sentence in Parkhurst Prison on the Isle of Wight. On the evening of 24 October 1969, a serious disturbance occurred in a recreation area of the prison where Golder happened to be. On 26 October Golder, together with other prisoners suspected of having participated in the disturbance, was segregated from the main body of prisoners. On 28 and 30 October he was interviewed by police officers. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 July 1994 by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain. It originated in an application (no. 19382/92) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Netherlands national, Mr Antonius Adrianus van der Tang, on 2 December 1991. The applicant had complained of the unreasonable length of pre-trial detention but who had absconded and evaded trial after being released on bail. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. Antonius Adrianus van der Tang was found driving a lorry which contained 1,300 kg of hashish. He was also found in possession of a pistol with its serial number chiselled off and of a radio pre-tuned to a station which coincided with that of another set found. The Court heard addresses by the three of them as well as replies to its questions. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on 20 February 1995. The case was heard by the President of the Chamber, who gave the Government's representative leave to address the Court in Spanish (Rule 27 para. 2) According to the applicant's statement to the police, an unknown person had approached him sometime in March and again in May 1989 and offered him 20,000 Netherlands guilders to transport 1,300 kg of “dope“ (droga) Mr van der Tang had finally accepted. Late in the evening of 25 May 1989, following the unknown person's instructions, he had taken his truck to Bayona, where another man had loaded the drugs and then gone away. The applicant had only been driving for about ten minutes when he was arrested. At least eight more people were subsequently detained for allegedly being involved in a three-stage operation to deliver about 7,000 kg of hashish. Mr van der Tang lodged with investigating judge no. 1 his first applications for provisional release. Arguing that he had throughout been unaware of the real nature of the consignment, he insisted that he was not involved with any drug-trafficking organisation. He further complained that during his four-month detention he had only been questioned twice by the judge - in May and June 1989. The ground for the decision was the seriousness of the offences - illegal possession of a firearm and drug trafficking in large quantities. The second offence in itself attracting a prison sentence of “prisión menor en su grado medio’ (that is, from two years, four months and one day to four years and two months) Authorities had launched a nationwide operation (Operación Nécora) to combat a large-scale drug-trafficking organisation which operated mainly in Galicia. The applicant's case was considered to be closely linked with other files relating to NéCora and was therefore transferred to Madrid on 29 October 1990. On 8 January 1991 central investigating judge no. 5 issued an order (auto de procesamiento) whereby new charges were added against the applicant without any alteration to the established facts. An appeal by the applicant against these orders which included a request for release was eventually rejected on 8 July 1991 by the Third Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional. Van der Tang was arrested in January 1991 and detained for two years. The public prosecutor asked for his detention to be extended to the statutory maximum of four years. His constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible by the Constitutional Court on the ground that none of the issues raised by the applicant were of a constitutional nature. The case was sent to the Third Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional for trial. Mr van der Tang has been in detention for over three years. He was released on bail on 11 June 1992 subject to the following conditions: (a) the applicant was to pay in cash a security of 8 million pesetas; (b) he was to give an address and inform the court of any subsequent change; (c) he had to report daily to the police in Vigo. It is possible to rule out his being able to conceal or suppress evidence. Mr van der Tang was of good behaviour and participated in several prison activities. He also worked as a clerk in the prison bursar's office. The court did not consider that the accused's foreign nationality constituted an insurmountable obstacle to reaching this conclusion. This is particularly so as the accused has shown, at least to some extent, that he is able to remain on Spanish territory and obtain a contract of employment there which would enable him to engage in a lawful activity for the duration of the contract. He could have been tried in Galicia several months ago when the Pontevedra public prosecutor did not oppose his provisional release. On 23 December 1992 the applicant travelled by car from Spain to the Netherlands. He had no means of subsistence and wanted to spend Christmas with his family. The Audiencia Nacional refused his request to stay in Spain. On 9 July 1993 the police informed the court that the applicant's whereabouts were unknown. He was ordered to appear before it on 23 July 1993 at a hearing concerning the forfeiture of the bail. But the summons could not be served on him, as he no longer lived at the address he had originally given the Spanish authorities. The case file ran to more than 22,000 pages. In respect of the applicant, the public prosecutor demanded a total prison sentence of 14 years. On 31 July 1993 the Audiencia Nacional dismissed the objection and ordered his arrest. The trial took place in Madrid from 20 September 1993 to 24 May 1994. Mr van der Tang did not attend it and could therefore not be tried pursuant to section 841 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Luciano Núñez (see paragraph 8 above) was held to have played a leading role in importing very large quantities of hashish. He was accordingly sentenced to a total of thirteen years' imprisonment and a fine of 100 million pesetas. It does not appear from the facts set out in this judgment that the applicant was involved in drug-trafficking activities beyond the transporting of 1,300 kg ofHashish for which he was arrested.

The law leaves it up to the person having custody, as a rule the mother, to determine whether, and to what extent, the father should be able to spend time with his child. The main reason for the weaker legal position of the father of a child born out of wedlock is his different social position. It is not enough for such contact to be consistent with, or not contrary to, the child's interests, it must serve those interests and promote them. The Regional Court is convinced that the father in this case is motivated by attachment to [G.] and genuine affection for her. The case originated in an application (no. 27644/95) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by twelve Swiss nationals. The applicants complained that they had not had access to a “tribunal” within the meaning of Article 6.0. The Commission declared the application admissible on 7 April 1997. On 14 January 1999 a panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand chambers. The applicants live in the villages of Villigen, Würenlingen, Böttstein and Kleindöttingen. They either own or rent property. The Beznau II nuclear power plant consists of a dual-loop pressurised water reactor. The site is situated five kilometres from the German border. The application for an operating licence was made on 18 December 1991. More than 18,400 objections were lodged by virtue of these provisions with the Canton of Aargau. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial and replied to the questions of the Court. The Grand Chamber decided (by sixteen votes with one abstention) not to apply Rule 39 in the present case. Complainants requested the Federal Council to refuse an extension of the operating licence and to order the immediate and permanent closure of the nuclear power plant. The Federal Council dismissed all the objections as being unfounded and granted NOK a limited operating licence expiring on 31 December 2004. The licence was subject to compliance with various specific conditions concerning threshold levels for radioactive substances, tests of the safeguard system, improvements of the feedwater system, for ageing surveillance and various other continuous technical improvements. NOK was also requested to submit periodically updated safety reports. More than 99% of the objections were photocopies. The complainants disputed the impartiality of the administrative bodies involved in the proceedings. The Federal Council considered each of the objections in turn. The report gave the results from the point of view of nuclear safety and radiation protection. The Federal Council was satisfied that certain complainants lived in zone 1 around the nuclear power plant and were therefore entitled to take part in the proceedings. The results of the probabilistic safety analysis carried out at the Beznau II nuclear power. plant showed that a nuclear accident was unlikely. It referred to the emergency standby system and improved power supply system (NANO), put into operation in 1992, and the filtered containment venting system. It concluded that on the basis of the evidence submitted no relevant deficiencies could be established. The Federal Council stated that the reactor of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant was technically not comparable to a light-water reactor like that of the Beznau II power plant. Council further observed that by voting against the popular initiative of 23 September 1990 (see paragraphs 20-21 below) “For the Progressive Abandonment of Nuclear Energy” the Swiss people and the majority of the cantons had expressed the wish to continue using nuclear energy. With regard to the complaint based on the right to life, the Federal Council pointed out that this right was protected by the Constitution and drew attention to the position under the Federal Court's case-law. The condition of the power plant with regard to nuclear safety and radiation protection had been rated as good. Since 1996, the Beznau II power plant had followed an ageing surveillance programme as a permanent task for its safety-relevant plant components. The relevant documentation examined by the HSK had not revealed any safety- relevant gaps in the maintenance programmes. The licence at issue continued to tolerate the serious safety deficiencies which had already been mentioned in the institute's previous expert reports of 1992 and 1994. It was stated that the modernisation which was both technically possible and had been required in the case of pressurised water reactors of the same generation had not been carried out. The report criticised the safety systems for their failure to ensure that the back-up components were physically separate. Lack of protection against outside influences rendered the plant much more vulnerable to a plane crash or to action by third parties. No demand had been made for an actual emergency system, such as was required for the more recent western European pressurised water reactors. The standards applied in the licensing procedure at issue were far below those applying in other central European countries – i.e. risks were accepted that would no longer be tolerated in other countries. The report further referred to the OSART mission which was conducted in 1995 and the criticism expressed by the experts with regard to the organisational structures and management at the Beznau II power plant.

Measures remain in force for a maximum of three months and may be renewed only on fresh application (Article 1 para. 5, sub-paragraph 3). The person concerned is not to be notified of the restrictions affecting him. The competent Minister must, at least once every six months, report to a Board consisting of five Members of Parliament on the application of the G 10. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. If the Commission declares any measures to be illegal or unnecessary, the Minister must terminate them immediately. The Commission members are appointed for the current term of the Bundestag by the above-mentioned Board of five members of Parliament after consultation with the Government. They are completely independent in the exercise of their functions and cannot be subject to instructions. The Government, moreover, intend proposing to Parliament to make such prior consent obligatory. According to Article 1 para. 9, sub-paragraph 5, of the G 10: “... there shall be no legal remedy before the courts in respect of the ordering and implementation of restrictive measures.” The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. For this reason, notification to this person is out of the question. For the same reason, it must be avoided that a person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance. Government may supply information or produce documents to enable it to verify for itself the individual’s allegations. The authorities are bound to reply to such a request even if the information asked for is secret. It is then for the Constitutional Court to decide whether the information and documents so obtained can be used. The latter may reject the application on the ground that the applicant is unable to adduce proof to substantiate a complaint. It may decide by a two-thirds majority that their use is incompatible with State security and dismiss the application. The Agent of the Government admitted that this remedy might be employed only on rare occasions. The persons concerned are informed of the measures taken as soon as notification can be made without jeopardising the purpose of the investigation. The applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 violate Article 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. On 18 December 1974, the Commission declared the application admissible. Some of the applicants are barristers and it is theoretically excluded that they are in fact subject to secret surveillance in consequence of contacts they may have with clients who are suspected of anti-constitutional activities. The applicants must be considered to be entitled to lodge an application even if they cannot show that they were victims, the report stated. The Commission then expressed the opinion:by eleven votes to one with two abstentions, that the present case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 6-1. The report contains various separate opinions. case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) in so far as the applicants relied on the notion “criminal charge’. The applicants could claim to be ‘victims’ of a violation of their rights guaranteed by the Convention by reason of the system of surveillance established by the so-called G 10 Act. The Registered Partnership Act also contains a comprehensive range of amendments to existing legislation. Unlike married couples, registered partners are not allowed to adopt a child. The rules on the choice of name differ from those for married couples. Artificial insemination is also excluded (section 2(1) of the Artificial Procreation Act – Fortpflanzungsmedizingesetz). The most important differences, however, concern parental rights. The law also provides registered partners with the same status as spouses in various other fields of law, such as inheritance law, labour, social and social insurance law, tax law, the law on administrative procedure and data protection.

The Court of Appeal will then decide whether or not to grant the couple permission to marry and the case will be heard again on August 28, 2015. The applicants alleged a breach of their right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions. They argued that in the event that one partner in a homosexual couple died, the other was discriminated against since he would be in a much less favourable position under tax law. On 12 December 2003 the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) dismissed the applicants’ complaint. The European Court of Human Rights found in its Cossey [v. the United Kingdom] judgment of 27 September 1990 that the restriction of marriage to this ‘traditional’ concept was objectively justified. The essence of marriage is not affected in any way by the fact that divorce (or separation) is possible. The Constitutional Court’s judgment was served on the applicants’ counsel on 25 February 2004. It is unnecessary in the instant case to examine whether, and in which areas, the law unjustifiably discriminates against same-sex relationships by providing for special rules for married couples. Nor is it the task of this court to advise the legislature on constitutional issues or even matters of legal policy. Instead, the complaint must be dismissed as ill-founded. The Registered Partnership Act, Federal Law Gazette (Bundesgesetzblatt) vol. I, no. 135/2009, came into force on 1 January 2010. The rules on the establishment of a registered partnership resemble the rules governing marriage.  registered partnership. involves cohabitation on a permanent basis and may be entered into between two persons of the same sex having legal capacity and having reached the age of majority. A registered partnership must not be established between close relatives or with a person who is already married or has established a still valid registered partnership with another person. The partner who is in charge of the common household and has no income has legal authority to represent the other partner in everyday legal transactions. Registered partners have the same obligations regarding maintenance as spouses (section 12). Dissolution of a registered partnership occurs in the event of the death of one partner (section 13). It may also be pronounced by a judicial decision on various other grounds. European Union law does not allow same-sex couples to marry. Artificial insemination is also excluded from the law. In a few countries, e.g. in the Netherlands and in Belgium, marriage between people of the same sex is legally recognised. There is no explicit reference to ‘men and women’ as the case is in other human rights instruments, it may be argued that there is no obstacle to recognise same- sex relationships in the context of marriage.” ‘It is important to point out that the name ‘registered partnership’ has intentionally been chosen not to confuse it with marriage. This new institution is, consequently, as a rule only accessible to couples who cannot marry’ Currently, six out of forty-seven member States grant same-sex couples equal access to marriage. Directive 2004/38/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 concerns the right of citizens of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the member States. 13 member States do not grant same.-sex couples access tomarriage, but have passed some kind of legislation permitting same- sex couples to register their relationships: Andorra, Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Iceland, Luxembourg, Sweden and Spain.’Family member’ means the partner with whom the Union citizen has contracted a registered partnership, on the basis of the legislation of a member State. There are 19 member States in which same-sex couples either have the possibility to marry or to enter into a registered partnership. The legal consequences of registered partnerships vary from being almost equivalent to marriage to giving relatively limited rights. In most of the States concerned, registered partners obtain a status similar to marriage. The possibilities for registered partners to undergo medically assisted insemination or to foster or adopt children vary greatly from one country to another. Other consequences include the use of the partner’s surname, refusal to testify, entitlement to compensation following the wrongful death of a partner, and lawful organ donation. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Mr J. Peter. The applicant’s complaint concerning the length of proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court and the lack of an effective remedy was communicated to the Government on 3 June 2013. On the same day the President of the Section sitting in a single-judge formation declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The circumstances of the case are as follows: In 2001 the Civil Partnership Act (Gesetz über die eingetragene Lebenspartnerschaft) entered into force and introduced civil unions for same-sex couples. The Federal Constitutional Court delivered its judgment in a case (no. 1 BvR 1164/07, hereinafter “the 2007 case’) which had been brought in 2007 concerning the pension rights of a surviving partner in a civil partnership. It found that denying a partner in. a civil union the right to a survivor’s pension from the civil servants’ pension scheme. violated the principle of non-discrimination. The Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) was to be introduced. In December 2011 the Court informed the applicant of the enactment of the new domestic remedy and drew his attention to the transitional provision of that Act. On 6 February 2012 the applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. However, the judge maintained that it had been in the applicant's best interest to wait for the court's ruling in the 2007 case. Subsequently, it became clear that the 2007 Case did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the applicants constitutional complaint. The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint under section 97a of the Federal Constitutional court Act. The court noted that the actual duration of the proceedings – four and a half years – was unusually long, but not excessive. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and it served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. decisions and judgments of the Constitutional Court had binding inter omnes legal effect and for this reason had to be drafted with the utmost diligence, the court said. It added that it was in the nature of constitutional court proceedings that chronological case management was of subordinate importance. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered by the Federal Constitutional Court. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay must be lodged in writing, set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. Complaint must be admissible twelve months at the earliest after the case has been lodged with the Federal Constitutional Court. The complaints panel shall decide by a majority. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The decision is not subject to appeal. The complaint had to be lodged by 3 June 2012 at the latest. It was not necessary to raise a complaint of. undue delay (Verzögerungsrüge) prior to filing a complaint claiming compensation.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of effective access to court and that the State had failed to provide him with sufficient protection against allegations that violated his right to privacy. In the show, the applicant, who was unknown to the broader public, appeared in pictures and was mentioned by name. He was singled out as the central figure of organised crime within media and advertising and as being guilty of several counts of fraud and other economic offences. Swedish TV personality X was accused of being a central figure of organised crime. The applicant claimed damages in the amount of 250,000 Swedish kronor (SEK; approximately 27,000 euros) X disputed the claim on the grounds, inter alia, that he was not the responsible editor of the show. The Stockholm District Court dismissed the claim in so far as it was based on the Constitutional Law. It referred to the Supreme Court judgment in an almost identical case, NJA 2002 p. 314 (see paragraphs 28-31 below), and held that Chapters 1-9 of the Constitutional law were not enough. The court held that Chapters 1-9 of the Constitutional Law were not applicable to the programme in question. The Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) upheld the District Court’s decision. The applicant appealed, repeating what he had stated in his earlier submissions. He argued that all companies involved in the case were Swedish, including the receiving company in London, allegedly named Viasat AB, with its seat in Stockholm. X contested the arguments and submitted that it was the company Viason Broadcasting UK Ltd, whose seat was in the United Kingdom, which was responsible for the programme service and decided on the final content of the programmes. The applicant requested that a question concerning the interpretation of the Brussels I Regulation be referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union (ECJ) for a preliminary ruling. According to the applicant, the regulation entitled a person claiming non-contractual damages to bring actions where the harmful event occurred. The position hitherto taken by the Swedish courts ran contrary to Community law. The Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s referral request and refused leave to appeal in the case. The applicant subsequently withdrew his remaining claims before the District Court since there was no practical prospect of success in a continued procedure. He was convicted of aggravated fraud and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.

The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (förvaltningsrätten) of Stockholm. On 19 April 2007 the court, after having held an oral hearing, upheld the Social Insurance Office's decision in full. The court found that, although it was scientifically known that employees in the food industry had a statistically high risk of injury, the circumstances in the applicant's case had to be taken into account. On 17 March 2008, the Administrative Court of Appeal granted leave to appeal. On 5 September 2008 the court rejected the request. It referred to the nature of the case and to the fact that an Oral hearing had been held before the County administrative Court. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Högsta förvaltningsdomstolen) He complained of the lack of reasoning in the Administrative Court of Appeal’s judgment. The applicant argued that that court's refusal to hold an oral hearing had infringed his right to a fair trial within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. He requested 50,000 Swedish kronor (SEK) for non-pecuniary damage. On 15 January 2015 the Chancellor of Justice rejected the applicant's claim. He argues that his back-related and other problems can thus – as has been found also by the County Administrative Court and the Social Insurance Office – not be defined as a work-related injury. The Administrative Court of Appeal had taken a stance on the central and decisive question in the case, that is, whether the applicant had been exposed to harmful influences in his work. The Chancellor of Justice noted that it would have been preferable, for pedagogical reasons, for the court to have given clearer grounds for why the applicant’s evidence had not been sufficient. But she concluded that the reasoning was not so deficient that the applicant's right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention had been infringed under the Convention. The case was heard in accordance with the Court's case-law, a less strict standard applied to the requirement to hold a hearing before the appellate court. The administration of justice before the administrative courts is regulated by the Administrative Court Procedure Act (Förvaltningsprocesslagen, 1971:291) The standard of proof was somewhat mitigated on 1 July 2002, but that amendment did not apply to the applicant’s case. According to section 30 of the Act, the determination of a case by a court must be based on what is contained in the documents and what has otherwise been established in the case. The decision must state the reasons that determined the outcome. was highly probable (Chapter 2, section 2). The decision was made to rule that the applicant was not entitled to a trial by jury.

Ms Halford claims she was discriminated against on grounds of sex. within Merseyside and other police authorities. She alleges that certain members of the Merseysidhes Police Authority launched a ‘campaign’ against her. This took the form, inter alia, of leaks to the press, interception of her telephone calls and the decision to bring disciplinary proceedings against her in 1990. She challenged the above decisions by way of judicial review in the High Court. The hearing before the Industrial Tribunal took place in June 1992. On 14 July 1992 the proceedings were adjourned pending negotiation between the parties, which led to settlement of the case. As Assistant Chief Constable, Ms Halford was provided with her own office and two telephones, one of which was for private use. These telephones were part of the Merseyside police internal telephone network, a telecommunications system outside the public network. No restrictions were placed on the use of these telephones and no guidance was given to her. She alleges that calls were intercepted for the purposes of obtaining information to use against her in the discrimination proceedings. It was agreed that she would retire from the police force on medical grounds (arising out of an injury to her knee in 1989). In addition, the Home Office agreed to implement various proposals put by the Equal Opportunities Commission, inter alia to update and review selection procedures. On 20 April 1995 the judge imposed on the applicant a sentence of five years' imprisonment. In his appeal he raised, inter alia, the following ground: The judge should have reacted to the juror's complaint by dismissing the jury. The juror who had written the complaint should not have been segregated from the other members of the jury in the early stages. The judge was right to confront the jury with the problem and ask them to consider it. Judge dealt with possibility of tensions among the jurors perfectly sensibly in the direction he gave to them. However, it would be unrealistic to suppose that the jury would not have wanted to know who the author of the complaint was. Other members of the jury, as this led to his identification, were also questioned by the judge. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty of the charge of perverting the course of justice. The judge ruled the jury should not have been allowed to deliberate on the question of whether to convict the defendant of perjuring the jury in the first place. The verdict was overturned on appeal and a new jury was brought in to decide the case.

He appealed the sentence but was later released on bail. He has three children with a woman he met in Denmark. The three children have been raised by their mother. The father of the children is in prison awaiting sentencing for drug trafficking in 1998. The mother of the child is in jail awaiting trial for drug smuggling. The son is in the care of a relative. The daughter has been taken care of by her mother. The applicant had served two-thirds of his sentence and was due to be released on parole. Since he did not consent to the deportation and refused to leave the country voluntarily, he was detained as from that date in accordance with the Aliens Act. The applicant appealed against this decision to the Refugee Board (Flygtningenævnet), which on 16 April 1999 requested the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to provide more information on the situation in Iran. By judgment of 14 February 2000 the City Court revoked the decision to expel the applicant. The High Court of Western Denmark quashed the above decision and dismissed the applicant's request for reconsideration of the expulsion order. The applicant was released from his detention on 11 May 2000. On 7 September 2000 the Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision of 3 March 2000 as it agreed that a request for a review of an expulsion order pursuant to section 50 of the Aliens Act could only be examined once by the courts. The applicant was never charged with any offence and was never convicted of any offence. The application was settled in court by the applicant's legal team and was dismissed with costs of more than £100,000. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECH) for its review of the expulsion order. The ECH ruled that the appeal could not be heard unless the case was heard by an international court of human rights.

Under the Civil Procedure Rules, which came into force on 26 April 1999, hearings, including those in small claims cases, are to be held in public. There is a discretion for the court to hold a hearing in private where: (a) publicity would defeat the object of the hearing; (b) it involves matters relating to national security; (c) it is confidential information (including information relating to personal financial matters) and publicity would damage that confidentiality; (d) a private hearing is necessary to protect the interests of any child or person suffering from mental incapacity; or it is a hearing of an application made without notice and it would be unjust to the respondent for there to be a public hearing.

The applicant, Mr Thomas John Crompton, is a British national who was born in 1954 and lives in Stalybridge, Cheshire. In 1989 the applicant joined the Territorial Army (“TA”) as a pay and accounts clerk, a military post. In July 1993 the applicant was informed that he was to be made redundant, following organisational changes in the TA pursuant to a process of civilianisation. The applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal. His claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over matters involving military personnel. The matter was then placed before the Army Board. The Army Board found in the applicant's favour as regards his argument that he ought to have been, but was not, given priority before five selection boards. An award of compensation was notified to the applicant on 10 August 2001, but he disputed the calculation of the compensation. In November 2001 a further offer of settlement was made to him, which he rejected. In April 2003 the Army board made a further compensation offer of GBP 94,016.67. The High Court ruled that the offer did not cover the full cost of the redundancy. A new offer of GBP 147,000 was made in 2004, but was rejected. In 2007 the High Court again ruled in favour of the offer, and ordered the original offer to be paid in full. The appeal was rejected again in 2008, this time on grounds that the original award did not take into account the length of time that it had taken to make the offer. The case was settled out of court in 2010, with the judge returning the offer to the claimant. The final offer was made on the basis that the full amount had already been paid, and the case had been settled for good. The Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47 on 24 May 2005. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005 on the ground that the Army Board's decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. It is not known whether the applicant has ever received any compensation from the British government. The case is described as one of the UK's highest-profile cases of compensatory damages in recent years.

(Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (“the 1978 Act’) They were informed that they were being arrested under this section and that this was because the arresting officer suspected them of being terrorists. They were also told that they could be detained for up to 72 hours. No charges were brought against either applicant. The first applicant was released at 11.40 a.m. on 7 February 1986 and the second applicant five minutes later. Excluding the time taken to bring them to the police station, the first applicant had thus been detained for 44 hours. He was informed at the time of his arrest that he was being arrested as he was suspected of being a terrorist. Mr Hartley was suspected of involvement in a kidnapping incident in Ballymena. A young man and woman were forcibly taken away by masked armed men. Those involved in the kidnapping were thought to have connections with the IRA. The motive behind the kidnapping was believed to have been an attempt to force the young woman to retract an allegation of rape made the previous year as a result of which a person had been convicted and sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment. The decision by the Supreme Court led to a legal challenge to the law. The case was dismissed by the Court of Appeal. The legal challenge was dismissed and a new law was enacted. The new law means that the tax bill is not enforceable by a court of law, but by a vote of the public. The law does not require the tax payer to pay the tax, it only requires that the public pay the same amount. The public does not have to pay taxes on the proceeds of the sale of the sales of the land.

As a result, the NSC can continue to operate without paying the tax. The NSC decided that the tax should be paid for the services provided by NSC, rather than the individual members of NSC. The decision was overturned in December 2013. NSC ruled again in March 2014 that it is not necessary for NSC to pay the tax, as NSC had already paid the tax in the first place. It will now pay the bill for the service.

It was extended to include earnings made on the sale of goods and services, and not on the basis of earnings made from the use of the earnings. In 1978, it was extended again to include the purchase of goods, services and services. The Act was also extended to cover the cost of the purchase and use of equipment to ensure that the income tax was paid for at least 10 years. As a result, the rate was reduced to the rate of 1.6 per cent per year. The tax rate was set at 4.5 per cent for the first five years. In 2000, it fell to 3 per cent.

It was noted that there was no dispute that the reading of prisoners’ correspondence was governed by law, and that it was directed to the prevention of crime and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. It considered that although it was of course possible to verify the existence, address and qualifications of the applicant’s external medical specialist (whose bona fides was not in question), there was. no way of ensuring that the latter would not be intimidated or tricked into transmitting illicit messages. The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. It did not exclude the possibility that in another case it might be disproportionate to refuse confidentiality to medical correspondence in the prison context. It recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse, for example, if the applicant's prison life or treatment was made more difficult because of what he was observed to be writing. However, the risk, having been minimised by virtue of confining surveillance to the prison medical officer, was outweighed by the above-mentioned factors. The process by which the measure had been decided upon was not found to be arbitrary. In particular, it had not been the result of the rigid application of a policy. At the beginning of the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping cases’ (selskabstømmersager) came into existence in Denmark. It covered a criminal activity by which the persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud by buying up and selling numerous inactive solvent private limited companies. According to surveys made by the customs and tax authorities, approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion Danish kroner (DKK) were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such benefit was payable to widowers under United Kingdom law. The application was rejected and he was left with no choice but to apply to the Court of Appeal.

The applicant was released the following morning and went to the medical centre. He submitted that his examination established that he had not had a nose bleed the night before. On 22 December 1997 at approximately 2 p.m. he was informed that he would have to appear before his company commander. On 7 June 1996, at approximately 6.00 a.m., two detective police officers left Limerick city in an unmarked police car escorting a post office van carrying significant sums of money. When the two vehicles arrived at the post office in Adare, the police car was rammed from behind by a stolen vehicle and immediately surrounded by five heavily armed and masked individuals dressed in paramilitary style uniforms. One of the five opened fire at point blank range on the police officers and one of those officers died instantly and the other was seriously wounded. The police suspected a local unit of the Irish Republican Army (an unlawful paramilitary organisation known as the IRA) and the IRA later claimed responsibility for the murder. As part of the investigation that followed, a number of persons suspected of being members of the IRA were arrested and charged.

The applicant was arrested under section 30 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 (“the 1939 Act’) on suspicion of being a member of the IRA. He was questioned on eight occasions during two 24-hour consecutive periods of detention. He saw his solicitor on three occasions during the time he was in detention. The applicant’s brother was charged with conspiracy to commit robbery (in relation to the Adare incident), possession of ammunition and of membership of the. IRA. A total of 63 persons were arrested and asked to account for their movements at particular times surrounding the attack, including the remaining members of the applicant's family except his two sisters. All of those persons who were asked to explain their movements did so.

The applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the Ankara State Security Court, who questioned him about his statements during the same television programmes. The applicant was charged with aiding and abetting members of the PKK on account of his statements made during the television programmes shown on MED-TV. The court decided to defer the imposition of a final sentence on the applicant, pursuant to Law no. 4616. On the same day, the single judge at the Ankara State Security Court ordered the applicant’s release from detention, having regard to the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence. On 21 December 2000 new legislation on the suspension of proceedings and the execution of sentences regarding offences committed before 23 April 1999 came into force.
